items.title: A new tab stays dark until its page has drawn
items.author: RanaOsamaAsif
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
## What

A link that opens a new tab (`target="_blank"`, e.g. the post links on https://near.blog) flashed white in dark mode before the page appeared. The new tab's web view was put on screen before it had drawn anything, and a `WKWebView` that has never drawn is opaque white.

Fresh web views now start at `alphaValue = 0` over the window's ground (`Palette.ground`), and fade in (0.12s) as soon as the page has something to show.

## How

- **Tab.swift**: `PageView.holdForFirstFrame()`, called from `Tab.build()`, asks WebKit to report `_WKRenderingProgressEventFirstVisuallyNonEmptyLayout` and hides the view. `showFirstFrame()` fades it in.
- **Browser.swift**: `_webView:renderingProgressDidChange:` reveals the view on that event. `didFinish` reveals it too, for a page that never lays out anything visible.
- **Stage.swift**: `StageView` no longer forces `alphaValue = 1` on a view that hasn't painted yet.

## Notes for review

- This relies on private WebKit names, like the existing `_isPlayingAudio` and `_webView:navigationDidFinishDocumentLoad:` hooks. It's guarded with `responds(to:)`: if WebKit doesn't answer, the view is shown straight away, as before.
- I checked with a standalone probe on macOS 26 (Darwin 25.6): for near.blog/unusual-holidays the event fires at about 0.53s, after commit (0.44s) and before finish (0.69s).
- It also covers typing an address into a blank tab and waking a sleeping tab.
- If a new tab's load is cancelled or becomes a download, the tab stays on the dark ground instead of white. Failed loads are still covered by the existing error screen.
- Release build compiles, and I launched it. I haven't checked the flash visually in the app.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

items.title: Feature request: Spaces / profiles (like Arc)
items.author: lusqua
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
Hi! Really enjoying how small and quiet Search is. The one thing keeping me from using it as my main browser is **Spaces**, as in Arc: separate sets of tabs with their own cookies and logins that I can switch between.

## Use case

I'm logged into the same sites (Google, GitHub, AWS, Slack…) with different accounts for different contexts: personal, and a couple of clients. In Arc, each context is a Space tied to a profile, and I switch between them from the sidebar or with a shortcut. Right now Search has one cookie jar for everything, and private tabs don't help because they forget everything when they close.

## What it could look like

Kept as minimal as the rest of the app:

- **A Space** = a name, a color/icon, its own tab list (pinned + open), and its own `WKWebsiteDataStore`, so cookies, localStorage and logins are isolated.
- **Still one window.** Switching a Space just swaps the tab list and the data store. No new windows, in keeping with "Tabs are the only kind of 'new' there is."
- **Switching:** a small indicator at the top of the sidebar/tab strip, plus a shortcut (e.g. `⌃1`–`⌃9` or `⌃⌘[` / `⌃⌘]`).
- **A single default Space** for anyone who never creates a second one, so nothing changes for them.

## Implementation notes

WebKit already supports this on macOS 14+ with `WKWebsiteDataStore(forIdentifier:)`. `Store.websites` already uses it for the test path, so the plumbing is mostly there. Roughly:

- `Tab.swift`: pick the data store from the tab's Space instead of the global `Store.websites`.
- Persist tabs per Space. History and bookmarks could stay shared or be per Space (open to your preference).
- Passwords: keep them in the keychain, optionally tagged with the Space.
- No new dependencies and nothing leaves the Mac.

Open questions I'd like your take on before writing any code:
1. Is this in scope for Search, or does it go against the "nothing in the way" philosophy?
2. Should history/bookmarks be shared across Spaces or isolated?
3. Should extensions be per Space or global?

If this direction fits, I'd be happy to implement it and open a PR, split into small pieces (data store per Space first, then the UI).

items.title: Floating video is black on YouTube, and the tab is empty after it lands
items.author: Chinteyley
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
**What I did**

1. Play a YouTube video.
2. Press ⇧⌘P, or switch to another tab so the video floats on its own.
3. Press ⇧⌘P again.

**Expected:** the video plays in the floating window. After step 3, the page is back in its tab.

**What happened:** the floating window is black. If the page was scrolled, the whole window is black; otherwise a black band covers the top. After step 3 the tab is empty, with no page and no "playing in the floating window" line. It stays empty until the window is resized or another tab is picked.

**macOS:** 27.0 (26A428), Search 1.0

**Cause** (reproduced on `main` @ cc8aa58 in a `SEARCH_PROBE` build)

1. **Black window.** `Isolate.on` pins the video with `position: fixed`, but WebKit still clips it to its ancestors' overflow: `#movie_player { overflow: hidden }` and `#full-bleed-container { overflow-x: clip }`. In the 440×247 float, YouTube lays the player out at y=56, so the top 56pt is black. With the page scrolled, the player box is entirely off screen, so the whole window is black. The video's `getBoundingClientRect()` reads 0, 0, 440, 247 the whole time. Layout is correct; only the paint is clipped.
2. **Empty tab.** `Page` passes the same `tab.web` to `WebStage` before, during and after the float. SwiftUI sees no change, so it never calls `updateNSView` when the float lands. `Float.drop()` has already removed the web view from the panel, which leaves the view with no superview and no window. The stage's layout-time self-heal only runs when something else triggers a layout. Picking another tab works because `activeID` changes. Pressing ⇧⌘P again on the same tab, or the float's ×, does not.

I've opened a PR with a fix.

items.title: Floating video shows the whole picture, and its page lands back in the tab
items.author: Chinteyley
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Fixes #8.

- **Black window** (`Float.swift`): while a video floats, every ancestor of the marked video gets `overflow: visible`, via `html.office-floating body :has([data-office-float])`. The rule sits in the same sheet, so `Isolate.off` removes it. It also follows the mark when the watch re-marks a new video. `html` and `body` keep `overflow: hidden`.
- **Empty tab** (`Stage.swift`): `Page` hands `WebStage` nil while `tab.floating` is true. Landing then changes nil to the page, which SwiftUI passes on to `updateNSView`, and the stage takes the page back right away.

Tested in a `SEARCH_PROBE` build on macOS 27.0 with a YouTube video:

| Case | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| ⇧⌘P, page at top | 56pt black band | full picture |
| ⇧⌘P, page scrolled 900px | all black | full picture |
| Switch tabs (auto float), then pick the tab again | band; page back | full picture; page back, still playing |
| ⇧⌘P again on the same tab | empty tab | page back, still playing |

`swift build` passes, and the two changed files add no warnings. I only tested YouTube.

items.title: [Feature Request] Proxy extension iGuge UI opens, but fails to enable proxy features
items.author: Jirentian
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
### Description
The extension [iGuge (Chrome Web Store)](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/iguge/ncldcbhpeplkfijdhnoepdgdnmjkckij) can be installed and its popup/interface opens without issue in the Search browser, but the core proxy/acceleration switch cannot be turned on (or fails to route traffic).

### Observed Behavior vs Chrome
- **Google Chrome**: The extension UI opens and the proxy switch toggles on normally. Chrome delegates proxy settings to the extension with the banner: *"This setting is enforced by an extension: iGuge"*, properly routing traffic and network acceleration.
- **Search Browser**: The extension popup opens and renders correctly, but clicking to enable the proxy either does not toggle or throws an error silently without applying proxy routing. This is likely due to unimplemented extension proxy APIs (e.g., `chrome.proxy.settings`).

### Expected / Requested Solution
Please consider supporting extension proxy management APIs (`chrome.proxy` or WebKit proxy configuration integration) so that proxy-based extensions like iGuge can properly toggle and apply proxy rules. Thank you!

items.body:
## Why

Search has a flat tab list. People with many open tabs need a way to keep related tabs together and hide a group without closing its pages. The roadmap lists tab groups as later work.

## Proposed behavior

- Add an optional Tab Groups setting, off by default.
- Create a named, colored group from a tab's context menu. Use "Group N" until the user sets a name.
- Show group labels in both tab layouts. Click a label to expand or collapse its tabs.

- Save normal tabs and group state across launches. Keep private tabs temporary and pinned tabs outside groups.
- Keep existing keyboard tab navigation and make selected tabs visible by opening their group.

The change should use Search's current SwiftUI controls and add no dependency.

items.title: A tab switcher with previews on ⌃Tab, off until turned on
items.author: farchanrifai
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Takes **A tab switcher with previews (⌃Tab held down)** off the roadmap.

## What it does

With **Settings › Tabs › Recently used tab switcher** on, holding ⌃ and pressing Tab shows up to ten tabs as pictures, in the order you last looked at them — the way Firefox and Arc do it. Letting go of ⌃ goes to the one picked.

- Tab / ⇧Tab and the arrow keys move through the tabs while ⌃ is held.
- Esc, or leaving the window, stays on the tab you're on.
- The pictures are the ones tab sleeping already takes, so nothing extra is drawn for this.

## Off by default

Per CONTRIBUTING, it's off until someone turns it on in Settings › Tabs. While it's off, ⌃Tab and ⌃⇧Tab step through the row exactly as they do on `main` today.

## Code

- `TabSwitcher.swift`: the recently-used order and the walk through it, with tests in `Tests/SearchTests/TabSwitcherTests.swift` (`swift test`; `Package.swift` gains the test target).
- `App.swift`, `Browser.swift`, `Tab.swift`, `Sleep.swift`: feed it, and draw the overlay.
- CHANGELOG gets its line under Unreleased, and ROADMAP loses the item.

## Tested

- Built on current `main`; `swift test` passes.
- Switcher off: ⌃Tab and ⌃⇧Tab step both ways through the row, checked with `./bench press` on a test run.
- Switcher on: the previews, moving through them, switching on release, and Esc were tried by hand.

items.body:
## Page-colored tab row

Adds an optional **Match the page color** setting for the horizontal tab row, off by default. The sidebar is unchanged. It keeps the toolbar-free window and the existing traffic-light placement.

The page reports its top-edge color from a Swift-embedded WebKit script. CSS colors update directly; animated headers pass their transition timing to the strip. Painted headers use a bounded snapshot fallback (at most eight sampled looks per page). The strip stays mounted across tab changes, so switching tabs changes the color at once; opening a blank tab no longer animates the page underneath its address field. The tint reads are throttled, snapshots wait for the page to settle, and the fallback waits were shortened after previewing them.

This incorporates the review on the original experiment: no toolbar, no `Bundle.module` script, and an opt-in setting. The sampling helper now lives with `PageTint.swift`. Merged current `main`, including folded tabs and the new bench controls, and resolved the four conflicts.

Verified with `./build.sh release app` after the merge.

items.author: lusqua

items.body:
Closes the roadmap item "Middle-click closes a tab."

The middle button on a tab closes it, as in other browsers — in the row across the top and in the column, rows and pinned squares alike. It goes through `Browser.close(_:)`, so a pinned tab is put down as with ⌘W, not removed.

SwiftUI has no middle-button gesture, so each tab gets a small NSView overlay (`MiddleClick`, in TabBar.swift) whose `hitTest` only answers for `otherMouseDown`/`otherMouseUp` with button 2 — the same idea as `DragStrip` refusing the tabs' run. Left click, drag-to-reorder and the right-click menu still reach the tab underneath. It closes on release, only if the pointer is still over the tab. A middle-click on a link in a page is unchanged (still opens a new tab).

Checked on a `SEARCH_PROBE` build, both layouts, with mouse events posted through the app's event queue: middle-click closed the tab under it; a pinned tab went to sleep and kept its place; press-and-release-elsewhere and button 3 closed nothing; left-click still selects, drags still reorder rows and pins, right-click still opens the tab menu. A hardware middle button also closed tabs in the row. `swift build` adds no warnings.

items.body:
Closes the roadmap item "The sidebar hides by itself until the pointer reaches the edge, as an option on top of ⌘S."

A switch in Settings › Tabs, "Hide the sidebar until the pointer reaches the edge", shown while the tabs are down the left and off by default. With it on, the ⌘S fold is where the column rests: at launch, after switching layouts, and when the switch is flipped. The left edge brings it out over the page as before, and ⌘S still brings it out to stay and puts it away again.

Folded for good, the column waits for the pointer to rest on the edge for 0.15 s, so crossing the edge on the way to the Dock doesn't flash it. A ⌘S fold still comes out at once. The traffic lights now hide once the window exists, so a column folded at launch doesn't leave them over the page's corner (`hideLights()` returns early before there is a window). The column also stays out while a tab's address is being typed into its row — this last one applies to a plain ⌘S fold too.

Built on top of 1df70b5 (the lights riding on the column's spring, `Browser.peek(_:)`), not around it.

Checked on a test world, driving the pointer from inside the app and reading `bench probe` plus window captures and `bench film peek`: folded at launch with the lights hidden; out after resting on the edge, not when crossing it; back in after the pointer leaves; ⌘S out and back; kept out while a row is being edited; with the switch off, ⌘S and the edge behave as before. Not yet tried with a physical mouse. `swift build` adds no warnings. `bench ui hides on|off`, and `probe` reports it.

items.author: SamarthaB10

items.body:
## What changed

- Add optional tab groups in the top tab row and sidebar. The setting is off by default and appears in Settings and the welcome screen.
- Add group creation from a tab menu, ten colors, custom names, collapse and expand, and drag targets for moving tabs between groups or back to the normal tab area.
- Save normal tab groups with each Space. Keep private tabs in groups only for the current run. Restore a closed group with one Reopen Closed Tab command.
- When the active group is closed, New Tab and New Private Tab create a tab outside groups.
- Add design notes, a changelog entry, and remove Tab groups from the roadmap.

items.title: Floating video window makes WindowServer do extra GPU work
items.author: AxxzyWasTaken
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
When a video leaves its tab for the floating window, WindowServer does more GPU work for the same video than when it plays in the tab.

I measured the GPU time the kernel bills to WindowServer (coalition `gpu_time`, the number `powermetrics` reports) over 10 s windows. The test was Big Buck Bunny on YouTube in a test build of `main`, first with the tab in front, then after switching to another tab so the video floats.

| | 1080p | 4K |
|---|---|---|
| Playing in its tab | 22% | 19% |
| Floating, as it is now | 28% | 24% |
| Floating, `panel.hasShadow = false` | 16% | 16% |

The shadow is the cause. I tried an opaque window, square corners and a continuous corner curve, and none of them moved the number. Taking the shadow off is the only change that did. With no shadow, a floating video costs less than one in the tab, because the small window has fewer pixels to put on screen.

Search's own processes (the app plus its WebKit GPU, WebContent and Networking helpers) use the same CPU either way, about 15–25% depending on resolution. The 250 ms `setInterval` in `Isolate.on` doesn't show up in that number.

This came up because a user saw Activity Monitor's Energy Impact go from 40–100 to 200–300 when switching tabs with a video playing. On the same Mac I didn't reproduce a jump that big in Search's own processes. It showed up in WindowServer's share and nowhere else, and I don't know what accounts for the rest.

Measured on macOS 27, Apple Silicon, built-in Retina display.

items.title: The floating video window has no shadow
items.author: AxxzyWasTaken
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Closes #33.

This is a one-line fix: `panel.hasShadow = false` in `Float.lift`.

A window with a shadow gets composited by WindowServer on every frame of the video. Without the shadow, a floating video costs less GPU time than the same video in its tab.

WindowServer GPU time (coalition `gpu_time`, 10 s windows, YouTube, switching to another tab so the video floats):

| | 1080p | 4K |
|---|---|---|
| In its tab | 22% | 19% |
| Floating, before | 28% | 24% |
| Floating, this PR | 16% | 16% |

I also tried an opaque window, square corners and `cornerCurve = .continuous`. None of them changed anything, so this PR leaves them alone. The rounded corners stay and so does the clear background. With no shadow the window's edge is less obvious against a dark background, but it's still clear against anything else.

Tested with `./build.sh release` and a `SEARCH_PROBE` world driven by `./bench`, on macOS 27 with the built-in Retina display. The build adds no new warnings.

Takes **Your own keyboard shortcuts** off the roadmap.

![Settings › Shortcuts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/farchanrifai/Search/pr-assets/settings-shortcuts-v2.png)

## What it does

**Settings › Shortcuts** lists every menu command with its key, one card per menu, at the usual Settings width.

- **Find:** a search field narrows the list by name or by key ("tab" or "⌘T").
- **Change a key:** click the box and press the new one. If another command already has it, the box says so and a second press moves it. macOS's own keys (⌘Q, ⌘C, ⌘V…) and ⌘1–⌘9 are refused, and so is a key without ⌘, ⌥ or ⌃.

- **The menus** always show the current keys.

## Nothing changes by default

Only what someone changes is stored, on top of the keys the menus already have, so a default that changes later still reaches everyone who never touched it.

## How it works

- **`Shortcuts.swift`:** the menu commands with their default keys, and `ShortcutStore`, which keeps the changes.
- **`App.swift`:** the menus read their keys from the store. The existing key handling is untouched; one block in front of it runs a command on a key you gave it, and lets a key you took off a command go on to the page.
- **`ShortcutsPage.swift`:** the Settings page.
- Only menu commands can be remapped; ⌘1–9, ⌃1–9, Tab and Esc stay as they are.
- CHANGELOG gets its line under Unreleased, and ROADMAP loses the item.

## Tested

- On a test run with `./bench press`: the default keys work as before; with New Tab moved to ⌥⌘T, ⌥⌘T opens a tab and ⌘T goes on to the page.

items.title: Quits on launch on macOS 14: NSApp is nil in Preferences.init
items.author: serhiitroinin
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
**What I did:** downloaded Search.dmg from officecommun.com/search, moved Search.app to /Applications, opened it.

**Expected:** a window.

**What happened:** it quits right away, no window, no dialog. Same when running the binary directly: `/Applications/Search.app/Contents/MacOS/Search` exits with 133 (SIGTRAP), on every launch.

**macOS:** 14.3 (23D56), Apple Silicon. Search 1.0, build 202609231444. I think this is the same crash as the 14.8.3 one on the roadmap.

There is no `~/Library/Application Support/Search/crash.log` — it dies before anything gets written. The system crash report has `EXC_BREAKPOINT / SIGTRAP` on the main thread. Symbolicated with the dSYM from the v1.0 release (UUID `57483994-D48F-398A-B03E-5BA13D248EBD`, matches the installed binary):

```
0  Search     Preferences.init()          Prefs.swift
1  Search     Browser.init()              Browser.swift:34
2  Search     @objc Browser.init()
3  SwiftUI    … StateObject / AttributeGraph update
```

The trapping instruction is a `brk #1` right after `ldr x20, [_NSApp]; cbz x20`, so the implicitly unwrapped `NSApp` is nil. In source that's `Sources/Search/Prefs.swift:134`:

```swift
NSApp.appearance = chosen.appearance
```

On macOS 14 SwiftUI builds the App's `@StateObject` before it has created the NSApplication, so `NSApp` isn't there yet. Newer macOS seems to create the app earlier, which is probably why it doesn't reproduce on your machine. #22 changes the default look to System, but it still goes through `NSApp` here, so it doesn't change this.

Minimal repro on 14.3 (plain SwiftUI app, `@StateObject` whose `init` sets the app's appearance): `NSApp.appearance = …` exits with 133, `NSApplication.shared.appearance = …` runs. `shared` creates the app if it doesn't exist yet, so the look is still applied before the first window, as the comment above that line wants.

Opening a PR with that one-line change right after this.

items.title: Search opens on macOS 14 again
items.author: serhiitroinin
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Fixes #37.

On macOS 14 Search quits on launch with SIGTRAP. `Preferences.init` sets the chosen look through `NSApp`, but SwiftUI builds the App's `@StateObject` (Browser, and the Preferences it holds) before it has created the application, so `NSApp` is still nil and the implicit unwrap traps.

The fix is `NSApplication.shared.appearance` instead of `NSApp.appearance`. `shared` creates the application if it doesn't exist yet, so the look is still set before the first window, not deferred, as the comment there wants. Everything after it in `Browser.init` then sees a real `NSApp` too.

Also in this PR: the line under **Unreleased › Fixed** in CHANGELOG.md, and the macOS 14.8.3 item taken off ROADMAP.md.

**Tested:** I couldn't run `swift build` here: this Mac has Xcode 15.4 (Swift 5.10), and the package needs Swift 6 plus the macOS 15.4 SDK for the web extension APIs. What I did check on macOS 14.3: a minimal SwiftUI app with the same shape (`@StateObject` whose `init` touches the app's appearance) exits with 133 using `NSApp` and runs using `NSApplication.shared`. It would be good if someone with the current toolchain runs `swift build` before merging.

items.title: The field leaves an extension's new tab page
items.author: meta-boy
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
## What happened

Install any extension that replaces the new tab page with `chrome_url_overrides.newtab` and say Keep It. I used [Tabby Cat](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/tabby-cat/mefhakmgclhhfbdadeojlkbllmecialg). Type an address or a search into the field on that new tab and press Return. Nothing happens, and the tab stays on `chrome-extension://…/public/index.html`.

## Why

Search shows an extension's page in a view built from that extension's `webViewConfiguration`, and WebKit only lets that view load the extension's own pages. `replace(_:going:)` already swaps such a tab for a normal one. It runs from `decidePolicyFor`, though, and WebKit only asks that about navigations the page starts. When the field calls `submit()` → `tab.go(to:)`, the load never reaches the policy check and dies quietly.

## Fix

Each `Tab` now records which extension its view was built for (`home`, nil for the web), set by a new `Tab(for: url)` initializer. `go(to:)` compares that with the destination. When they differ it calls `onCross`, and the browser swaps the tab in place with `replace(_:going:)`.

The check lives in `go(to:)`, so no caller has to remember it. The field, suggestions, ⌘⇧V, bookmarks, history rows, links from other apps, a reopened closed tab and `chrome.tabs.update` all get it without changes.

## Tested

I ran a test world with `./bench --world tabby` and loaded Tabby Cat unpacked.

- With Tabby Cat as the new tab, I pressed ⌘T, ⌘L, typed `example.com` and pressed Return. Before, the tab stayed on `chrome-extension://local-…/public/index.html`. After, it loaded `https://example.com/`.
- I opened the extension's page in a bench tab with `ext-page` and sent it to `https://example.org` with `go`. The tab was swapped and loaded the site.

I only tried an address, not a search, but a search takes the same path through `submit()`. `swift build` shows no new warnings, and CHANGELOG has a line under Unreleased › Fixed.

items.title: Extension popups open at their size, and their button closes them
items.author: nicostassart
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Two things about extension popups, both seen with a pinned extension whose popup fills itself in from a script (most of them do).

**Opening.** The popover was shown as soon as the document was built. At that moment the popup had nothing in it yet, so the first measure was a sliver (25 × 76 for the one I was using), and the popover came in narrow and short, then stretched down, then across, over about half a second as `grow()` caught up. The host view controller's `preferredContentSize` was also left at zero, so even the remembered size never took. Now the popover stands unseen (window alpha 0, not animating) while the page is measured again every 40 ms. Once two measures agree and the page has loaded, it fades in at that size in 0.15 s. It is up the whole time, so the page runs as it did. Slow pages still get a cap: seen at 0.6 s after the first measure, or 0.8 s after opening if the document takes longer than that. After it is seen, everything is as before.

**Closing from its button.** A transient popover closes on the press, and a press on its own button is outside it. The button's action then arrives on the release and `press()` opened it straight back up, so the button could never close its popup the way it does in Chrome. `popoverWillClose` now notes a press that landed on the extension's own button, and `press()` lets that click only close. The note is dropped on the next press, or after a second, so a press dragged off the button doesn't swallow the next click.

**Bench.** `./bench ext-tap ID` (test runs only) clicks a pinned button the way a hand does: the press goes through the app's event queue, where the transient popover sees it, and then the action comes. The release can't reach a button in a window that isn't key, and a test run's window stays behind. That's how both bugs were reproduced and checked. Before the fix, the second tap left the popup open. The popover window's size over time went 53×105 → 53×586 → 366×586. After the fix, it is at alpha 0 until it holds 362×586, then fades in.

`swift build` adds no warnings.

items.title: Search with the engine you pick in Settings, Google by default (#43)
items.author: karadoganyi
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Closes #43.

Settings › General gets a **Search with** menu: Google (still the default), DuckDuckGo, Bing, Ecosia, Startpage, Kagi, or **Custom**, an address with `%s` where the words go, the way Chrome and Firefox do it. Nobody who leaves it alone sees any change.

### What follows the choice
Everything that searched with Google before:
- the address field, and the name on its search row
- editing a tab's address
- paste and go (⇧⌘V)
- `chrome.search.query` for extensions

### How it works
- `Google.swift` becomes `Engine.swift`: the six templates plus a few pure functions, Foundation only.
- The choice is saved in `Preferences` as `search.engine` and `search.custom`.
- `Browser.searchURL(for:)` and `Browser.destination(for:)` are the one path from the setting to a URL.

### Custom addresses
- A custom address has to be http or https, have a host, and contain `%s` after the host. Anything else (a typo, `javascript:`, `file:`) isn't used: searches stay on Google, and Settings says why.
- The words are encoded once. An address copied with its own spaces, `ü` or `[ ]` in the query still gets the words exactly as typed.

### Privacy
Nothing new leaves the Mac. The query goes to the engine you picked instead of Google, and there are still no suggestion requests.

### Testing
- 53 checks on `Engine`, run with `swiftc` against the file on its own. They cover every preset, the round trip of `c++ & rust`, `a+b=c`, `100% sure`, Turkish and Japanese, templates with `%s` in the path, bad custom addresses and the Google fallback. I left them out of the PR because the repo has no test target. Happy to add one if you'd like.
- Each preset's address answers (Kagi asks you to sign in first, as expected).
- In the app: DuckDuckGo from the address field, the search row's name, a custom Brave address, and a bad custom address falling back to Google.
- `swift build`: no new warnings.

### Not in this PR
Right-clicking selected text still offers macOS's own "Search With Google", which never went through `Google.swift`. It could follow this setting in a small follow-up.

Fixes #17.

### Overview

  - In `Passwords.swift`, added an "Apple Passwords…" import button in the Passwords panel alongside Dia, Chrome, Arc, and CSV.

items.title: feat: add tab groups, space emojis and extension controls
items.author: K-NRS
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
Tabs can now be grouped in both the sidebar and horizontal strip, with collapse, rename, emoji or native icons, and a new-tab action per group. Spaces also accept emoji markers. This extends the existing spaces implementation: per-space sessions, current icons, shared or separate sign-ins, download folders, Control-1–9 and sidebar swiping are preserved. Groups, markers and custom tab names survive space switches and restart. Pinning removes membership; ungrouping keeps tabs. Selection and resizing keep the selected tab visible.

Search runs extension-declared shortcuts but previously had no way to change or clear them. Settings → Extensions now offers a recorder, Clear and Reset for each command, with bindings restored after reload, disable/re-enable and browser restart. The recorder rejects unsupported keys and conflicts with browser/menu/space shortcuts or another enabled extension. Dispatch uses exact modifiers, preserves non-US keyboard characters, skips private tabs and reuses the existing popup path.

Offscreen dictionary lookups can fail because document discovery returns no contexts and iframe messages cannot reach the hidden parent page. This adds owned offscreen lifecycle management, filtered context discovery, readiness before creation completes, iframe messages and replies, and cleanup on reload or disable. Lokal can translate without a temporary tab in the strip. Uninterested extension pages no longer preempt slower replies after ten seconds. Ordinary inactive tabs retain their existing behavior; `runtime.getContexts` currently reports Search-managed offscreen documents only.

Float Video keeps centered videos inside the floating viewport and preserves Netflix's separate subtitle layer above the picture. Returning to the page restores its original styles; unrelated player controls stay hidden while floating. No dependencies added.

Validation on the final combined packaged release:
- Release build and ad-hoc signature verification passed.
- All 602 checks passed with production scheduling: 111 group/session checks, 37 native group UI checks, 110 extension-shortcut checks, 13 background-tab checks, 315 offscreen checks and 16 floating-video checks.
- Group tests cover legacy space metadata, named tabs, per-space persistence, collapse, marker validation, shared/isolated WebKit cookies and local storage, private/bench exclusion, reopen, replacement and canonical reordering.
- Native heading clicks and sheet controls were exercised in both layouts. Native scroll bounds and inspected screenshots verify first-tab pin updates, emoji/icon rendering, selected-tab reveal and a 640px dark tab strip. Pointer dragging itself was not automated.
- Regressions were reproduced before fixes for cross-group move rejection, unavailable-space ghosts blocking reopen, closing to the wrong displayed neighbor and selected tabs leaving view after resize.

Earlier feature-specific verification retained from this PR:
- Unchanged Lokal 1.5.9 returned 43 Tureng rows for an uncached lookup and 46 after reload, using one offscreen document without changing visible tabs or foreground selection.
- Native Settings layout, shortcut restart persistence and floating/returned video snapshots were checked separately. Netflix floating playback and Return were confirmed by the user; Netflix subtitle visual confirmation remains pending.
- Offscreen discovery/lifecycle/iframe failures, premature empty replies, shortcut interception, Turkish-key misidentification, space-shortcut conflicts and video/subtitle issues were reproduced before their fixes.

items.title: Mute a tab from its right-click menu
items.author: merttopuz
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Every other browser lets you silence a tab from its speaker icon without stopping the video - WKWebView has no call for that (it can pause media, but pausing stops it rather than muting it), so this does it in the page's own JavaScript instead: every `<audio>` and `<video>` element, present now or added later (tracked with a MutationObserver, for players like YouTube's that build their `<video>` element after the page loads), gets its `muted` property set. It runs in every frame, and is re-armed on each navigation, so a tab muted before it went somewhere else is still muted once it gets there.

"Mute Tab" / "Unmute Tab" is in a tab's right-click menu, in both the row across the top and the column down the side. A muted tab's speaker icon turns to a slash so the row still says which tab it is, same spot the playing icon already used.

items.title: A middle-click on a link opens it in a new tab
items.author: Dodothereal
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Closes #45.

A middle-click on a tab has closed it since #27, but a middle-click on a link did nothing at all: the page kept the click, and no tab was opened.

## Why the old code could not have worked

Next to the ⌘-click check in `webView(_:decidePolicyFor:)` there was an `action.buttonNumber == 2` test meant to catch a middle-click. Two things were wrong with it.

WebKit hands the browser a `WKNavigationAction` for a ⌘-click and **none at all** for a middle-click — the page gets the click and the delegate is never called — so the test never ran. And it was comparing against the wrong number: WebKit answers `buttonNumber` with a **mask**, not a button index. From WebKit's `WebEventFactory::toNSButtonNumber`:

```
Left   -> 1 << 0  = 1
Right  -> 1 << 1  = 2
Middle -> 1 << 2  = 4
```

So `== 2` is the *right* button; the middle one is 4. Confirmed against the running app: a ⌘-click reports `buttonNumber = 1`, which is the Left mask.

## What this does

The page can see the click even where the delegate can't, so the page is asked. A new `MiddleRelay` follows the existing `ImageRelay` / `StoreRelay` pattern: an injected script listens for `auxclick` on the middle button, walks up to the enclosing `<a href>`, and posts the address. The relay opens it beside the current tab — `Browser.open(url, foreground: false)` — and leaves you where you are, the same thing ⌘-click does.

Guards, so a page cannot open tabs by asking:

- the event must be a real click, not a synthesized one (a page dispatching its own `auxclick` gets nothing);
- it is listened for on the way up, so a click the page has already answered with `preventDefault` is left alone;
- the message must come from the main frame, and the address must be `http` or `https`.

The stale `buttonNumber` test is removed and the comment beside it now says why, so it does not get put back.

## Testing

Driven through `./bench` against a `--test` world, with a real middle-click posted at both buttons in the running app:

| | result |
|---|---|
| middle-click on a link | opens in a background tab, `activeUnchanged: true` |
| five page-dispatched `auxclick`s | open nothing |
| ⌘-click | still opens beside, foreground false |
| ⌘⇧-click | still opens in front, foreground true |

`swift build`: no new warnings.

## Notes

- Main frame only, deliberately: a middle-click on a link inside an ad iframe is that frame's business, and its link is not this tab's to open.
- No dependency, no network, nothing new leaves the Mac.
- CHANGELOG entry added under **Unreleased** as CONTRIBUTING asks.

items.title: Search selected text in a new tab, with the engine from Settings (#66)
items.author: karadoganyi
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Fixes #66.

Right-clicking selected text and choosing "Search with Google" opened the search in the Mac's default browser (Safari for most people), and always said Google whatever was chosen in Settings › General › Search with.

### Why
The item is WebKit's own (identifier `WKMenuItemIdentifierSearchWeb`, action `forwardContextMenuAction:`). WebKit hands the text to macOS, which opens the default browser, so nothing in Search ever saw the click.

### What changes
- `PageView.willOpenMenu` finds that item by its identifier, renames it "Search with <engine>" from Settings (the host for a custom engine), and points it at the page view.
- The selection is read when the menu opens, in WebKit's isolated script world so the page can't change it. The click then opens the search in a new foreground tab with `searchURL(for:)` and `open(_:foreground:)`, as "Open Image in New Tab" does.
- From a private tab, the search opens in a private tab too. `open(_:foreground:atEnd:shy:)` gains a `shy` argument, defaulting to false, so nothing else changes.
- Whitespace-only selections do nothing.
- When the main frame can't see the selection (text selected inside an iframe, a PDF), the click goes back to WebKit's own action, so those cases behave exactly as before.
- It works on macOS 14: the callbacks run Browser → Tab → PageView like `onImageMenu` and `onPull`, with no dependence on `Extensions.shared`.
- If a future WebKit renames the identifier, the item is left alone and behaves as it does today.

### Testing
- In an isolated test profile set to DuckDuckGo, the item reads "Search with DuckDuckGo" and opens a new tab in Search at duckduckgo.com. After switching to Google, the title and the search follow.
- From a private tab: the search opens in a private tab, and the query appears in neither History nor the saved session. A normal-tab search is recorded, as expected.
- Text selected in the page first, then inside an iframe: the page's old selection isn't searched, and WebKit's own action takes over.
- `swift build`: no new warnings.

items.title: Frame rate setting: 60, 120, or 120 while plugged in
items.author: AxxzyWasTaken
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Closes #75.

I noticed Search was stuck at 60fps on my 120 Hz MacBook Pro. It turned out to be WebKit's "Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps" feature flag, which Safari also ships with on. I added Settings › General › Frame rate with three choices:

- **60**: the default, same as now.
- **120**: turns the flag off for every page.
- **120 plugged in**: 120 on the power adapter, 60 on battery. I listen for macOS's power source notification, so nothing polls.

I kept it off by default, per CONTRIBUTING.

## What it costs

I ran a short test on my MacBook Pro with the window at 1728×994 and Search in front. These are Activity Monitor energy impact numbers for Search's own processes:

| Page | 60 | 120 |
|---|---|---|
| Static page | 0.7 | 2.1 |
| One CSS animation | 9–11 (60fps) | 15 (120fps) |
| 1080p video + rAF counter | 20 (60fps) | 23 (120fps) |

WindowServer stayed about the same. A page that animates costs me roughly half again as much at 120, which is why I didn't make it the default and why I added the plugged-in option.

## One rough edge

WebKit reads the flag when a page is made, so new tabs and reloads get the new rate right away. Tabs I already had open didn't fully follow. Going up to 120, they caught up the next time I switched to them. Going back down to 60, they only changed after a reload. That applies to the plugged-in option too: if I unplug, my open tabs stay at 120 until I reload them.

I tried hiding and showing the view to make WebKit re-read it, but that only worked when the page actually left the screen. Reloading every tab would lose typed text, so I left it and mentioned it in the setting's description. If you know a cleaner way to get WebKit to re-read it on a live page, I'm happy to change it.

## Notes

- The flag isn't public API. I set it through `WKPreferences._features` / `_setEnabled:forFeature:` and check `responds(to:)` at each step, so a WebKit without it just stays at 60.
- I added `./bench ui framerate standard|smooth|plugged` so it can be set from a script.
- It builds with no new warnings. With bench and a rAF counter I checked that it's 60 by default, 120 after choosing 120, that the choice survives a relaunch, and that "120 plugged in" runs at 120 on AC. I haven't tested the battery side yet.
- I added a CHANGELOG line under Unreleased.

## Summary
- The bookmarks popover (`BookmarksDropdown` in `Sources/Search/Bookmarks.swift`) closed as soon as the pointer moved over the bookmark list, making it impossible to click a bookmark or the "Add This Page" / "Manage Bookmarks..." buttons.

items.title: Allow pages to use full display refresh rate (#75)
items.author: SamarthaB10
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
## Change

- Disable WebKit's near 60 FPS preference before Search creates a page view.
- Apply the setting to normal and private tabs, and to views made from a configuration supplied by WebKit.
- Expose the preference state in `bench probe` and add an Unreleased changelog line.

## Cause

WebKit enables `PreferPageRenderingUpdatesNear60FPSEnabled` on a new `WKPreferences`. Search did not change it, so pages could stay near 60 FPS on a 120 Hz display. WebKit has no public switch for this setting. The change checks for its feature API and uses it only when available.

## Checks

- `./build.sh debug` passes on the latest `main`.
- The runtime probe reported `prefersNear60FPS: [true]` before the fix and `false` after it. On the rebased build, normal, private, and site opened tabs all reported `false`.
- `swift test` builds, then reports `no tests found` because this repository has no test target.
- A live 120 Hz FPS result needs a foreground ProMotion check. This automation desktop changes window focus during frame timing.

Closes #75

items.title: Customization Settings Tab
items.author: PeterTheMango
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
> **Split into separate issues**, each with its own pull request, so they can be discussed and merged one at a time:
>
> - #101 Settings › Customization page (PR #105)
> - #102 Tab size (PR #106)
> - #103 Where the zoom level shows (PR #107)
> - #104 New tab at the foot of the sidebar (PR #108)

---

A **Customization** page in Settings would give people one place to change how their Search looks and feels.

Today these settings are spread out. The Light / Dark / System switch sits on the General page next to spelling, middle-button scrolling and the bench socket. How tabs look is on the Tabs page, mixed in with sleeping tabs and Spaces. Several open proposals would add more options of this kind, and each would need a place in Settings:

- An address bar above the page (#15, #56)
- A tab row in the page's colour (#25)
- Bookmarks in the column, above the tabs (#58, #69)

A Customization page, between General and Tabs, could be the home for all of these. It would start with the Light / Dark / System switch, moved from General as it is, and the three options below. Each new option defaults to how Search works today, so nobody sees a change unless they turn it on.

### 1. Tab size
Tab titles are 12.5 pt and a sidebar row is 28 pt tall, in both the sidebar and the row across the top. That's too small for some people to read quickly. I find it easier to spot the tab I want when the tabs are a bit bigger.

- **Tab size:** **Regular** (today, the default) or **Large**. Large makes the tab's title and icon bigger and makes rows taller to fit, e.g. 14 pt titles and 34 pt rows. Pinned squares grow with them.
- Only two sizes, no slider.
- **How others do it:** Firefox has a density setting (Compact / Normal / Touch) that changes the tab height. On the Mac, Finder and Mail sidebars follow System Settings › Appearance › Sidebar icon size.

### 2. Where the zoom level shows
When I zoom a page (⌘+ / ⌘− / pinch), the percentage appears in the capsule that rises from the bottom of the window, the same one that says "Address copied." I don't look at the bottom of the window while zooming, so I usually miss it. Chrome and Firefox show the zoom level at the top right, next to the address, so that's where I look first.

- **Show zoom at:** **Bottom middle** (today, the default), **Top middle**, **Top left** or **Top right**, chosen from a dropdown or a small picker showing the four spots on a window outline. It uses the same capsule and the same fade in whichever spot is picked. The spots are measured from the page, not the window, so they stay clear of the sidebar and, with tabs across the top, sit just below the tab row.
- Only the zoom percentage moves. "Address copied" and the other messages stay at the bottom.

### 3. New tab at the foot of the sidebar
In the sidebar, the **New tab** row sits right below the last tab, so its position changes as tabs open and close. Once the column scrolls, it scrolls away with the tabs. I'm used to having New tab in a fixed place at the bottom left, so I can reach it without looking for it.

- A switch that moves New tab to the foot of the sidebar, as a **+** button next to the bookmarks button (and the Spaces dot and extensions, when those are shown). It looks like the other buttons there. **Off by default**: New tab stays under the last tab.
- Shown only when Tabs in a sidebar is on. The row across the top isn't affected.
- The foot is where I'd put it, but I'm open to other places, e.g. the top of the column above the tabs, which is where Arc keeps it.

---

None of these depend on each other, so each can be its own small pull request. The page doesn't change what Search does. It only gives these opt-in options a place people can find.

Closes #83.

With enough tabs to scroll, the column's system scroll bar was drawn over the rows' right edge, which is where the cross on the tab under the pointer sits. The two were hard to tell apart, and it was easy to grab one when aiming for the other.

The column now hides the system bar (as the row across the top already does) and draws its own: a thin line in the margin between the rows and the column's hairline, clear of the cross. items.title: feat: add Universal binary (Intel + Apple Silicon) support
items.author: Assim-Genshi
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
## Summary

This PR enables building Search as a **Universal 2 macOS application (`arm64` + `x86_64`)**, allowing the app to run natively on both Apple Silicon and Intel Macs. It also fixes an immediate launch crash caused by early `NSApp` access and resolves Swift 6 concurrency warnings and toolchain compatibility issues.

---

## Key Changes

### 1. Universal Binary Build (`build.sh` & `Package.swift`)
- Updated `build.sh` to compile separate `arm64-apple-macosx` and `x86_64-apple-macosx` slices and combine them into a single fat binary using `lipo`.
  - *Note:* This avoids the known SwiftPM / Xcode build system bug with duplicate intermediate outputs (`.abi.json`) when attempting to pass multiple `--arch` flags in a single invocation.
- Added explicit `.executable` product declaration in `Package.swift`.
- Added `ARCHS` environment variable override in `build.sh` for fast single-arch local development builds (`ARCHS=$(uname -m) ./build.sh`).

### 2. Fix Early Launch Crash (`Prefs.swift`)
- **Bug:** When launching the app, SwiftUI initializes `@StateObject` properties before AppKit finishes instantiating `NSApplication`. Accessing `NSApp.appearance` in `Preferences.init()` caused an immediate fatal crash (`EXC_BAD_INSTRUCTION`) because `NSApp` is an implicitly unwrapped optional (`NSApplication!`) and was `nil` during early struct allocation.
- **Fix:** Used optional chaining (`NSApp?.appearance = ...`) and dispatched appearance updates to `DispatchQueue.main.async` so that it cleanly applies as soon as the main runloop starts. Added defensive optional chaining in `Icons.swift` and `Design.swift`.

### 3. Toolchain & SDK Compatibility (`Extensions*.swift`)
- Guarded `WKWebExtension` APIs (which require macOS 15.4 / Xcode 16.3 SDK) behind `#if compiler(>=6.1)` with lightweight fallback stubs for older toolchains.
- The project now builds cleanly across both macOS 14 / Xcode 16.2 and newer toolchains without breaking forward compatibility.

### 4. Swift 6 Concurrency & Warning Cleanups
- **`History.swift` & `Icons.swift`:** Marked static file/folder properties `nonisolated` and captured them locally before dispatching to background utility queues.
- **`Icons.swift`:** Wrapped background `NSImage` decoding in an `@unchecked Sendable` struct (`SendableImage`) to eliminate actor boundary transfer warnings.
- **`Links.swift`:** Properly annotated the `onceShown` completion handler with `@Sendable @MainActor` and used `MainActor.assumeIsolated`.
- **`Bench.swift` & `Browser.swift`:** Silenced unused `fcntl` return value warnings and added `@preconcurrency import WebKit`.

---

## Verification

1. **Universal Binary Verification:**
   ```bash
   $ lipo -info build/Search.app/Contents/MacOS/Search
   Architectures in the fat file: build/Search.app/Contents/MacOS/Search are: x86_64 arm64

items.title: Report the installed Safari version in the user agent
items.author: peter-bf
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
The user agent hardcoded Version/26.5, but web views run on the system's WebKit, which can be older (for example, Safari 18.6 on macOS 15 instead of the hardcoded 26.5). 

Sites that choose code paths by browser version could serve features the engine does not support and bot protection that compares the claimed version against the engine's actual features may treat the mismatch as suspicious traffic.

Read CFBundleShortVersionString from the installed Safari at launch, checking the cryptex location first and then /Applications. If neither is readable, fall back to the Safari version that shipped with the running macOS, the oldest the system WebKit can be.

items.title: A hidden sidebar opens at the edge and closes when you leave it, every time
items.author: caisergan
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Closes #114.

With "Hide the sidebar until the pointer reaches the edge" on, the column didn't always follow the pointer. After opening and closing it quickly a few times, either the left edge stopped bringing it out, or it stayed out after the pointer had left it.

The cause was the hover events `Fold` relied on: SwiftUI's `onHover` over a 6pt band at the edge to open, and over the column itself to close. A view that appears under a pointer that isn't moving never gets "entered", so it never gets "exited" either. The column coming back under the pointer never closed, and the band could think the pointer was still on it and ignore it coming back.

`Fold` now reads the pointer's actual position on every move, through local and global `NSEvent` monitors, and compares it with the window:

- At the left edge (the top edge for the strip), it starts the dwell and opens.
- Off the column once it's out, it starts the grace and closes. The grace now counts from when the pointer left, not from its latest move.
- Another app's window over the edge doesn't open it. One of Search's own windows, such as a popover from the column, counts as part of the column.
- It works with another app in front too.

The strip folded across the top used the same code and gets the same fix.

Side effects:
- The edge bands are gone, so the page's left 6pt takes clicks again.
- The main window now accepts mouse-moved events (`acceptsMouseMovedEvents`), so the monitor sees moves anywhere over it.

All of it is in `Sources/Search/Fold.swift`. The changelog gets its line under Unreleased › Fixed.

### Testing
- [x] `swift build`: no new warnings
- [x] In the app, window maximized: opened and closed the sidebar quickly many times; it opened at the edge and closed on leaving every time

items.title: 1Password never finishes signing in: its worker freezes on new WebSocket()
items.author: anyrobert
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
**What I did**

Installed 1Password from the Chrome Web Store (stable 8.12.37, later Nightly 8.12.42) and signed in, both through the 1Password Mac app and through the "Sign in" page on my.1password.com. The Mac app refuses Search until it's added under 1Password › Settings › Browser › Add Browser, so I did that first.

**What I expected**

The extension picks up the account and unlocks.

**What happened**

The popup never gets past its loading spinner, and the my.1password.com sign-in tab spins forever. The extension's own log (its `b5x-diagnostics` IndexedDB) stops right after the Mac app hands it a session:

```
[AppIntegration] [DesktopApp] Initiation complete - B5X is connected to desktop app
[DelegatedSessions] Signing in with delegated session
[AppIntegration] Received message <NmRequestDelegatedSession> from native core. Duration: 274ms
```

Nothing after that, and no account gets saved. Search notices and restarts the extension ("its worker stopped answering"), but the new one never starts either.

**Why**

`sample` on the WebContent process that hosts the worker gives the same stack in every sample:

```
WebCore::WorkerMainRunLoop::postTaskForMode
  WebCore::EventLoop::run
    WebCore::MicrotaskQueue::performMicrotaskCheckpoint
      WebCore::constructJSWebSocket1
        WebCore::WebSocket::create → WebSocket::connect
          WebCore::WorkerThreadableWebSocketChannel::WorkerThreadableWebSocketChannel
            WebCore::waitWithSTWParticipation
              WTF::BinarySemaphore::waitUntil
```

WebKit runs an extension's service worker on the main thread of its process (`WorkerMainRunLoop`). A WebSocket made from a worker goes through `WorkerThreadableWebSocketChannel`, which sets the connection up on the main thread and waits for it. The worker is the main thread, so it waits on itself. It never runs again, and a restarted extension gets handed the same stuck worker.

For 1Password the socket is its notifier (`this.websocket = new WebSocket(e)` in `@1password/web-api/notifier.js`), opened as soon as the session is set up.

It reproduces without 1Password. A worker with only this in it never replies, and nothing else gets through to it after that:

```js
chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener((m, sender, reply) => {
  const ws = new WebSocket("wss://echo.websocket.org");
  ws.onopen = () => reply("open");
  return true;
});
```

This might also be the Bitwarden item on the [roadmap](https://github.com/driceroland/Search/blob/bbc0c6e1f580cae01a2db853a790125fc8bf0fc0/ROADMAP.md?plain=1#L14) ("goes blank after signing in"). Bitwarden's worker connects to its notifications hub over SignalR once you're signed in, with `transport: WebSockets, skipNegotiation: true` in its `background.js` (2026.8.0). I don't have a Bitwarden account, so I haven't checked.

macOS 27.2, Search 1.0.1.

items.title: An extension worker's WebSockets are opened by the browser
items.author: anyrobert
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
Fixes #116.

It might also fix the Bitwarden item on the [roadmap](https://github.com/driceroland/Search/blob/bbc0c6e1f580cae01a2db853a790125fc8bf0fc0/ROADMAP.md?plain=1#L14) ("goes blank after signing in"), since Bitwarden's worker opens a SignalR WebSocket once you're signed in. I couldn't test that without an account, so I left the roadmap line alone.

**What it does**

The details of the freeze are in #116: WebKit runs an extension's service worker on the main thread, and a WebSocket made from a worker waits on the main thread, so it waits on itself.

The shim now replaces `WebSocket` in extension workers only. The replacement opens a `connectNative("search.websocket")` port, and `ExtensionSocket.swift` makes the actual connection with `URLSessionWebSocketTask`, passing text and binary frames both ways. Extension pages keep WebKit's own WebSocket, which works there.

The request is the one the worker would have made: same URL and subprotocols, `Origin: chrome-extension://<id>`, the worker's user agent, and whatever cookies Search's store has for that host. The same connection to the same server, just started from the app instead of WebKit, so nothing new leaves the app.

One thing that surprised me: WebKit drops messages posted on a native port before the delegate has set its `messageHandler`, and the worker posts right after `connectNative()`. Without a handshake, most connections never opened. So Search replies `ready` and `opening`, and the worker re-sends its `open` every 250 ms until it hears back, giving up after 10 s as if the connection had been refused.

**Testing**

- A small test extension whose worker opens `wss://echo.websocket.org`, sends text and binary, then closes. On `main` the worker freezes in `new WebSocket` with the same stack as in #116. With this change: open, both echoes, close 1000 clean, and the worker still answers messages afterwards. Nine runs in a row, all the same.
- An unknown host and a refused port: `error`, then `close` 1006.
- Four sockets at once: three closed cleanly, and the fourth got a 1006 because echo.websocket.org turned its handshake down (`-1011`), which is what a browser reports too.
- 1Password Nightly 8.12.42 with a real account: signs in, syncs, and keeps working, where it used to stop right after getting its session.
- `swift build`: no new warnings.

items.title: A new tab from a private tab is private too
items.author: PeterTheMango
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Closes #121

A tab opened from a private tab is now private too. Before, ⌘T, ⌘-click on a link, ⌘D, Open Image in New Tab and a bookmark opened with ⌘ all made an ordinary tab, even from a private one. That tab went into the history and tomorrow's session. Only links that ask for a new window (`target=_blank`, `window.open`) were already kept private.

### How
- `newTab()`: on a private tab, it hands off to `newShyTab()`. So ⌘T, the menu's New Tab and the + in the sidebar and in the row across the top all open a private tab there. The rule of never having two empty tabs still applies, through `newShyTab()`'s own reuse of an empty private tab.
- `open(_:foreground:atEnd:from:)`: a new `from` argument, the tab it was opened out of. A private one's opens private, in **the same** non-persistent store, so a link followed out of a site you signed in to privately is still signed in. That matches what `createWebViewWith` already does with the configuration WebKit hands over. Extension pages keep their own configuration.
- `from` is passed by ⌘/middle-click on a link, ⌘D (and Duplicate in the tab's menu), Open Image in New Tab, and `visit` (a bookmark opened with ⌘ held).
- Left public: tabs an extension opens, links from other apps, History menu items and links dropped on the tab row. None of these come out of a page.
- `Web.configuration` takes an optional `store`, and `Tab.store` exposes its `websiteDataStore`.
- CHANGELOG line added.

### Behaviour worth a look
While a private tab is in front, ⌘T and + can't make an ordinary tab. You switch to an ordinary tab first, the way a Chrome incognito window works. If ⌘T should stay ordinary and only links should stay private, that's the first block of `newTab()` taken out.

### Testing
- `swift build`: no new warnings.
- Driven end to end in the app: from a private tab (⌘⇧N), the new tabs opened by ⌘T, ⌘-click on a link and ⌘D are private, and none of their pages appear in History.

items.title: Addresses that redirect, like youtube.com, open the page instead of downloading a file
items.author: danielferrazs
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
When navigating to an address like `youtube.com`, the server returns an HTTP 301 redirect to `https://www.youtube.com/`, but includes a header of `Content-Type: application/binary`.

Because WebKit cannot natively render that MIME type, `response.canShowMIMEType` evaluated to `false`. Without inspecting the HTTP status code, Search interpreted the response as an unrenderable file download and initiated a `WKDownload`, saving a `.html` file into the user's Downloads folder instead of following the redirect to the site.

### What it does

- In `Browser.webView(_:decidePolicyFor response:)`, any HTTP redirect response (status code in `300...399`) is now unconditionally `.allow`ed so WebKit follows the `Location` header to the destination resource.
- Legitimate file downloads (DMGs, ZIPs, etc.) continue to download as expected because they are served with a `200 OK` status and a non-displayable MIME type.
- Adds an entry to `CHANGELOG.md` under `## Unreleased` › `### Fixed`.

### Testing

- [✓] `./build.sh`: clean build, 0 new warnings.
- [✓] In the app:
  - Typing `youtube.com` into the omnibox now navigates straight to YouTube without triggering a file download.
  - Tested file downloads with redirects (e.g. GitHub release assets) to verify that redirect chains leading to real file downloads still trigger the download when reaching the 200 OK file response.

items.title: ⌘W no longer bounces between pins: a pin already put down stays down
items.author: armin-ahmadii
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
With two pinned tabs and no other tab open, ⌘W bounces between them: ⌘W on A lands on B, and ⌘W on B wakes A again, back and forth, so you can never get out of the pins.

The pin branch of `close()` already avoids this when an ordinary tab exists ("⌘W bounced between the two instead of getting you out of them"). With only pins, the last fallback still picked a pin that had just been put down and woke it. This removes that fallback: once no other tab is awake, closing a pin leaves an empty tab through the `newTab()` that was already there, as closing the last tab of all does.

**Before:** two pins, ⌘W, ⌘W, ⌘W… → A, B, A, B…
**After:** two pins, ⌘W, ⌘W → B, then an empty tab; ⌘W again closes the window as before.

Tested with `./build.sh`:
- two pins, no other tabs: ⌘W twice → empty tab, then the window closes
- pins + an ordinary tab: ⌘W on a pin → back to that tab (unchanged)

**Testing**

[✓] `swift build`: clean build, 0 new warnings.
[✓] In the app (`./build.sh`):
Two pinned tabs, no other tabs: ⌘W on one pin lands on the other, and ⌘W again now leaves an empty tab instead of waking the first pin, so it no longer bounces between them. ⌘W on the empty tab closes the window as before.
Pins plus an ordinary tab: ⌘W on a pin still goes back to the ordinary tab, unchanged.

items.title: 1Password works: sign-in, autofill and passkeys
items.author: iuriio
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
With the 1Password extension installed, signing in never finished, nothing was offered on Google or any other page, and passkeys stored in 1Password failed. This PR has three commits, one per cause.

## 1. A worker's WebSocket froze the whole extension

WebKit runs an extension's service worker on the main thread of its web process (`WorkerMainRunLoop`). A worker's `new WebSocket()` builds a `WorkerThreadableWebSocketChannel`, which waits synchronously for the main thread to set up the channel. In this case the worker *is* the main thread, so it waits on itself forever. `sample` of the frozen process:

```
WebCore::WebSocket::connect
WebCore::WorkerThreadableWebSocketChannel::WorkerThreadableWebSocketChannel
WebCore::waitWithSTWParticipation(WTF::BinarySemaphore&, JSC::VM&)
```

1Password opens its notifier socket right after SRP sign-in succeeds, before it saves the account. The worker, the popup and the inline menu all froze, and the account was never added.

- **`ExtensionSocket.swift`** (new): the socket is made by Search with `URLSessionWebSocketTask` (one shared session, a per-task delegate) and its frames are carried over a native port (`search.socket`): text as it is, binary as base64. The handshake sends the Origin and user agent Chrome would send.
- **Shim, worker only**: `WebSocket` is replaced with a standards-shaped class on that port: `readyState`, `binaryType`, `protocol`, `on*` plus `addEventListener`, `send` in order (string, ArrayBuffer, view, Blob), `close` with code validation, and `error` + `close 1006` on failure.
- WebKit silently drops a native port that a worker opens in its first moments. Search acknowledges each port (`{ready: true}`), and the shim opens it again with a short backoff when no acknowledgement comes.
- `ExtensionTab.loadURL`: an extension sending a website's tab to one of its own `chrome-extension://` pages gets the tab swapped for one built from its configuration. 1Password does this after an auth-only sign-in. `Browser.replace` already did the reverse.

## 2. The passkey object was hidden even when an extension could answer

Without Apple's browser entitlement, or with passkeys off in Settings, `FormRelay.withoutPasskeys` deleted `PublicKeyCredential`, so GitHub said "Webauthn isn't supported" even with 1Password installed. The object is now a getter that stays hidden only until an extension claims the requests: it puts its own `get`/`create` on `navigator.credentials`, or reads `PublicKeyCredential` from an extension script (checked through `Error().stack`). The browser refuses publicKey requests that the extension leaves to it right away, with `NotAllowedError`; a conditional request waits instead. With no such extension, behaviour is the same as before.

## 3. `tabs.sendMessage` never reached the extension's own frames

In WebKit, `tabs.sendMessage` reaches only a tab's content scripts. In Chrome it also reaches the extension's pages framed in that tab. 1Password updates its in-page sign-on banner that way. On GitHub's two-factor page the banner stayed on the password suggestion, was dismissed after about 7 s, and the pending `get-credential` came back as `fallback-requested`. Worker log:

```
00:44:39.823 get-credential
00:44:39.840 [Webauthn] Spawning USO banner for tab 45
00:44:46.961 uso-dismiss
00:44:46.967 get-credential → {reason: "fallback-requested"}
```

In a worker, `tabs.sendMessage` now also hands the message (by runtime message) to the extension frames that `webNavigation.getAllFrames` finds in that tab, or to the one `frameId` names. The frame in that tab runs its listeners, every other page stays silent, and the first answer from either path wins.

Unlocking through the 1Password desktop app is a separate path. Its BrowserSupport host answers `BrowserVerificationFailed: UnknownBrowser` for browsers it doesn't know, so the user adds Search in 1Password › Settings › Browser › Add Browser. The changelog line mentions this.

## Testing

In a `--test` world with a fresh profile and 1Password 8.12.37:
- **Sign-in and autofill:** web sign-in → Add account → the account is saved and unlocked, and the inline menu offers logins on Google and other sites.
- **GitHub passkey:** sign out → sign in → the passkey stored in 1Password is offered on the two-factor page and accepted on the first try. Before the fixes: "Webauthn isn't supported", then "Authentication failed" until a reload.
- **WebSocket probe:** a worker opening `ws://127.0.0.1` against a local echo server as its first statement gets open with subprotocol, text and binary echo, and `close 1000`, on 4/4 fresh installs. A closed port gives `error` → `close 1006`.
- **Frame probe:** an extension iframe in a page now receives the worker's `tabs.sendMessage`, both tab-wide and by `frameId`, and its reply reaches the worker.
- **webauthn.io:** `PublicKeyCredential` is present with 1Password enabled and absent with it disabled, when passkeys are off.
- `swift build`: no new warnings.

items.title: Prevent webpage hover behind full-page panels
items.author: luca-dupont2
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse

items.body:
## Problem

A web page can keep its CSS hover state when Search opens Settings over it. I reproduced this on Search 1.0.1 and macOS Tahoe 26.6.2 with a local page that marks hovered elements. The same native overlay path is used by History, Downloads, Bookmarks, and Passwords; the Hidden list, Welcome panel, and address field can cover the page too.

## Change

Give WebKit a transparent pointer target in the active page while a full-page overlay is visible. Remove it when the overlay closes. Reapply it after navigation and when the active tab changes. This keeps page hover from showing through Search's panels without adding a dependency or a preference.

## Verification

- Before the change, the local page kept a hovered element after Settings opened.
- With the final build, moving the pointer inside Settings or History left no site element hovered. Closing the overlay removed the guard and restored normal hover.
- Checked the address field, tab switches while Settings was open, and navigation while Settings was open.
- Swift build succeeded with no new warnings. Existing deprecation and unused-result warnings remain on unchanged lines.

items.title: Extensions: hold the browsing APIs to what the manifest asked for
items.author: Hyp4tia
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
## What

The layer that fills in the Chrome APIs WebKit lacks answers from the browser itself: bookmarks, history, downloads, the open tabs, closed tabs, top sites, browsing data, the reading list. Until now the permission checks for those answers lived only in the injected script (`search-shim.js`), which runs beside the extension's own code, while `Extensions.swift:250` hands every extension `nativeMessaging` at every load and `runtime.sendNativeMessage("search", …)` reaches `ExtensionShims.answer` directly (`Extensions.swift:868-871`). An extension that skips the script can ask the browser itself.

Demonstrated on `bbc0c6e`, in an isolated SEARCH_PROBE world, driven through the app's own bench socket. An extension whose manifest declares only `storage` ran:

```js
chrome.runtime.sendNativeMessage("search", {api:"history.search", args:[{text:"", maxResults:5}]})
```

and got real history entries back, titles and URLs included. The same shape answers `tabs.describe` (every open tab's URL and title), `bookmarks.getTree`, `downloads.search` and `sessions.getRecentlyClosed`, none of it mentioned in the install prompt.

## The change

One gate in `ExtensionShims.run`, before the dispatch switch, on the families whose answers leave the extension's own origin:

- `gates` maps the seven families to the Chrome permission of the same name, plus one exact-name entry: `tabs.describe` is the single call where the permission guards reading a tab rather than moving or selecting it, so `tabs.move`/`discard`/`activate` are left alone.
- `allowed(id)` reads the names the extension's own manifest asked for, plus any optional permission already granted through `permissions.request` (the same `extensions.granted.<id>` list the shim's own `granted()` consults), so an extension that asks at runtime is not broken by this.
- A family that was never asked for is refused the way Chrome refuses an API it lacks, so an extension's own error paths see it.

The checks inside the shim stay as they are; they read well as UX. This makes the native side the boundary, which is where a boundary can actually hold.

## Testing

- `swift build` clean, no warnings added.
- In a test world: the no-permission extension above now gets `{"error":"The extension never asked for “history”"}`, and a control extension that declares `history` in its manifest still receives its answer, unchanged.
- Extension code that declares what it uses sees no difference: the store extensions this layer exists for (password managers, Raindrop) declare their permissions.

If you would rather keep the script as the only gate on purpose, that is your call to make and I will close this; from the outside this reads as one data path with a check a hostile caller can walk around.

---
