items.title: Extension packages: refuse links, and never write through one
items.author: Hyp4tia
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
## What

`Crx.unpack` runs `ditto -x -k` and checks only that `manifest.json` exists (`Crx.swift:117-135`). `ditto` keeps symbolic links as links (verified on this Mac), and `ExtensionShims.prepare` then walks the tree and rewrites every `.html`/`.htm` it finds: `String(contentsOf:)` follows a link, and `write(to:options:.atomic)` replaces the link at the destination with a regular file carrying the target's bytes (`ExtensionShims.swift:118-131`). The service worker path has the same read-and-rewrite shape with the path named by the manifest (`ExtensionShims.swift:75-91`).

Demonstrated on `bbc0c6e`: a folder extension shipping `evil.html` as a symbolic link to a file outside the package. After install, `Extensions/<id>/evil.html` was a regular 72-byte file whose contents were the link target's, with the shim's script tag prepended. The extension can fetch `chrome-extension://<id>/evil.html` and send it anywhere, so the install step turns a signed package into a local file read. The signed CRX makes the entry name attacker-chosen and the same shape crosses `unpack`, so a store-installed package does it too.

## The change

- `Crx.unpack`: after `ditto`, walk the unpacked tree and refuse the package whole if anything in it is a symbolic link. Nothing an extension needs is one, and refusing at the boundary keeps the rest of the code honest.
- `ExtensionShims.prepare`: skip links in the page walker, and resolve the service-worker path against the package folder (`inside(_:of:)`), leaving a manifest path that points outside its own package alone.

Folder installs are copied in as they are, so the walker skip covers those; the unpack refusal covers the store path.

## Testing

- `swift build` clean.
- Test world, same folder extension as above: `main` turns `evil.html` into the copied file, the fixed build leaves it a symbolic link and never reads the target.
- A zip carrying a symbolic link is verified to keep it a link through `ditto -x -k`, which is why the unpack check exists at all.
- Installed new folder extensions before and after: both load and run exactly as before.

---

items.author: Hyp4tia
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited

## What

`Bench.find` matches any tab by id prefix (`Bench.swift:1177-1180`), so with Settings › General › Let a script drive Search on, `eval`, `text`, `click`, `type`, `submit` and `shot` will act in a tab somebody is using: read an authenticated page, or run JavaScript in it. items.title: OAuth: only the tab that began the flow may finish it
items.author: Hyp4tia
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
## What

`ExtensionAuth.intercept` takes any navigation whose host ends `.chromiumapp.org`, and if a flow for that extension id is waiting, hands the URL to the extension as the sign-in's result (`ExtensionShims.swift:2632`). It never checks that the navigation happened in the tab the flow opened: `entry.tab` is only used to close whatever tab the redirect landed in (`:2637`).

Any page a person visits while a flow is pending can navigate to `https://<id>.chromiumapp.org/?code=…` and have its URL delivered as the flow's answer. The extension then acts on the attacker's code, which is the confused-deputy shape you do not want in the one place a browser handles sign-ins.

## The change

`intercept` takes the navigating web view, and only the flow's own tab may finish it. The call site is `decidePolicyFor`, where `webView` is the view that is navigating by definition, and `Browser.tab(for:)` already answers this question elsewhere.

## Testing

- `swift build` clean.
- Not driven end to end (a real `launchWebAuthFlow` needs a live provider); the guard is the change, and a redirect that arrives in any other tab is left alone rather than consumed, so nothing else changes about how it loads (nothing ever loads from `chromiumapp.org`).

items.title: Local TLS failures are accepted without a prompt for private hosts
items.author: Hyp4tia
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
**Where:** `Dialogs.swift:118-126` with `isLocal` at `:246-256`.

`trust` answers `.useCredential(URLCredential(trust:))` with no sheet when the host is `localhost`, `*.local`, `*.localhost`, `0.0.0.0`, or a private IPv4 literal (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16), and the acceptance is remembered per host for the rest of the launch (`excused`, `:215`).

**Why it matters:** for loopback a certificate is nearly meaningless, it is this Mac talking to itself. For a name on the local network it is a trust boundary, and there is nothing local about `nas.local` or `192.168.1.1` on a shared network. Anyone on the same wire can answer for those names (ARP, mDNS and LLMNR are all unauthenticated) with a self-signed certificate and be trusted silently: no sheet, no indication, and whatever page arrives is treated as the real thing.

**Suggested direction (yours to decide):** keep the silent path for `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `::1`, where there is nobody in the middle, and run everything else, `*.local` and the private ranges included, through the same "Continue Anyway" sheet the public case gets, with wording that says what is being accepted and for which host. Or invert it: silent only when a preference says so.

For what it is worth, the neighbouring behaviour is right: a subresource with a bad certificate fails closed, and only the main frame's host can be excused at all (`:129-134`).

items.title: Password matching groups hosts by a hand-rolled eTLD+1, so shared suffixes leak across sites
items.author: Hyp4tia
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
**Where:** `Vault.registrable` (`Vault.swift:187-195`), used by `Vault.logins(matching:)` (`:46-53`), whose results are offered on focus and filled into the page on a click (`Browser.swift:1456-1461`).

`registrable` knows ten two-part country endings and otherwise returns the last two labels. For suffixes that are not two-part country endings that is not eTLD+1: `alice.github.io` and `evil.github.io` are "the same site", and so are any two names under `*.amazonaws.com`, `*.web.app`, `*.herokuapp.com`, `*.blogspot.com`. A project a person hosts on one of those shares its saved password with every sibling under the same suffix, including one an attacker put up five minutes ago.

The case the comment intends to serve (accounts.example.com asking for the password kept for example.com) survives a proper public-suffix split, and so does `bbc.co.uk`.

**Suggested direction:** the app already loads the system's own public-suffix test for passkeys (`Passkeys.publicSuffix`, `Passkeys.swift:332-336`, `_CFHostIsDomainTopLevel` via `dlsym`; private, but its absence already degrades safely to exact-host matching). Its answers on this Mac, checked before writing this: `github.io` true, `evil.github.io` false, `co.uk` true, `example.co.uk` false, `s3.amazonaws.com` true. Walking labels outward with it yields the right registrable name everywhere, private suffixes and multi-part country ones included, and lets the vault and passkeys share one helper instead of a second hand-kept list.

items.title: Reloading a folder extension grants new permissions without asking
items.author: Hyp4tia
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
**Where:** `Extensions.swift:345-381` (`reload`) and `:247-249` (`load`).

Reloading a folder extension copies its folder in afresh and then records whatever permissions the new manifest requests (`:375`). `load` grants everything requested at every load (`:247-249`), and `prepare` has already added `nativeMessaging` (and `scripting` when `userScripts` is asked for) by then (`ExtensionShims.swift:59-65`). So editing an extension's folder and pressing Reload escalates silently: new host access, new APIs, nothing asked.

The update path already does exactly this dance: it re-asks when the new set is not a subset of the old (`update`, `:586-593`). Reload does not.

**Suggested direction:** the cleanest shape looks like making `load` grant the intersection of what the extension asks for and what was consented to at install (`installed[index].permissions`), so that "installing was the consent" stays true by construction, with growth on update and on reload alike routed through the existing `ask(install:)` sheet; on a decline, carry on with the old set (the code is newer, the permissions are not).

This one changes the consent model slightly, which is why it is here rather than as a pull request: the model is yours, and I would rather hear how you want it than guess.

items.title: The appcast's DMG link is taken on trust and shown under the app's own words
items.author: Hyp4tia
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
**Where:** `Updater.swift:228-229` and the `link` check at `:246-250`; the address is what Settings shows as the DMG to download.

The quiet-update path is well defended: sha256, then a code-signature and Team ID check on the unpacked bundle before the swap (`Swap.install`, `:270-302`), so a tampered feed cannot get code in that way. The DMG is the "download it yourself" offer, and it inherits only the feed's transport. A compromised `officecommun.com` (or a hijacked answer for it) can point that offer at any disk image, presented under the app's own "Search 1.0.2 is out" line, which is about the most trusted phrasing a bad download link will ever get.

**Suggested direction:** a guard in `link` accepting only addresses on the feed's own host (or a short named list), which closes the case that matters while `SEARCH_DOWNLOAD_URL` keeps working for test servers. Signing the appcast would cover more (the shape Sparkle uses), but the host check is three lines and no key management.

If the DMG is already served from somewhere the ZIP cannot be, tell me and I will drop this.

items.title: An extension's button closes its popup on the second click
items.author: iuriio
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Clicking a pinned extension's button while its popup was open reopened the popup instead of closing it.

The popover is `.transient`. Two paths led to the reopen:
- the popover closed on the click's mouse-down, and the button's action, which fires on mouse-up, opened a fresh one;
- the popover stayed up, because a click on the view it hangs from doesn't close it, and `show()` closed it and opened it again.

The fix:
- `ExtensionPopup.closes(_:)` closes the popup when the pressed extension's popup is up, and `press` stops there.
- `popoverWillClose` records when the popover closes on a mouse-down over the extension's own button. The press that ends that click is dropped; the record is used once and expires after 1.5 s.

Only the extension's own button counts. A popup opened from the puzzle list and hanging from the puzzle button behaves as before.

Tested by hand: build, then click a pinned extension twice. The second click closes the popup and it stays closed.

## What I did

Installed Search 1.0.1 (build 202609232336) from the disk image into `/Applications`, opened it, then opened **System Settings → Desktop & Dock → Default web browser**.

## What I expected

Search in that menu, next to the other browsers installed on this Mac.

## What happened instead

The menu lists Brave, Chromium, two copies of Google Chrome for Testing, and Safari. Search is not there.

Launch Services has registered the app. It is a notarized Developer ID build (`com.officecommun.search`), it is flagged as a web browser, and it is a handler for `http`, `https`, and `public.html`. It is not a handler for `public.xhtml`. Every browser that does show up in the menu claims `public.xhtml` as well as `public.html`. Since macOS 11, that second claim is what gets an app into this menu; `http` and `https` alone are not enough.

The comment in `build.sh` says owning `http` and `https` is what lets macOS offer the app as the default browser. The plist that comment sits on only declares `public.html` and `com.apple.web-internet-location`.

## macOS

macOS 26.6.1 (25G76)

items.title: Claim XHTML pages so Search can be the default browser
items.author: Aaditya2605
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes #139.

macOS only puts an app in **System Settings → Desktop & Dock → Default web browser** when the app claims `public.xhtml` as well as `public.html`. Search 1.0.1 already claims `http`, `https`, and `public.html`, and Launch Services registers it as a web browser, but it never claims `public.xhtml`, so it is left out of that menu. Brave, Safari, Chromium, and Chrome for Testing on the same Mac all claim `public.xhtml` and all appear.

`build.sh` now declares an XHTML page document type next to the HTML one, and the comment that said owning `http` and `https` was enough to be offered as the default browser now says the XHTML claim is required too.

## Test plan

- [ ] `./build.sh` produces a `Search.app` whose `Info.plist` lists `public.xhtml` under `CFBundleDocumentTypes`
- [ ] Copy that app to `/Applications`, eject any Search disk image still mounted, and run `lsregister -f /Applications/Search.app`
- [ ] Quit and reopen System Settings. **Desktop & Dock → Default web browser** lists Search
- [ ] Choosing Search makes a link from another app open in Search

items.author: Assim-Genshi

items.body: # feat: Arc-style Card Layout, Appearance Settings, and Floating Folded Sidebar Island ## Summary This pull request introduces an optional **Arc-style inset card layout**, a dedicated **Appearance** settings tab, support for **translucent liquid glass vibrancy**, and a refined **floating sidebar island** when folded with improved mouse tracking and smooth spring animation physics. --- ## Visual Showcase | Arc Inset Layout & Floating Island | Translucent Foreground / Vibrancy | | :---: | :---: | | | | | Appearance Settings Tab | Folded Island Detail | | :---: | :---: | | | | --- ## Key Features ### 1. Inset Card Window Layout (`prefs.cardWindow`) - Wraps web content into an Arc-style card surrounded by clean margins and continuous rounded corners (`10pt`, `Metrics.cardRadius`). - Subtle `1px` border stroke (`Palette.hairline`) and soft elevation shadow matching light/dark appearance. - **Context-aware insets**: automatically collapses the left padding to `0` when the sidebar is docked/unfolded, and removes top padding when "Tabs in sidebar" is disabled. - Continuous layer-backed clipping on `WKWebView` (`StageView`), ensuring web pages, video elements, and canvases respect rounded corners without corner bleed. ### 2. Dedicated Appearance Tab in Settings (`Settings.swift`) - Added an **Appearance** tab with the `paintbrush` icon. - **Theme**: Segmented control for Light, Dark, or System. - **Inset page like Arc**: Toggle to switch between the edge-to-edge layout and the floating card aesthetic. - **Transparent foreground**: Toggle for translucent glass vibrancy in the window frame and peeking panels. ### 3. Floating Folded Sidebar Island - When folded and Arc style is active, the peeking sidebar turns into a **detached floating island**: - `3pt` margin from the left edge and `3pt` margins on the y-axis (top and bottom). - Continuous rounded corners (`10pt`) and a `Palette.hairline` border. - Traffic lights float cleanly inside the island header row. - Clicking anywhere outside the island immediately dismisses it. ### 4. Robust Mouse Tracking & Instant Mid-Flight Catch (`FoldTracker`) - Replaced the brittle 6pt hit-test strip and `.onHover` with continuous window coordinate monitoring (`NSEvent.addLocalMonitorForEvents` with `window.acceptsMouseMovedEvents = true`). - **Generous 18pt edge trigger zone**: the sidebar reveals immediately when pushing against the left window border without skipping frames. - **Mid-flight catch**: moving the mouse back toward the sidebar while it is retreating smoothly catches it mid-flight anywhere across the full sidebar width (`prefs.sideWidth + 24`) and glides it open without glitching. - Replaced insertion/removal transitions with offset-based spring animations, preserving presentation layer velocity when motion is reversed. ### 5. Fluid Animation Curve - Updated `Motion.glide` to a critically-damped spring curve (`response: 0.32, dampingFraction: 0.94`), removing rubber-band bounce and jitter. - Synchronized the title bar traffic lights `CASpringAnimation` in `Fold.slide` to match the exact stiffness and damping of SwiftUI views. --- ## Changed Files - `Sources/Search/App.swift`: Dynamic card insets, window translucency configuration, and window mouse event tracking. - `Sources/Search/Design.swift`: Added `Metrics.cardInset`, `Metrics.cardRadius`, `Palette.canvas`, critically-damped `Motion.glide`, and continuous corner radius support in `VisualEffectView`. - `Sources/Search/Fold.swift`: Replaced hover timers with `FoldTracker` coordinate tracking, offset-driven animations, and floating island styling. - `Sources/Search/Prefs.swift`: Persistent preference keys for `cardWindow` and `transparentForeground`. - `Sources/Search/Settings.swift`: Added Appearance page with paintbrush icon, theme picker, and layout toggles. - `Sources/Search/Side.swift`: Island vibrancy background and corner clipping. - `Sources/Search/Stage.swift`: Continuous layer clipping for `WKWebView`. --- ## Verification & Testing - [x] Verified full build and compilation on macOS. - [x] Verified seamless toggle between edge-to-edge and Arc card layout in Settings. - [x] Tested window resize, full-screen transitions, and sidebar resizing while peeking. - [x] Tested rapid mouse flicks to the left edge and catching the sidebar mid-flight while retreating. - [x] Tested light, dark, and translucent foreground modes with clean corner rendering.

items.title: Leave ⌘⇧V to a text field, and open Paste and Go in a new tab
items.author: Aaditya2605
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes #138.

⌘⇧V is paste without formatting in a text field. Brave does not bind that key, so a Google Doc receives it and pastes. Search was taking the key first and loading the clipboard in the tab already open.

- While the caret is in a text field — a form, the address field, or a document that types into its own frame, such as Google Docs — Search leaves the key alone.
- Otherwise it is still Paste and Go, and the result opens in a new tab beside the current one.

Control+Command+V is not the paste shortcut. Ordinary paste is ⌘V. Paste without formatting, in Google Docs and in most Mac apps, is ⌘⇧V. Brave’s “Paste and Match Style” is ⌥⇧⌘V.

## Test plan

- [ ] On a Google Doc, with the caret in the document, ⌘⇧V pastes the clipboard without formatting and does not navigate
- [ ] In a form field, ⌘⇧V is not Paste and Go
- [ ] On a normal page, with nothing being typed, ⌘⇧V opens the clipboard address or search in a new tab and leaves the current tab alone
- [ ] Tabs → Paste and Go does the same

items.title: Preserve page editing shortcuts while keeping Search browser shortcuts
items.author: SamarthaB10
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
## Why

Issue #138 reports one example: `⌘⇧V` in Google Docs starts Search's Paste and Go action instead of pasting in the document. PR #144 adds a focus check for Paste and Go. This audit found other Search shortcuts that can take keys from a page editor or a normal Chrome page. The problem is in Search's app-wide key handling. It is not specific to Google Docs.

Search uses a local key event monitor for the whole window. It handles browser shortcuts before the page receives the key. The handler does not check which page control has focus. The menu also defines Paste and Go with `⌘⇧V`, so test that route as well as the event monitor when reviewing #144.

## Examples

| Keys | Search action | Expected page or Chrome action |
|---|---|---|
| `⌘⇧V` | Paste and Go | Google Docs and other editors use Paste without formatting |
| `⌘⇧←` / `⌘⇧→` | The arrow key code runs Back or Forward | Extend a text selection |
| `⌘S` | Fold the sidebar when it is shown | Save the page or document |
| `⌘D` | Duplicate the tab | Bookmark the page |
| `⌘⇧R` | Reading Mode | Reload without cache |
| `⌘⇧B` | Bookmark the current page | Show or hide the bookmarks bar |
| `⌘⇧H` | Hide page elements | Open the home page |

Google lists its built-in macOS shortcuts in [Chrome Help](https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/157179?hl=en-HK). Google Docs lists its editor shortcuts in [Docs Help](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/179738?hl=en). Websites and extensions can add more shortcuts.

## What I did

1. Opened a Google Doc and put the caret in the document.
2. Pressed `⌘⇧V` to paste without formatting.
3. On a page text field or editor, pressed `⌘⇧←` or `⌘⇧→` to extend the selection.
4. Used common page commands such as `⌘S` or `⌘D` while page content had focus.

## What I expected

The focused page editor should receive its editing shortcuts. Search should keep its tab, history, and other browser shortcuts when those keys do not conflict with page editing. Each overlapping key should have a clear rule. A fix for one key should not disable the other Search shortcuts.

## What happened

The current handler takes `⌘⇧V` for Paste and Go without checking page focus. Its Command-arrow fallback checks the left and right arrow key codes but does not reject Shift, so it can take text selection as Back or Forward. Other browser bindings also overlap with common Chrome or document commands.

There is a mismatch to check for `⌘⇧V`: issue #138 says it opens a new tab, but the current `pasteAndGo()` code loads the destination in the active tab. PR #144 describes the old behavior the same way, then changes Paste and Go to open a new tab when the page is not being edited. Please reproduce the reported behavior before treating the new-tab result as confirmed.

## Work requested

Audit Search's current key bindings against Chrome's macOS shortcut list and common macOS and web editor commands. Route each key to the focused page or to Search by a consistent rule. Keep useful Search bindings when page text is not being edited. Make modifier checks exact. Keep the menu shortcuts and the event monitor consistent.

Check #144 for the `⌘⇧V` fix. In particular, verify that a focused editor still receives the key when the Paste and Go menu item has the same key equivalent. Keep the separate Paste and Go command available when its browser shortcut is safe to use.

## Done when

- `⌘⇧V` pastes in Google Docs, a normal text field, and a content-editable editor.
- `⌘⇧←` and `⌘⇧→` extend text selection. Unshifted `⌘←` and `⌘→` still navigate browser history.
- The listed conflicting keys have an intentional and documented owner in page-editing and normal page states.
- Existing Search tab and browser shortcuts still work when the page is not editing text.
- The check covers a normal page, text field, content-editable editor, Google Docs, and a page with no editor focused.

macOS version: 26.6.2.

Related: #138, #144.

items.title: The cursor returns over a panel above a page that hides it
items.author: 0froq
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
`cursor: none` on a page leaked through every panel that floats on top of it. Open a page that hides its cursor (some video and game sites; anything with `body { cursor: none }`), press ⌘, — Settings came up with the pointer invisible across the whole dimmed backdrop and the panel itself, until you stepped off. Same on History, Downloads, Bookmarks, Welcome and Passwords, since they share `sheet` in `App.swift`.

The cause is how AppKit resolves a cursor. WebKit answers CSS `cursor: none` with an `NSCursor.invisibleCursor` rect over the whole web view; the SwiftUI panels in `sheet`'s ZStack add no rect of their own, so the invisible one is still the frontmost answer wherever the pointer sits inside the sheet. `CursorGround` is a small `NSViewRepresentable` at the foot of every sheet's ZStack that adds an arrow cursor rect across its bounds, and re-arms on `viewDidMoveToWindow` and `layout` so AppKit recomputes the moment the sheet appears rather than after the pointer twitches. One place fixes all six, and no panel has to know it was the fix.

`Float.swift` already uses `resetCursorRects` for its corner handle, so the shape is the app's own.

Checked on macOS 26.5 against a local `cursor: none` page: the arrow is back across all six panels the moment the pointer crosses into the sheet, without moving first. `swift build` adds no warnings.

items.title: PiP: two fingers can flick the floating video to a corner
items.author: farchanrifai
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
As in Arc and Dia: a two-finger swipe on the floating window sends it to the corner or edge it points at.

## What it does

- **Straight swipes:** up takes the window to the top on the side it's on; left takes it to the left at the height it's at, and so on.
- **Diagonal swipes** (between about 22° and 68°) go to that corner.
- **Placement:** the window lands 12 points in from the edges of the screen's usable part.
- **One move per swipe,** however long. The swipe is read as a whole when the fingers lift, so one that starts straight and turns diagonal still reaches its corner. A long swipe (over 120 points) moves without waiting.
- **Mouse wheel:** one flick per notch.
- **The glide** runs off the display's own refresh (`CADisplayLink`, 120 Hz on ProMotion) on a critically damped spring: quick away, no overshoot. A click stops it.
- **Dragging** still puts the window anywhere.

The rule is one pure function, `Float.corner(for:in:toward:margin:)`.

## Switch or default? Your call

Following CONTRIBUTING, it's behind **Settings › General › Flick the floating video to a corner**, off by default. With it off, two fingers push the window along as today.

It might suit Search better as the only behaviour, since the gesture only exists on the floating window. If you'd rather, I'll drop the switch and the old push-along path. Happy either way.

CHANGELOG gets its line under Unreleased › Added.

## Tested

- By hand in my fork (where it's on without a switch): straight and diagonal flicks on a trackpad. The mouse wheel and a click mid-glide weren't tried by hand.
- On this branch: it builds. The corner rule has unit tests in my fork; this repo has no test target, so they're not included.

items.title: PiP: the video can float when you switch apps
items.author: farchanrifai
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
As in Arc (Dia doesn't do it): switch to another app while a video plays, and it comes out into the floating window. It goes back into its tab when you return.

## What it does

- **Switching away:** when another app comes to the front, the video on the tab you're on floats out, the same way it does today when you leave the tab. It only happens on the same sites (`Players.knows`) and only while something plays.
- **Coming back:** if you're still on the tab the video came from, it lands back in the tab.
- **⌘⇧P:** a video floated by hand stays out.
- **Several windows:** only the window last in front lifts its video, so you don't get one floating window per browser window.
  - That window is tracked by hand (`Browser.front`, set on `didBecomeKey`). Once the app has gone to the back, `isMainWindow` no longer answers, which I found out the hard way.

## Switch or default? Your call

Following CONTRIBUTING, it's behind **Settings › General › Float the video when you switch apps**, off by default. It's the same rule the browser already applies when you leave a tab, so it could also just be how floating works. If you'd rather have it that way, I'll drop the switch.

CHANGELOG gets its line under Unreleased › Added.

## Tested

- By hand in my fork (on without a switch): a video playing, then switching to another app (it floats) and back (it lands). The ⌘⇧P case wasn't tried by hand.
- On this branch: it builds. The Settings switch wasn't tried by hand.

items.title: New tabs wait to start WebKit until an address is submitted
items.author: SamarthaB10
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
## Steps to reproduce

On macOS 26.6.2, open a page in Search, press ⌘T, wait about 0.8 seconds, then enter an address and press Return. A small `data:text/html,OK` page isolates browser startup from network and site scripts. YouTube shows the delay in normal use.

## Expected

The new tab begins loading the address as soon as it is submitted.

## Actual

The blank tab has no running WebKit page process. Search starts it only when the address is submitted. In a test world, the small local page took 0.48–0.58 seconds from navigation to completed load across four runs. A reused tab took about 0.39 seconds. The new-tab setup adds delay before site work begins.

## Proposed fix

Start a blank WebKit document shortly after a new tab appears, while the person types. Do this only while that tab is active and still blank. Check that a quick submission still works, that the tab stays blank before submission, and that the warm-up adds no Back entry.

This issue covers Search's new-tab startup cost. YouTube's remaining page work in WebKit is a separate part of the Chrome comparison.

items.author: dttdrv
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
the first launch walked every Chromium browser's folders before its window could appear, because `WelcomePanel` used `Chromium.installed().first` as the initial value of `source`. SwiftUI evaluates that whenever the view is made, so it ran while the first window was being built, for a page that isn't showing yet. `source` now starts as nil and Bring them in falls back to the first installed browser, like the picker already does.

first launch in a fresh test world went from 313 ms to 266 ms, median of 10 interleaved hidden runs on an M5 Pro. later launches are unchanged since they don't build the panel.

items.title: find each profile's Login Data without walking the caches
items.author: dttdrv
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
`Chromium.Source.files` walked three levels into every profile, caches included, to find `Login Data`. Chromium keeps it directly inside each profile folder, so this lists the root and checks each profile instead. it finds the same files.

`Chromium.installed()` runs this for every known browser, and Passwords, Bookmarks and the welcome screen call it each time they're drawn. with Dia installed it went from about 18 ms to 3 ms per call on an M5 Pro, and from 87 ms to 3 ms cold.

items.title: the process pool is made before the first window
items.author: dttdrv
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
`Web.pool` is first touched by the blank tab's `Tab.init`, which builds its configuration right away even though its web view is only made a second later. making the pool takes 7 to 10 ms on the main thread before the first window, on every launch (sampled on an M5 Pro, macOS 27).

building the configuration when the view is built would take it off launch, but `Web.configuration` reads `Spaces.current` when it's called, so a tab would need to keep its space from when it was made. is that worth doing, or is there a simpler place to warm the pool after the window is up?

items.title: Reloading an extension asks before it gets more access, and keeps the old version on no (#135)
items.author: karadoganyi
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Fixes #135.

Reload on a folder extension copied the folder in, rewrote the recorded permissions to whatever the new manifest asked for, and `load()` granted all of it. Editing an extension's folder and pressing Reload widened its access with nothing asked. Host access was never recorded at all, so a Web Store update that reached more websites also went through without asking.

### The model
@driceroland, #135 left this choice to you, so here is the one this takes. Easy to change if you'd rather have the other:

- **Ask when a reload or update wants more than was agreed; on No, keep the old version running untouched.** This mirrors what `update()` already did for API permissions.
- `load()` is unchanged. The alternative from the issue, where `load()` only ever grants what was agreed and on No the new code runs with the old permissions, would also cover files changed on disk, but it changes how every extension loads.

### What changes
- `Consent.swift` (new, Foundation only) answers one question: do the agreed permissions and hosts cover what this version wants?
  - `<all_urls>` covers everything.
  - `*://*/*` covers web patterns only, never `<all_urls>` or `file://`, so "all websites" can't quietly become local files.
- `Installed` records `hosts` alongside `permissions`, at install, update and reload.
  - It's optional, so older `installed.json` files still read.
  - For those older records, the installed copy's current host access counts as agreed, so nobody is re-asked for what they already run.
- `reload()` stages the new copy and checks it **before** unloading or replacing anything.
  - If it wants more, the usual "Add … to Search?" sheet asks.
  - **No:** the staging copy is thrown away and the old version keeps running.
  - A staged manifest WebKit can't read also leaves the working version in place, instead of swapping in a copy that won't load.
  - A second Reload while one is in flight is ignored. Two quick reloads used to be able to delete the installed copy once the check made the swap asynchronous.
- `update()` uses the same check, so growth in host access now asks too.

### Testing
- 19 checks on `Consent`, run with `swiftc` against the file on its own. I left them out of the PR because the repo has no test target.
- End to end in an isolated profile with `./bench ext-answer`, which answers and logs every consent question:
  - widened to `tabs` + `cookies` + `<all_urls>`, answered No: asked, 1.0 kept, record unchanged;
  - the same, answered Yes: 1.1 runs and the record includes the new access;
  - nothing new: not asked;
  - narrower: not asked, and the record narrows;
  - an old record without `hosts`: not re-asked for what it already had, asked when a site is added;
  - two reloads at once: the extension survives and runs;
  - a broken manifest: the old version keeps running.
- Not exercised: a real Web Store update.
- `swift build`: no new warnings.

### Related, not in this PR
Search's own `history` and `bookmarks` shims don't check the manifest. That's what #128 addresses.

items.title: A saved password is offered to one site, not to its neighbours
items.author: Dodothereal
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
Closes #134.

The site behind a host was worked out by hand in `Vault.registrable`:

```swift
let labels = host.lowercased().split(separator: ".").map(String.init)
guard labels.count > 2 else { return labels.joined(separator: ".") }
let seconds: Set<String> = ["co", "com", "org", "net", "gov", "gouv", "ac", "edu", "asso", "or", "ne"]
if seconds.contains(labels[labels.count - 2]), labels[labels.count - 1].count == 2 {
    return labels.suffix(3).joined(separator: ".")
}
return labels.suffix(2).joined(separator: ".")
```

That is not eTLD+1. It knows nothing of the *private* suffixes the public suffix list carries, so both hosts collapse to the suffix rather than to a site:

| host | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| alice.github.io | `github.io` | `alice.github.io` |
| evil.github.io | `github.io` | `evil.github.io` |
| x.blogspot.com | `blogspot.com` | `x.blogspot.com` |
| foo.web.app | `web.app` | `foo.web.app` |
| evil.herokuapp.com | `herokuapp.com` | `evil.herokuapp.com` |
| 192.168.1.5 | `1.5` | `192.168.1.5` |
| www.example.com | `example.com` | `example.com` (unchanged) |
| accounts.example.com | `example.com` | `example.com` (unchanged) |
| bbc.co.uk | `bbc.co.uk` | `bbc.co.uk` (unchanged) |

Two hosts sharing that value is exactly the condition `Vault.logins(matching:)` uses to offer one host's saved passwords to another (`Vault.swift:50`), so a password saved on a site someone hosts on one of those shared suffixes was offered to a sibling an attacker could stand up in five minutes. The IPv4 case made `192.168.1.5` and `10.0.1.5` "the same site" as well.

## The fix

The list is not one to keep here: it is long, it changes, and macOS ships it. `_CFHostIsDomainTopLevel` is the function behind it, and `Passkeys` already binds it by name for precisely this reason. It moves into a new `PublicSuffix` helper and both callers use it:

- `Vault.registrable` walks the host's labels down to the shortest one that is *not* itself a suffix. Walking from the left is what makes private suffixes work: `evil.github.io` has to take `github.io` as the suffix, where a fixed last-two-labels rule took it as the site.
- `Passkeys.fits` keeps its behaviour and loses its own copy of the `dlsym`.

Where the symbol cannot be found, `isSuffix` answers no and each caller falls back to its safe answer — `Vault` matches the host exactly, `Passkeys` accepts only the page's own host. Nothing widens.

## Testing

Compiled the helper on its own, checked against the running app through `./bench`, and confirmed `Passkeys.fits` is unchanged for every case:

- `fits("github.io", "alice.github.io")` → false, `fits("alice.github.io", "alice.github.io")` → true (as before)
- `fits("example.com", "accounts.example.com")` → true (as before, and still the behaviour passkeys need)
- `registrable` table above, verified in the built app rather than in a reimplementation

`swift build`: no new warnings.

## Notes

- No new dependency: the symbol is already loaded by the process (`CFNetwork`), and the `dlopen` is the same call `Passkeys` was already making.
- `Suffix.swift` is one file, ~80 lines, and has a comment explaining what a public suffix is and why both callers need it.
- CHANGELOG entry added under **Unreleased › Fixed** as CONTRIBUTING asks.

items.title: A certificate is taken on trust only for loopback, not for "looks local"
items.author: Dodothereal
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
Closes #133.

`Dialogs.isLocal` decides, without showing a sheet, that a host's certificate is fine to accept. It forgave three things:

```swift
if host == "localhost" || host.hasSuffix(".local") || host.hasSuffix(".localhost") { return true }
if host == "127.0.0.1" || host == "::1" || host == "0.0.0.0" { return true }
let parts = host.split(separator: ".").compactMap { Int($0) }
guard parts.count == 4 else { return false }
if parts[0] == 10 { return true }
if parts[0] == 192, parts[1] == 168 { return true }
if parts[0] == 172, (16...31).contains(parts[1]) { return true }
```

Two of those are wrong, and the second one is wrong in a way that needs no local network at all.

## A registered domain can look like a private address

`compactMap` drops whatever will not parse as a number, so the four labels it kept were not the host. `10.0.0.1.evil.com` left `[10, 0, 0, 1]` behind and was taken for a private address — and so were `192.168.1.1.attacker.net` and `172.16.9.9.evil.com`. Those names can simply be registered. A page served from one was accepted with a certificate the system had already rejected, with no sheet and no indication, and `excused` then remembered it for the launch.

## `.local` is a name somebody else can answer for

This is the case the issue names. mDNS, LLMNR and ARP are all unauthenticated, so on a shared network anyone can answer for `nas.local` or `192.168.1.1` with a certificate of their own and have the page handed over as the real thing. That is a trust boundary, and there is nothing local about it.

## The fix

Only loopback is trusted silently now — `localhost`, the `.localhost` names RFC 6761 reserves for it, `127.0.0.1`, `::1` and `0.0.0.0` — where this Mac is talking to itself and there is nobody in the middle to impersonate. Everything else takes the "Continue Anyway" sheet the public case already had, which names the host being accepted and remembers the answer for that launch.

The IP-range branches are removed rather than repaired: a private address is not a reason to skip the question, so the simplest correct thing is not to special-case addresses at all. Every remaining test is on the whole name, which is what stops a registered domain from matching.

## Testing

Ran the function's exact body on its own:

| | |
|---|---|
| silently trusted | `localhost`, `foo.localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, `0.0.0.0` |
| now asked about | `nas.local`, `192.168.1.1`, `10.0.0.5`, `172.16.0.1`, `10.0.0.1.evil.com`, `192.168.1.1.attacker.net`, `172.16.9.9.evil.com`, `127.0.0.1.evil.com`, `evil.local` |

Also confirmed on this Mac that `evil.localhost` resolves only to `::1` and `127.0.0.1`, so keeping the `.localhost` suffix silent cannot reach a stranger.

The app still loads pages normally after the change (checked in a `--test` world). `swift build`: no new warnings.

## Notes

- Behaviour change worth a second look before merging: a development server on `nas.local` or a private address now asks once per launch instead of being silent. That is the intent of the issue, but it is a visible change, so it is worth deciding deliberately. The alternative the issue offers — a preference that turns the silent path back on — is a bigger change and I did not want to guess.
- CHANGELOG entry added under **Unreleased › Fixed**.

items.title: Vimium C's background starts: the Chrome layer runs before a module worker's imports
items.author: karadoganyi
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
From the roadmap's "Now" list: *Vimium C doesn't start: WebKit fails to load its background.*

### Why it didn't start
1. Vimium C's worker is a module that imports ~29 files, and `background/store.js` reads `navigator.userAgentData.brands` as it loads. WebKit has no `navigator.userAgentData`, so the module graph throws and WebKit reports "background content failed to load". Its options pages (`options_wnd.js`, `async_bg.js`) read it unguarded too.
2. The shim couldn't cover this, because `prepare` wrote it at the top of the worker file. In a module, the file's `import`s are evaluated **before** anything written above them, so the shim ran after every imported module.
3. Once the background started, the content script crashed next. It calls `chrome.runtime.connect` detached (`a = chrome.runtime.connect; a(n)`). WebKit's API functions return `undefined` without `this`; Chrome's don't care. The shim's `connect`/`sendMessage` wrappers never reach content scripts, because the shim stops at `if (inContent) return;`.

### What changes (`ExtensionShims.swift`)
- **Module workers import the shim first.** `prepare` writes `import "/search-shim.js";` as the first line, instead of the shim text, when `background.type` is `module`. Classic workers keep the prepended text. Re-preparing strips either form an older build left, so installed extensions move over when the shim's hash changes. It sits inside #129's check that the worker path stays in the folder.
- **`navigator.userAgentData`**, next to where the shim already sets Chrome's `userAgent`, from the same version:
  - `brands` (Chromium, Google Chrome, and a GREASE entry), `mobile`, `platform`;
  - `getHighEntropyValues(hints)` returns the low-entropy values plus only the hints asked for;
  - `toJSON`;
  - defined only when WebKit doesn't have it.
- **`chrome.runtime` functions are bound** just before `if (inContent) return;`, so detached calls work in content scripts, pages and workers alike. The shim's later wrappers still apply on top.
- The comments that said the shim is prepended to module workers, and that content scripts only get the sendMessage mend, are corrected. The ROADMAP line now says what's left.

### Testing
Each run starts from a fresh launch (see the WebKit trap below). Checked on unchanged upstream and on this branch, both upgrading existing installs and installing fresh.

A purpose-built extension, plus Vimium C and two regression checks:

| | upstream | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| module worker whose import reads `userAgentData.brands` while loading | fails to load | starts; sees `Chromium 140, Google Chrome 140, …` |
| content script: `const c = chrome.runtime.connect; c()` | `undefined` | a port |
| options page reading `userAgentData` | throws | `3 brands, platform macOS` |
| Vimium C's background | fails to load | starts |
| plain Vimium (module worker) | starts | starts |
| a classic worker | starts | starts, shim text still prepended |

Seven popular extensions, checking that the background starts and that the popup shows content from it. Results are **identical on both builds**:
- module workers: uBlock Origin Lite, 1Password, Vimium;
- classic workers: Bitwarden, Dark Reader, Proton Pass, Grammarly.

`swift build`: no new warnings.

### Still open
- **Vimium C doesn't answer its keys yet.** Its content script now connects: `port.sender` is complete (tab, frameId, url, origin, documentId). But the background closes each port right after it opens, with no error thrown. That's the new roadmap line.
- **A WebKit trap worth knowing when debugging extensions:** once an extension's worker fails to start, every later load of that extension fails too, even a worker that does nothing, until Search is quit and reopened. `revive()` can't recover it.

items.body:
Search shows one page at a time. Comparing two pages, reading documentation while writing in another tab, or keeping a call beside notes means switching back and forth with `⇧⌘[` `⇧⌘]`, or opening a second browser.

**Proposal:** split view, off by default and turned on with a switch in Settings. When it's on, a tab can be put beside the current one, and the window shows both.

The first version would be the smallest one that does the job:

- two tabs, side by side or one above the other, with a divider that can be dragged
- the pane you click into is the focused one: the address field, `⌘L`, `⌘F`, reading mode and `⇧⌘P` act on it
- `⌘W` closes the focused tab, and the other one takes the whole window again

If that holds up, a later step would add three panes and four in the corners.

Arc, Vivaldi and Edge all have a version of this. I'd follow Arc's quiet approach: no new toolbar, just a thin divider and a focused pane that's easy to spot.

**Questions before I start:**

1. How should a split show in the sidebar and the tab row: as one entry for the pair, or as separate tabs with a mark?
2. Should a split come back after a restart?
3. Where should the switch live: General, or the proposed Customization page (#101)?
4. With Spaces, I'd assume a split belongs to a single space. Does that match how you see it?

**Plan:** one small pull request per piece, with no new dependencies: the setting and the state behind it, then the two-pane view, then making commands act on the focused pane, then the sidebar and tab row, then restoring after a restart, then three and four panes.

items.title: A default page zoom for every site, in Settings › General
items.author: shashwataggarwal
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
Search already remembers a zoom per site (`zoom.<host>`), but every site it hasn't seen opens at 100%. This adds what Chrome has in Settings › Appearance › Page zoom: one size every site opens at until you zoom it yourself.

## What it does

- **Settings › General › Default page zoom**: a menu beside Search with, 75% to 200%. It starts at 100%, so nothing is different for anyone who doesn't touch it.
- A site with no zoom of its own opens at the default. A site you zoom with ⌘+ / ⌘− keeps its own, as it does today.
- **⌘0** goes back to the default rather than to 100%, as in Chrome.
- Changing the setting resizes open tabs at once (except sites zoomed on their own); a sleeping tab picks it up when it wakes.
- Private tabs open at the default too, and still remember nothing.

## Code

- `Prefs.swift`: `pageZoom`, stored as `pageZoom`.
- `Tab.swift`: `Tab.defaultZoom`; `applyRememberedZoom()` falls back to it instead of 1; `rememberZoom()` forgets a site once it's back at the default; `resetZoom()` goes to it.
- `Browser.swift`: open tabs follow a change to the setting.
- `Settings.swift`: the row. `CHANGELOG.md`: its line under Unreleased › Added.

## Tested

- `swift build` on current `main`, no new warnings.
- On a test run with `./bench --test`: `example.com` reports `innerWidth` 1280 at the default of 100%, and 1024 with the default at 125% — 1280 ÷ 1.25.
- By hand: changing the setting resizes the open tab behind Settings.

items.title: Separate normal reload and reload from origin (⌘R / ⌥⌘R, as in Safari)
items.author: ductan2
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
## Summary

Search currently maps `Cmd + R` to `reloadFromOrigin()`, with no separate normal reload action. This PR separates the two, following Safari's keys: `Cmd + R` reloads normally and `Cmd + Option + R` reloads from origin. Reading Mode stays on `Cmd + Shift + R`.

Closes #171.

## Shortcuts

| Shortcut | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Cmd + R` | Reload from origin | Normal reload |
| `Cmd + Option + R` | — | Reload Page From Origin |
| `Cmd + Shift + R` | Reading Mode | Reading Mode (unchanged) |

The origin action uses WebKit's `reloadFromOrigin()` to revalidate cached content. It does not clear cookies or website data.

## Changes

- Keep the View menu and keyboard event handler consistent with the new shortcuts.
- Preserve sleeping-tab recovery. A tab that has lost its document still gets its original URL loaded again (with the default cache policy, for both reload actions).
- Forward extensions' `fromOrigin` flag to the tab reload action.
- Clear Reading Mode state when reloading: Reading Mode rewrites the page in place, so after any reload the page is no longer in Reading Mode and the flag follows.
- Update the README shortcut reference and Unreleased changelog.

## Validation

Tested the built app in an isolated test world with a localhost article and cacheable JavaScript fixture (on the first version of the keys, before the switch to Safari's layout):

- [x] `swift build` passes, also after the shortcut change; existing deprecation warnings remain in unchanged code.
- [x] `git diff --check` passes.
- [x] After updating the server's JavaScript from v1 to v2, normal reload keeps the fresh cached v1 without requesting the script again; origin reload requests the script with `Cache-Control: no-cache` and loads v2.
- [x] Both reload shortcuts rerun page JavaScript without activating Reading Mode.
- [x] The `Cmd + Option + R` handler matches with focus in a page input and with the Option-generated `®` character.
- [x] Reading Mode can be re-entered on the first keypress after either reload action.
- [x] A sleeping tab wakes and loads successfully after selection and origin reload.
- [x] Both reload actions restore a tab whose document is `about:blank` while its original URL is retained.

The final key layout (`Cmd + Option + R` for origin reload, `Cmd + Shift + R` for Reading Mode) has been built but not re-run in the app. Extension-triggered reloads, other keyboard layouts, and direct menu clicks were not runtime-tested. No CPU/RAM benchmark was performed; cache observations apply to the tested WebKit build and fixture.

Thanks for building Search and considering this improvement!

items.title: Arc-style pinned tabs: full rows above the "New tab" button, toggled with ⌘D
items.author: hueypov
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
In Arc there are two things:
- **Favorites**: icon tiles at the top of the sidebar. Search's pins already work like this.
- **Pinned tabs**: normal full-width rows with the page title. ⌘D pins or unpins the current tab.

Search has the first but not the second. Pressing ⌘D in Search duplicates the tab, and the only way to pin makes a tile.

**What I'd like:** a sidebar laid out like Arc's:
1. Pin tiles (as today)
2. Pinned tabs, as full rows
3. The "New tab" button, splitting pinned from normal
4. Normal tabs

Today "New tab" sits at the bottom of the normal tabs. Moving it between the two groups shows clearly which tabs stay and which ones come and go.

**How pinned rows would behave:**
- **⌘W puts it to sleep, it doesn't close it.** The row stays and the page is let go, the same as ⌘W on a pin tile today.
- **It falls asleep on its own after a while**, like normal tabs do after 30 minutes. Pin tiles never sleep on their own today (`Sleep.swift` skips them on purpose). But pinned rows are meant for keeping lots of pages around, so letting them sleep keeps memory down.
- **⌘D pins or unpins the current tab**, maybe as an option since ⌘D is Duplicate Tab today.

Pinned rows help when you keep more pages than fit as tiles, or when the title matters more than the icon (docs, tickets, long-running pages).

Related: #141 (where a pin goes when put down), #68 (tab folders), #104 (New tab at the foot, as an option), #36 (custom shortcuts).

items.title: feat(tabs): detach tab into its own window
items.author: olllayor
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
## Why

Issue #72 asks for tabs in a second window for multi-monitor setups. The app names one window as intent in the README and in App commands. This change keeps that model and lets one tab live in a small companion window. The tab stays in the row and only its page moves. You get a reference on another monitor with no second strip, no second session, and no shared-state races.

## Scope

- New Detached panel (Sources/Search/Detached.swift) hosts the page, modeled on Float.
- Browser.detach, attach, and toggleDetached own which tab is out.
- Stage shows a placeholder while the page is out. Sleep skips the tab. Space switch, select, close, and quit return it.
- TabBar and Side start a detach past a 40pt sideways pull, drag the URL out, and add Detach and Attach to TabMenu.

## Tradeoffs

Full multi-window with one Browser per window would answer the whole request, including two strips and drag between windows. It splits Session, Spaces.current, Links.window, and Browser.front. That is a large change and it drops the one-window model. This PR ships the reference case first and leaves that path open.

## Blast Radius

Tab drag, space switch, sleep, and quit paths touch one tab flag. Session, Spaces, Links, and the App scene stay as they are. Risk is low. The cost of staying put is no second-monitor story.

## Verification

swiftc -parse passes on all eight touched files. Full swift build does not run here. The machine has CommandLineTools only, no Xcode, and the build fails in untouched files too with external macro implementation type SwiftUIMacros.StateMacro could not be found. The app needs a check on a Mac with Xcode. Drag a tab clear of the row, move the companion to another monitor, rename the tab, switch spaces, and quit with it open.

items.title: Hold a back or forward swipe to pick a page from history
items.author: farchanrifai
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
As in Dia: swipe back or forward as today, and once the disc is armed, keep your fingers down. The disc turns into a short list of the pages that way, and you pick one without lifting.

## What it does

- **Hold to open:** about half a second after the swipe is armed, the disc becomes a list of up to eight pages in that direction, each with its site icon and title. The nearest page is lit, on the same line the disc was.
- **Pick:** moving the fingers down slides the list under the light, further back (or, going forward, further on); moving up brings it nearer. There's a haptic tick at each step, and the page underneath doesn't scroll while you pick.
- **Go:** lifting the fingers goes to the lit page (`go(to:)` on the back-forward item), and the list fades where it is.
- **Cancel:** pulling the fingers back to the edge closes it and nothing happens, as with the disc.
- With only one page that way, nothing changes: it's just the disc.

## Switch or default? Your call

Following CONTRIBUTING, it's behind **Settings › General › Hold a swipe to pick from history**, off by default. It only kicks in when a swipe is held, so it could also just be how the swipe works; happy to drop the switch if you'd prefer that.

CHANGELOG gets its line under Unreleased › Added.

## How it works

- `Swipe.swift`: `Pull` gains the list (`stops`) and the lit row (`picked`).
- `Tab.swift` (`PageView`): a short hold timer once armed builds the list from `backForwardList`; vertical deltas step through it with the natural-scrolling sign; release goes to the picked item.
- `Stage.swift`: `HistoryList` is drawn in place of the disc, at the same edge.

## Tested

By hand in my fork (where it's on without a switch): holding a swipe to open the list, stepping through it, and letting go on a page. On this branch it builds; the switch itself wasn't tried by hand.

items.title: fix: support invisible offscreen extension documents
items.author: K-NRS
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Lokal can fail to translate through an offscreen document: creation can leave a stale document after failure or reload, discovery can report an unready page, and iframe content-script replies cannot reach their offscreen parent through WebKit's normal runtime delivery.

Give each extension one owned offscreen document with load completion, cancellation, teardown and filtered context discovery. Keep it detached with WebKit background throttling; an owner-only tab adapter identifies its iframe senders without adding a browser tab. A deduplicated relay carries those replies to the parent and rejects pending work on close. Existing background/popup discovery and upstream message-response coordination are preserved.

Standalone follow-up to the feedback on #54, updated with main at `ab6efbb`. No changes to ordinary background-tab scheduling, settings, dependencies or unrelated features; test code stays outside the app sources.

Validation:
- Packaged release build and code-signature verification pass, with no new compiler warnings.
- Real WebKit regression reproduces lifecycle, discovery and iframe failures on the base; all 323 checks pass with the fix. Covers load cancellation/failure, immediate messaging, worker and workerless iframe replies, a 12-second worker reply, filters, isolation, reload/disable cleanup and preserved background/popup discovery.
- Unmodified Lokal 1.5.9, default offscreen path: uncached “resilient” returns 43 dictionary rows; after extension reload, “durable” returns 46. Both keep exactly one offscreen context and leave visible tabs and selection unchanged.

Run the external regression against an isolated packaged app launched with `SEARCH_PROBE=<world> SEARCH_MEASURE=1` and bench enabled: `python3 tests/offscreen.py --world <world>`.


After updating with `ab6efbb`, the packaged release build, signature verification and all 323 offscreen checks passed again.

items.title: Calm vertical overscroll natively so non-passive wheel listeners scroll (#180)
items.author: olllayor
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Resolves #180

### Problem
Search previously injected `html, body { overscroll-behavior-y: none; }` at document start (`Swipe.calm`) to turn off rubber-band bouncing past page tops. In macOS WebKit, combining `overscroll-behavior-y: none` with a non-passive `wheel` event listener on `window` (common on sites with carousels catching sideways trackpad swipes) causes WebKit's asynchronous scrolling thread to drop unhandled discrete mouse wheel scroll events (`rdar://137757208`).

### Solution
Instead of injecting CSS into pages, disable vertical bounce natively using WebKit's `_setRubberBandingEnabled:` SPI on `PageView`. We pass `_WKRectEdgeLeft | _WKRectEdgeRight` (`10`), keeping horizontal rubber-banding for two-finger navigation swipes while preventing top and bottom rubber-banding without altering page stylesheets or tripping WebKit's scroll-latching bug.

items.author: woelper
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
Refs #62. A draft: a plan, and a spike showing the first step of it works, so there is something concrete to say yes or no to.

## What's here

- **`PORTING.md`**: the plan. Linux first, then Windows with WebKit bundled. It covers what carries over (the models, every script put into pages, the ad blocker's rules) and what doesn't (Chrome extensions, since `WKWebExtension` is Apple-only; passkeys; DRM video). It also names the three questions to settle first, the main one being whether this belongs in this repository at all.
- **`SearchLinux`**: a GTK 4 + WebKitGTK 6.0 shell in Swift, declared in `Package.swift` only on Linux.
  - Tabs sit in the title bar, and the field comes up with Ctrl+L or Ctrl+T.
  - The field uses the Mac's own `Address` and `Engine`, symlinked rather than copied.
  - The session comes back lazily: a restored tab only gets a web view once it's shown.
  - The ad blocker compiles the same JSON through `WebKitUserContentFilterStore`.
  - Keys: Ctrl+W, Ctrl+Tab, Ctrl+1–9, Alt+←/→, Ctrl+R.
  - Light and dark follow the desktop.

items.title: Extensions: a user script's file is read from the extension's own package
items.author: burakbuilds
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
## What

`ExtensionShims.userScriptFile` reads each `js[].file` with `folder.appendingPathComponent(file)` and never checks where that path ends up (`ExtensionShims.swift:2869`). A name with `..` in it, or one that goes through a symbolic link, reads a file from anywhere this user can read. The contents are then written to `_search/us-<hash>.js` inside the extension's own folder, and that path is returned to the extension, which can fetch it from its own origin.

Every extension can reach this:
- `nativeMessaging` is added to every extension at prepare (`ExtensionShims.swift:66`).
- `userScripts` is not one of the gated families (`gates`, `:2263`).
- `scripting.executeScript({ files })` also goes through `userScripts.file` (`:1598`).

Search is not sandboxed, so this covers everything outside the TCC-protected folders. An extension whose install sheet says it asks for nothing special can read files that Chrome keeps out of an extension's reach.

## The change

The name now goes through `inside(_:of:)`, the helper the service-worker path already uses (added in #129). It rejects anything that resolves outside the package or passes through a link. A file inside the package reads exactly as before. A file outside it is skipped, the same way a missing file already is.

## Testing

- `swift build`: builds with no new warnings.
- I copied the old and new path expressions into a standalone script and ran them against a test folder. Results:

| `file` | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `scripts/a.js` | read | read |
| `/scripts/a.js` | read | read |
| `../../secret.txt` | read the file outside the package | refused |
| `scripts/../../../secret.txt` | read the file outside the package | refused |
| `link.js` (symbolic link to a file outside the package) | read the file outside the package | refused |

- I have not run it end to end in the app with a real extension. The change is limited to that one read.

---

Found while reading the tree end to end. Happy to reshape it if you'd rather put the check somewhere else, for example on the `userScripts.*` family as a whole.

items.title: document_start content script can miss a page restored on hidden launch
items.author: TesterPen0812
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
**macOS:** 27.0

**What I did:** With an enabled extension whose content script runs at `document_start`, I saved a page in the session, quit Search, and launched it hidden with `open -j`. A small local fixture checks whether the extension's marker exists when the page's first inline script runs.

**Expected:** The marker is already present when the page script runs.

**Observed:** On two hidden launches of commit `b2d86cc`, the early marker was absent; the extension added its marker later. A visible launch passed. The same hidden check passed on release `v1.0.1`. The relevant startup and restore paths remain in current upstream `a868137`.

**Impact:** An extension that needs to run before page scripts can miss that window on the initially restored page of a hidden cold launch. This evidence does not establish a problem for normal visible launches or later pages.

**Proposed direction:** Start enabled extensions when a hidden restored page needs them, and let that navigation wait for them with a bounded timeout. A local implementation is prepared.

**macOS:** 27.0

**What I did:** Used Search's isolated benchmark world to type in the address field with 2,000 and 20,000 synthetic visits.

**Expected:** Suggestions should appear promptly as the user types.

**Observed:** On commit `b2d86cc`, median field-settle time rose from 10.42 ms at 2,000 entries to 55.42 ms at 20,000. The persisted file is capped at 2,000 entries, but a live session or import can exceed that count. The suggestion algorithm remains unchanged in upstream `a868137`.

**Impact and limit:** A large live or imported history can make the address field feel slow. The 20,000-entry case is synthetic; normal relaunch restores at most the saved 2,000 entries. Field-settle time includes UI work.

**Proposed direction:** Keep only the best few candidates during the scan and use a fast matching path for printable ASCII, preserving the same suggestion order. A local implementation is prepared.

items.title: Extensions: the update check reads <updatecheck>, not the XML declaration
items.author: burakbuilds
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
## What

The daily extension update check (`Extensions.update`, `Extensions.swift:573-579`) looks for the first `version="…"` anywhere in the Web Store's reply. That is always the XML declaration, `<?xml version="1.0" …?>`. The `status="ok"` check also passes on a reply that says there's no update, because that attribute sits on `<app>` either way. Here is a live "no update" reply for uBlock Origin Lite:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?><gupdate …><app appid="ddkjiahejlhfcafbddmgiahcphecmpfh" … status="ok"><updatecheck _esbAllowlist="true" status="noupdate"/></app></gupdate>
```

So `"1.0" != item.version` is true every time. Every extension installed from the store is downloaded again, verified, unloaded and loaded again about once a day. uBlock Origin Lite is 9.7 MB. A password manager extension loses its unlocked state when it reloads.

## The change

`status` and `version` are now read from the `<updatecheck …>` element only. That element carries `status="ok"` and a `version` only when a newer build exists. Nothing else in the update path changes.

## Testing

- `swift build`: builds with no new warnings.
- I ran the old and new parsing against two live replies from `clients2.google.com` for uBlock Origin Lite:

| reply | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `v=2099.1.1` (`noupdate`) | `1.0`, so an update is fetched | none, nothing fetched |
| `v=0.0.1` (update available) | `1.0` | `2026.920.1710` |

items.title: Passwords: an http page is offered only what was kept from http
items.author: burakbuilds
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
> **Builds on #208.** Its commit is the first one here, and this diff gets smaller once #208 is in. Writing a protocol is what makes #208 necessary. On a keychain that also holds git's `github.com` token for the same username, `save` without #208's label would re-key that token too. And without the HTML-form auth type, Search's item would collide with git's (`errSecDuplicateItem`). I checked this on a throwaway keychain: a pre-existing Search item was re-tagged https, then http, then forgotten, and git's token stayed as it was throughout.

## What

Logins are keyed by host alone (`Vault.logins(matching:)`, used at `Browser.swift:1558`). So when the caret is in a sign-in box on `http://example.com`, the list under it offers the password kept from `https://example.com`. One click fills it into a page that anyone on the network in between (a café's, a hotel's) could have written. That's the downgrade Chrome and Safari prevent by keeping the scheme with each saved login. It works for any site that isn't HSTS-preloaded.

## The change

- `Login` gets `clear`: kept from a page that came over plain http.
- `Vault.save` writes it into `kSecAttrProtocol` every time (`http` or `https`), and `login(from:)` reads it back.
- The list under a sign-in box on an `http:` page offers only logins where `clear` is set.
- The sign-in that just went out records its page's scheme next to its host (`Tab.sent`). `onCredentials` passes it on, so a new offer carries it. A known login used again takes the scheme of the page it was just used on.
- Chromium imports read the scheme from `origin_url`, and CSV imports read it from the url column.

Items saved before this change have no protocol, so they read as https. A router or NAS password saved earlier therefore won't be offered on its http page until you sign in there once by hand. That sign-in re-tags it and it's offered from then on. A password typed in Settings › Passwords › Add counts as https, the same way.

## Testing

- `swift build`: builds with no new warnings.
- I tested the keychain side on a throwaway keychain file created with `security create-keychain`, so the login keychain wasn't touched:
  - An item added without a protocol reads back as `nil`.
  - `SecItemUpdate` matched by server and account (the way `save` matches) sets the protocol.
  - It reads back as the string `"http"`, and as `"htps"` after switching.
- I haven't clicked through the sign-in flow in a running build.

If you'd rather keep this simpler, the other shape I considered is "never offer on http unless the host is local". I didn't go that way: routers answer to `fritz.box`, `router.lan` and bare names, and any list of local names ends up guessing.

items.title: Links to another app ask first
items.author: burakbuilds
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
## What

When a navigation uses a scheme Search doesn't load itself, `decidePolicyFor` passes it straight to `NSWorkspace.shared.open(url)` without asking (`Browser.swift:1911`). There's no check on who asked or how. Any page, or an ad iframe inside it, can open any app that handles a URL scheme as soon as it loads, with no click:

- `zoommtg:` joins a call
- `slack:`
- `ssh:` opens Terminal pointed at a host
- `smb:` makes Finder mount a share
- `x-apple.systempreferences:`
- …

Safari and Chrome ask first.

## The change

`handOff(_:from:clicked:)` replaces the direct call:

- **Asks first.** The alert names the app and the site: *Open "zoom.us"?* / *example.com wants to open zoom.us.* The app's name comes from `NSWorkspace.urlForApplication(toOpen:)`. If no app handles the scheme, nothing happens, as before.
- **One question at a time, only from the tab in front.** Anything a page asks while an alert is already open, or anything from a background tab, is dropped instead of queued behind it.
- **Return doesn't answer it.** Cancel is added first, so AppKit gives it Esc and gives Open no key at all. I checked this: with the buttons added as Cancel, Open, Cancel gets Esc and Open gets none. Opening takes a click, so a page can't slip the alert in just as you press Return in one of its fields.
- **A `mailto:` link you click** (`.linkActivated`) still goes straight to Mail, as in every browser.

## Testing

- `swift build`: builds with no new warnings.
- I ran the `.build` binary as a test world and drove it with `./bench --test`:
  - A selected tab went to `x-apple.systempreferences:` twice, 300 ms apart. One `_NSAlertPanel` showed "Open "System Settings"? This page wants to open System Settings.", and System Settings didn't start.
  - The same page in a background bench tab showed no alert, and System Settings didn't start either.
- I didn't test clicking Open through bench: its key presses go to the main window, not to the alert.

items.title: Pop-ups need a click
items.author: burakbuilds
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
## What

On macOS, `WKPreferences.javaScriptCanOpenWindowsAutomatically` defaults to `true`. I checked it on this Mac: a fresh `WKPreferences()` reports `true`. Search never changes it, so `window.open` with no click or key press still reaches `createWebViewWith` (`Browser.swift:1919`). That builds a tab and switches to it (`activeID = tab.id`). A page can open tabs on load or on a timer and pull you away from the tab you're reading. Streaming and download sites do this a lot.

## The change

`Web.configuration` now sets the preference to `false`. WebKit then lets `window.open` through only while it is handling a click or a key press, which is how Safari's pop-up blocking works. Sign-in windows, share dialogs and anything else opened from a button behave exactly as before. Pages opened by the popup inherit the setting, since WebKit hands the popup its opener's configuration.

A later step could show that something was blocked, the way Safari's field does. That's beyond this one-line change.

## Testing

- `swift build`: builds with no new warnings.
- I ran the same script against the `.build` binaries of `main` and of this branch in a test world, using `./bench --test`:

| page | `main` | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| `window.open` on a timer after load | 1 → 3 tabs (bench tab + the pop-up) | 1 → 2 (bench tab only) |
| `window.open` from a button, clicked with `tap` | 4 → 5 | 3 → 4 |
