items.title: Passwords: the keychain is asked only about Search's own items
items.author: burakbuilds
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
## What

Search reads passwords with `kSecAttrLabel: "Search"`, but `Vault.save` (the update) and `Vault.forget` (the delete) match on class, server and account only (`Vault.swift:119-123`, `:144-150`). That also matches internet passwords other apps keep for the same site. The usual example is `git-credential-osxkeychain`'s token for `github.com` under your GitHub username. Many developers' login keychains have one.

So if you save your GitHub web login in Search with the same username:
- `SecItemUpdate` targets git's item. macOS asks whether Search may use it. Say yes and the password replaces the token, and the item is relabelled "Search", so `git push` stops working. Say no and the update fails, so Search can't save the login at all.
- **Remove** in Settings › Passwords sends `SecItemDelete` for the same match, so it goes after git's item too.

## The change

- `save`'s lookup and `forget`'s delete now include the label, the same way reading already does.
- New and updated items are tagged `kSecAttrAuthenticationType = kSecAttrAuthenticationTypeHTMLForm`. That is accurate: they are web-form passwords. It also makes them a separate item from git's as far as the keychain is concerned. An internet password's uniqueness key is server, account, protocol, auth type, port and path. Without this tag, adding Search's item next to git's fails with `errSecDuplicateItem` whenever the protocol matches. I confirmed that; see below. It matters for #205, which starts writing the protocol.

## Testing

- `swift build`: builds with no new warnings.
- I tested on a throwaway keychain file (`security create-keychain`), not a real login keychain. It held a git-style item: `github.com`, `burak`, `htps`, label `github.com`. I ran Vault's logic against it: save, save again, then forget.

| step | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| start | `github.com=ghp_token` | `github.com=ghp_token` |
| save | `Search=web-password` (the token is gone) | `Search=web-password`, `github.com=ghp_token` |
| save again | `Search=web-password-2` | `Search=web-password-2`, `github.com=ghp_token` |
| forget | *(nothing left)* | `github.com=ghp_token` |

- On the same kind of keychain, with git's item present:
  - Search's item with no protocol (as today) adds fine.
  - With protocol `htps` it's refused as a duplicate.
  - With protocol `htps` plus the HTML-form auth type it adds fine.
- A real login keychain would show macOS's access prompt before the "before" column's overwrite. In the throwaway keychain the test process owns every item, so there's no prompt.

This touches the lines next to #205's change in `Vault.save`. Whichever lands second needs a trivial rebase, and I'm happy to do it.

items.title: Import bookmarks and history from Firefox and Zen
items.author: DagimAlemayehuu
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
## Summary

Search previously supported importing bookmarks, history, and passwords exclusively from Chromium-based browsers. Users switching from Gecko-based browsers such as Mozilla Firefox and Zen Browser were unable to bring over their existing browsing data.

This pull request adds support for importing bookmarks and browsing history from Firefox and Zen profiles on macOS.

## What changed

- `Sources/Search/Import.swift`:
  - Added `enum Mozilla` alongside `enum Chromium`.
  - Discovers profile folders for Firefox (`~/Library/Application Support/Firefox/Profiles/*`) and Zen (`~/Library/Application Support/zen/Profiles/*` and `Zen/Profiles/*`), sorted newest first by modification date.
  - Implemented `copyDatabaseWithWAL`: safely copies `places.sqlite` and `favicons.sqlite` along with `-wal` and `-shm` sidecars to an isolated temporary folder before reading with SQLite3 in read-only mode (`SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY`). This guarantees uncheckpointed transactions from active browser sessions are preserved without database locks.
  - Extracts browsing history from `moz_places` by querying `url`, `title`, `visit_count`, and `last_visit_date` (converting microsecond Unix timestamps to Apple reference dates).
  - Reconstructs bookmark hierarchies from `moz_bookmarks` and `moz_places` into `[Bookmark]`, preserving toolbar items, menu structures, and folders, while deduplicating entries across multiple profiles.
  - Extracts bookmark icons from `favicons.sqlite` when available.
  - Added unified `ImportSource` abstraction for browsers discovered across Chromium and Mozilla ecosystems.

items.title: Fix tab favicon host resolution and fallback (#181)
items.author: DagimAlemayehuu
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes #181.

Resolves an issue where tabs navigating across hosts could retain stale icons or receive icons from an asynchronous in-flight probe of a previous site (such as Meta AI wearing Google's G icon), and tabs on subdomains without explicit favicons (such as Swagger UI on an api. subdomain) remained stuck on a generic monogram letter 'A' instead of falling back to their own domain initial letter.

## What changed

- Sources/Search/Icons.swift:
  - Normalized host matching in Favicons.cached(_:) to check both bare and www. variants of the host, while keeping distinct subdomains isolated so they do not share cached icons across different origins.
  - Verified that a tab's current host still matches the target host before applying cached icons in Favicons.fetch(for:) completion blocks, avoiding stale icon assignment if the tab navigated during an async probe.
  - Resolved relative declared favicon hrefs against the page URL using URL(string:relativeTo:) so Swagger UI and relative favicon paths are properly recognized.
  - Included the browser's user agent in favicon download requests so sites that block automated requests (like Meta AI) serve their icons.
  - Prevented Sendable warning by capturing the cache directory before dispatching to the utility queue in Favicons.keep(_:for:).

- Sources/Search/Tab.swift:
  - Updated monogram to derive its letter from Vault.registrable(host) rather than naive string replacement of www., ensuring subdomain URLs (e.g. api.swagger.io) fall back to the site's domain initial letter ('S') rather than generic subdomain prefixes ('A').
  - Cleared icon to nil in adoptIcon() when address?.host() is missing or invalid.
  - Used lowercased host comparison in the URL observer so host changes consistently trigger icon adoption.

- Sources/Search/Browser.swift:
  - Updated decidePolicyFor to reset/adopt the favicon for nextHost as soon as a main frame navigation starts, preventing the previous host's icon from lingering while the new destination loads.
  - Allowed Favicons.shared.arrived to update tabs matching either bare or www. forms of the arriving host.

- CHANGELOG.md:
  - Added entry under ## Unreleased > ### Fixed crediting @olllayor.

## Test plan

- Authored reproduction script verifying:
  1. Monogram domain letter extraction for subdomains (api.swagger.io -> S, docs.github.com -> G, etc.).
  2. Relative favicon href resolution in Favicons.rank.
  3. Host checking in async evaluateJavaScript callback to prevent cross-host icon pollution.
  4. Host resolution for www and bare domain variants.
- Verified script failed before changes (exit code 1) and passed after implementation (exit code 0).
- Ran swift build and verified clean compilation (exit code 0) with zero new warnings.

items.title: iCloud Passwords pairs on the first code (Refs #17)
items.author: PeterTheMango
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Refs #17

## Problem

iCloud Passwords never paired in Search: every code you typed got a request for a new one. There were three causes, one commit each.

## Changes

1. **The worker's first message to Apple's helper was lost.** WebKit drops what a worker posts on a native port in its first moments. iCloud Passwords sends its hello then, and without it the helper never answers the pairing. The shim now holds those messages until the port is ready, then sends them in order.
2. **Helpers kept running.** When an extension reloads, is turned off or is removed, WebKit drops its native ports without calling their disconnect handler. Each restart left another helper running. `ExtensionNative.stopOrphans()` now stops the helpers whose ports are gone.
3. **Port messages arrived twice.** Messages posted as a `runtime.connect` port opens, between the popup and the worker, were delivered twice. This is WebKit's doing: it happens with the shim removed too. The shim now numbers messages on those ports and drops repeats. Content-script and native ports are left alone.

Each fix has its line under **Fixed** in `CHANGELOG.md`.

## Testing

All in a `--test` world. Apple's helper only runs under a notarized build, so I tested with a stand-in that runs the same SRP pairing.

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| First messages received by the host | 0 to 5 of 5 | 5 of 5, in order |
| Code typed into the popup | asked again, forever | pairs on the first try |
| Helpers after 3 reloads, then off and removed | one more each restart | 1, then 0 |
| Popup's state request | answered twice | answered once |

`swift build` adds no warnings.

**Not tested:** Apple's real helper. @driceroland, could you try this branch in your build? On a fresh launch, the first code should pair. Whichever way it goes, please reply with what happened (paired, asked again, or an error in the popup or the worker's console). That will show where to look next.

## Not in this PR

WebKit unloads an idle worker after about 2 minutes, even with a native port open. After that, iCloud Passwords asks for the code once more. Keeping the worker alive while a native port is open would be the follow-up.

items.title: Should Search block YouTube ads too, or is that a bridge too far?
items.author: ductan2
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
Search already blocks ads at the network level (`Shield.swift`): a compiled `WKContentRuleList` drops known ad/tracker domains before the request is even made — `doubleclick.net`, `googlesyndication.com`, and the rest. That works because those are third-party domains, separate from the page's own content.

YouTube doesn't play that way. Its video ads are stitched into the same stream and served from the same `googlevideo.com` domain as the actual video, so a domain-based blocklist can't tell the two apart without breaking playback entirely. Blocking it means something closer to what uBlock Origin / SponsorBlock-style extensions do: parsing YouTube's player response, skipping/removing ad segments, or hiding the ad UI with a page script — not a rule list.

## Questions to settle before building anything

- Is this in scope for Search itself, or something people should get via a Chrome extension (Search already supports those)?
- If in scope: server-side stream parsing (fragile, breaks whenever YouTube changes its player) vs. UI-level skip/hide (safer, less effective)?
- Default on, or a Settings toggle like the other blocking features (`Shield`, mute, etc.)?

Opening this to gauge interest and figure out the right approach before anyone writes code.

items.title: A video put full screen shows its picture, not black
items.author: StefanTodorov32
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
**What happened:** on YouTube (and any page using element full screen), pressing the video's full-screen button gave a black screen with the sound still playing. macOS 27, Search 1.0.1; still present on `main` at 1.0.2.

**Why:** WebKit enters element full screen by moving the page's `WKWebView` into a window of its own and leaving a placeholder view in the stage. In that same moment the page's `fullscreenchange` sets `tab.immersed`, the column / strip / bookmarks bar step aside, and the stage is laid out again. `StageView.settle()` runs on every layout: it removed WebKit's placeholder (not `wanted`) and, seeing `wanted.superview !== self`, took the web view back out of WebKit's full-screen window, leaving that window empty.

**Fix:** `settle()` leaves the page alone while `fullscreenState != .notInFullscreen`. WebKit puts the web view back where its placeholder was on the way out, and the next layout (the chrome coming back as `immersed` clears) sets its frame to the stage's bounds. `fullscreenState` is macOS 13+, so it's fine for the macOS 14 floor.

A line under **Unreleased › Fixed** in CHANGELOG.md.

**Tested:** `swift build` clean, no new warnings. Not yet run against a live video; would appreciate a check on your machine.

## Likely cause

items.author: farchanrifai
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
As in Dia: swipe the floating video into the side of the screen and it tucks away, leaving a sliver to bring it back by.

![Docking the floating video](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/farchanrifai/Search/pr-assets/pip-dock.gif)

## What it does

With **Flick the floating video to a corner** on (Settings › General, from #151):

- **Pull:** with the window against the left or right side, two fingers swiped at that side pull it with them, heavily (a third of the fingers' travel).
- **Dock:** let go past about 90 points and it slides off that side on its spring, leaving a 10-point sliver on screen.
- **Bounce:** let go short of that and it springs back out, a little past its place and back.
- **Bring it back:** a swipe towards the middle, a click on the sliver, or a mouse wheel's notch the other way returns it to where it was.
- Swipes anywhere else still flick to corners as before, and dragging still puts it anywhere.
- Closed while docked, it reopens where it was before docking, not as the sliver.

Since the window moves out from under the pointer as it's pulled, the fingers lifting can be delivered to whatever window is under the pointer instead; a pull that hasn't heard more for 0.2 s ends on its own, so it never sticks half out.

It rides on the existing flick switch rather than adding another; happy to give it its own if you'd prefer.

CHANGELOG gets its line under Unreleased › Added.

In my fork, by hand (the recording above). On this branch it builds.

items.title: Add AppleScript support for reading the current tab's URL
items.author: joshmedeski
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
Search's bundle has no scripting dictionary (`OSAScriptingDefinition`), so tools that read the front tab through osascript can't use it:

```
$ osascript -e 'tell application "Search" to return URL of current tab of front window'
syntax error: A property can't go after this identifier. (-2740)
```

Safari (`URL of current tab of front window`) and Chrome-family browsers (`URL of active tab of front window`) both support this. It's how launchers, Raycast/Alfred scripts, and CLI tools like [sesh](https://github.com/joshmedeski/sesh) (`sesh worktree connect --browser`) grab the current page.

A minimal sdef with `window` → `tabs` / `current tab` → `URL` and `name` would do it. Matching Safari's terms means existing scripts work with only the app name changed.

items.title: AppleScript can read the tabs: URL and name of the current tab (#232)
items.author: joshmedeski
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Closes #232.

Search had no scripting dictionary, so launchers, Raycast and Alfred scripts, and tools like [sesh](https://github.com/joshmedeski/sesh) (`sesh worktree connect --browser`) couldn't ask it for the page in front. Now it answers in Safari's words:

```
$ osascript -e 'tell application "Search" to return URL of current tab of front window'
https://www.wikipedia.org/
```

## What it does

- `Search.sdef` uses Safari's terms and four-letter codes: a `window` has `tabs` and a `current tab`, and a `tab` has a `URL` and a `name`. A Safari script works with only the app's name changed. Everything is read-only.
- It also declares the standard `count` command, because `repeat with t in tabs of front window` needs it.
- `Scripting.swift` gives the browser window's tabs to Cocoa Scripting. Tab references resolve back to the tab (`tab 2 of window id 402`). Other windows have no tabs, and the floating video panel isn't in the window list at all.
- `build.sh` copies the dictionary into `Resources` and sets `NSAppleScriptEnabled` and `OSAScriptingDefinition`.

A blank tab's `URL` and `name` are empty strings. Private tabs are listed too, as Safari does with private windows.

## Checked

Release build, run as a `SEARCH_PROBE` world, addressed by path with `osascript`:

- `URL` and `name` of `current tab of front window`, following tab switches
- `count of tabs of front window`
- `repeat with t in tabs of front window`
- `{name, URL} of tab 1 of window 1`
- `current tab of front window` itself → `tab 2 of window id 402`

`swift build` has no new warnings.

items.title: An ad-hoc build that cannot sign stops, rather than reporting a finished app
items.author: Hyp4tia
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
## What

`build.sh:161`, the no-certificate path that most builds take, signed with `2>/dev/null || true`. A signature that failed printed nothing and changed nothing: the script went on to `built: ...` and left behind a bundle macOS would refuse to open. `set -euo pipefail` is already on at the top of the script, so the `|| true` was the only thing between a failure and a stopped build. It is gone, and codesign's own words reach the person building instead of `/dev/null`.

The Developer ID path above it has no such guard, so the two halves agree now.

## Testing

- `./build.sh` on this branch: exit 0, `built: build/Search.app (1.0.2, build 202609241820)`, and `codesign -dv` reports the ad-hoc signature as before.
- I did not find a way to make ad-hoc signing fail on a healthy bundle, so the negative case is argued rather than shown: with `set -e` on and the guard gone, a failure exits non-zero.

## Not in here

`--deep` is deprecated by Apple for signing. The bundle carries no nested code today, so signing inside-out has nothing to gain yet; happy to do it as its own change if you would rather have it in place before a helper appears.

No CHANGELOG line: nothing a person using the app sees changes.

items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
## What

`Vault.all()` read every item's secret before the panel could draw. The keychain will list items or hand over one secret, not both in one call, so the list came back in one call and then `secret(host:user:)` ran once per row: on a Mac with a few hundred kept passwords that is a few hundred keychain round trips on the main path each time the panel opens, for rows that show a site and an account and nothing else.

The list is metadata only now, and a secret is read when one is asked for:

- `Vault.all()` returns `[Kept]` (site, account, last used, http or https) and makes no secret reads at all.
- `Vault.secret(of:)` is the way to one item's secret for the two places a password is wanted: the row's Show, and Copy. Both already ask the Mac who you are first, and Copy now says so if the read comes back empty.

`Kept` is a type of its own rather than a `Login` with an empty password on purpose: everything that writes a password or fills one into a page takes a `Login`, so a list row can never be handed on as though it held a secret. The compiler carried every use of the list over; only the panel and the list's own filter read from it. `Vault.logins(for:)` and `logins(matching:)`, which the fill path and the "is this one already kept?" check use, are unchanged and still read theirs.

## One thing changes on screen

The row's dots are a fixed ten now, where they were the password's length (6 to 12). A row cannot know the length without reading the secret, and a run of dots that spells out how long a password is is not worth keeping. Say the word if you would rather have the length back in the model; it would mean a read per row again.

## Testing

- `swift build` clean.
- Not driven by hand: Show and Copy need a kept item to read, and I was not going to put one in a keychain to try it. What the change does is statically checkable (`Vault.all()` no longer reaches `secret(host:user:)`, the panel's two actions do), and the compiler carried every list use over to `Kept`.
- A read that comes back empty leaves the row unmasked-free and logs the keychain status, as before; the panel itself stays quiet, where Copy announces it.

CHANGELOG: a line under Unreleased.

## Worth a look, not in here

`Browser.relist()` runs on the main thread and is called when the panel opens, and after saving, forgetting, taking another browser's store, or importing. It is one keychain list call now instead of one plus one per row, but on a very large drawer that single call is still made on the main thread.

items.author: isaiasroliveira
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry

items.body:
## Summary

Add optional, named tab groups to the sidebar and top tab bar. The feature is off by default in Settings > Tabs. A group starts from a tab's context menu, can be renamed, collapsed, reordered and ungrouped without closing its tabs, and disappears when its last tab leaves. Tabs can move through the menu or by dragging onto a group heading.

The sidebar heading uses secondary text and is shorter than a tab row; its chevron appears on hover. The top heading takes only the width of its name. A collapsed group shows just its name. Pinned and private tabs stay outside groups.

## Integration

Group membership, order and collapsed state are saved with each Space. The underlying tab order follows the displayed group order for keyboard navigation. The maintainer is handling the remaining integration work across Spaces, Move to Space, session compatibility, sleeping and private tabs, Peek, the tab switcher and the extensions tabs API.

## Validation

- `swift build` succeeds after rebasing on current `main`.
- Visually checked group headings in both tab layouts using an isolated test profile.
- Manual interaction checks for drag and drop and the broader integrations are still pending.

Related: #23, #68, #76.

items.title: fix(extensions): close popup instead of reopening on second click
items.author: kinnrai
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body: Clicking a pinned extension button while its popup is open can still close and immediately reopen it. The second click should leave it closed. Reproduced on Search 1.0.3 ([3482002](https://github.com/driceroland/Search/commit/3482002864db1e7639903f16d1ae840f04faea4c)) with Bitwarden 2026.8.0. Follow-up to #137. `popoverWillClose` can run during `leftMouseUp`, when `NSEvent.pressedMouseButtons` is already `0`. The guard added in #137 then returns without recording `closedByButton`, so the subsequent button action opens a new popup. The handler now uses `NSApp.currentEvent`, accepts either `leftMouseDown` or `leftMouseUp`, and checks the event's window and location against the popup's own button. This lets the existing `closes(_:)` logic consume the close record and prevent reopening. ## Reproduction 1. Use the top tab row and pin an extension with a popup, such as Bitwarden. 2. Click its button to open the popup. 3. Click the same button again. ## Before / after | Before | After | | --- | --- | | | | | The second click closes and immediately reopens the popup. | The second click leaves the popup closed; a third click opens it again. | ## Testing - Built both upstream [3482002](https://github.com/driceroland/Search/commit/3482002864db1e7639903f16d1ae840f04faea4c) and this branch ([a2ed99d](https://github.com/kinnrai/Search/commit/a2ed99d301bbdf75605eb1a964fe0eba99a48be6)) with `./build.sh debug`. - Compared them in separate test instances using the same Bitwarden version and mouse clicks at screen coordinates. The upstream build created a new popup page after the second click; the fixed build left no popup open. - Confirmed that a third click opens the popup again and Escape closes it.

items.title: fix(extensions): keep popups anchored after switching tab layouts
items.author: kinnrai
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body: After switching from the top tab row to the sidebar, a pinned extension's popup can open away from its button. It should stay attached to the pinned button in the new layout. Reproduced on Search 1.0.3 ([491f321](https://github.com/driceroland/Search/commit/491f3214063212fac176a7ad95467f0821040451)) with Bitwarden 2026.8.0. During the animated transition, the outgoing `Anchor` can receive `updateNSView` after the incoming view has registered itself in `makeNSView`. It overwrites `anchors[id]` with the outgoing view, which then disappears and leaves an empty weak reference. Opening the popup then falls back to another anchor instead of the pinned button. The anchor is now registered only in `makeNSView`, leaving `updateNSView` empty. This prevents an outgoing view from replacing the new layout's anchor, so the popup stays attached to its button. ## Reproduction 1. Use the top tab row and pin an extension with a popup, such as Bitwarden. 2. Click its button to open the popup, then click blank page space to close it. 3. Choose View → Show Tabs in Sidebar (⌘⇧S) and wait for the transition to finish. 4. Click the pinned button in the sidebar to open its popup again. ## Before / after | Before | After | | --- | --- | | | | | After switching to the sidebar, the popup opens away from its button. | After switching to the sidebar, the popup opens next to its button. | ## Testing - Built unmodified upstream [491f321](https://github.com/driceroland/Search/commit/491f3214063212fac176a7ad95467f0821040451) and this branch's source tree ([9531e2f](https://github.com/kinnrai/Search/commit/9531e2fb062e5996a6b7c5470cc0b2f7709c5089)) with `./build.sh debug`, with no additional compiler warnings. - Compared separate test instances using Bitwarden 2026.8.0. items.title: A folded sidebar comes out when the pointer overshoots the window's left edge
items.author: tomohiron907
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
With the sidebar folded, the way to get at the tabs is to move the pointer left until it reaches the window's edge. Today it has to *stop* on the edge for the sidebar to come out. That's easy when the window is flush with the screen's left edge, since the screen stops the pointer. When the window sits away from it, though, a hand reaching for the tabs almost always overshoots: the pointer sails past the edge onto whatever is to the left, the edge is never seen, and the sidebar stays folded. You then have to come back and land on a thin strip.

Other browsers with vertical tabs forgive this. In Zen Browser, for example, a collapsed sidebar opens even when the pointer overshoots the window's edge. This PR does the same in Search.

## What changes

- **Past the edge counts as the edge.** A pointer up to 48 pt beyond the window's left edge, beside the window (not above or below it), brings the sidebar out, just as if it had stopped on the edge.
- **Only when it came off the window.** This applies only to a pointer that has just left the window across its left edge. A pointer moving around over another app or the desktop to the left of the window, arriving from anywhere else, leaves the sidebar alone, so nothing pops out while you work next to Search.
- **Once out, a small overshoot doesn't put it back.** While the sidebar is out, going a little past the edge and coming back keeps it out, instead of folding it and bringing it out again.

Nothing changes when the sidebar is kept open, in the tab strip layout, or when the window is flush with the screen's edge (there's no room to overshoot).

## Implementation

All of it is in `Sources/Search/Fold.swift`:

- A new `overshoot` constant (48 pt) sets how far past the edge still counts.
- `pointer.crossing` records whether the pointer is over the window, or has just gone off its left edge from inside it. It's what tells a hand flung off the window apart from one that was already out there.
- The `beside` band (within `overshoot` of the edge and inside the window's height) is part of `over` while peeking, and arrives when `overshot` holds while folded.

There's also a CHANGELOG entry.

## Tested

I've tried each of the steps below by hand in a local build, and they behave as described.

1. Fold the sidebar and move the window well away from the screen's left edge.
2. Flick the pointer quickly to the left across the window's edge, going past it: the sidebar comes out.
3. With the sidebar out, go a little past the edge and come back: it stays out.
4. Move the pointer around in the space to the left of the window without starting inside it: the sidebar stays folded.

items.title: Floating video jerks on enter/exit — use WebKit's picture-in-picture instead?
items.author: Vedaant-Rajoo
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
## What happens

Floating a video (⌘⇧P, or switching tabs or apps) makes it jump in size. It first shows smaller than the black window, then grows to fill it. Landing it back in the tab does the same in reverse. It's most visible on YouTube.

Recordings on `main` (YouTube, 720×405 remembered window). The jerk shows at about 0.9 s in each:

Entering the float:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3c96f410-bb92-46f4-a676-1c4d65c27115

Landing back in the tab:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/075b8ea0-1777-485d-8de2-cf2905fd5655

## Why

`Float` moves the whole `WKWebView` into an `NSPanel` and stretches the video with `Isolate` CSS. Every enter and exit resizes the page, so WebKit's layout and YouTube's player lag behind the new window size for a moment:

- **Enter:** `Float.lift` builds `ground` at 440×247, but opens the panel at the remembered `float.frame`. Measured with a 720×405 window, the first frames fill only ~92% of the height, then fill.
- **Exit:** `land()` removes the `Isolate` CSS in the same pass that hands the page back to the stage. On YouTube the video briefly drops to 720×240 inside a 1180×728 viewport before settling.

Timing tweaks shrink this but can't remove it. Firefox, Zen and Chromium don't move the page at all; they pipe the video into a separate player window.

## A possible fix

The comment in `Float.swift` says WebKit won't allow picture-in-picture without a real click on the page. On macOS 27, calling the video's own `webkitSetPresentationMode('picture-in-picture')` from Search's injected JS does work without one. It needs one private preference, `_setAllowsPictureInPictureMediaPlayback:`, checked by name first, the same way `Muter` does it.

A prototype (native PiP first, Float as the fallback) measured:
- YouTube enter: page layout and video box unchanged across 40 samples; no jerk.
- Auto picture-in-picture on tab switch works.
- A video with `disablePictureInPicture` falls back to Float correctly.
- Closing the system PiP window clears Search's state, so ⌘⇧P works again.

## The trade-off (the decision this issue asks for)

The system PiP window belongs to macOS, not to Search. Going native loses what Float adds:
- flick to a corner (Settings › General)
- pinch to resize around the pointer
- the ±15 s skip buttons and the progress line
- the remembered window frame

macOS's window has its own behaviour instead: drag it, it snaps to corners, and it can be tucked off the edge of the screen.

Options:
1. Native by default, Float only as the fallback.
2. Native only when flicks are off.
3. Keep Float and fix its sizing: open at the video's `videoWidth:videoHeight`, and reveal the window only once the video fills it.

## Not yet verified

- macOS 14–26. Only tested on 27; the private preference may be missing on older WebKit, in which case it falls back to Float.

items.title: fix(site-info): prevent clipping in connection details
items.author: kinnrai
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body: Reproduced on Search 1.0.3 ([491f321](https://github.com/driceroland/Search/commit/491f3214063212fac176a7ad95467f0821040451)). With `https://github.com/`, Opening **Site Information… → Connection is secure** clips the explanation and buttons because the panel keeps the size of its initial page. It should resize to fit the connection details and shrink back when **Back** is clicked. SwiftUI can lay out the new content without calling the hosting view's `invalidateIntrinsicContentSize`, so the existing resize callback is missed. The hosting view now measures its fitting size after `layout()` and schedules the panel resize outside the layout pass, keeping its top edge below the address and skipping unchanged sizes. ## Reproduction 1. Open `https://github.com/`. 2. Right-click its tab and choose **Site Information…**. 3. Click **Connection is secure**. ## Before / after | Before | After | | --- | --- | | | | | The panel keeps its initial size, clipping the explanation and buttons. | The panel grows to show all content; **Back** restores its initial size. | ## Testing - Built this branch ([f1685a9](https://github.com/kinnrai/Search/commit/f1685a9164771728abe19f56438af683fb36a6cb)) with `./build.sh debug`, with no additional compiler warnings. - Checked **Back**, repeated navigation into the details, **Show Certificate…**, Escape, and dismissal by clicking outside.

items.title: Extension workers start again after a relaunch
items.author: sethmorton
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
Extensions with a popup (Bitwarden, Tampermonkey) spin for ever after Search is reopened.

**Cause.** WebKit keeps each extension's service-worker registration between launches and on macOS 26.4 never starts a kept one again. After a relaunch the worker answers nothing (`__searchPing` gets `undefined`), the popup's `runtime.connect` fails with "No runtime.onConnect listeners found", and `revive()` (unload + load) doesn't bring it back.

**Fix.** Drop service-worker registrations before extensions load, so each worker registers afresh. Extension storage (sign-ins, settings, scripts) lives elsewhere and stays.

**Cost.** WebKit lists no data records for extension origins, so sites' registrations go too; a site registers its own again on its next visit.

**Tested** in a copy of the app with its own bundle id (the real WebKit container, not an identifier store, which behaves differently), with Bitwarden and Tampermonkey installed:
- main, relaunched twice: both workers answer `undefined` both times
- this branch, relaunched twice: both answer `pong`, and both popups render (Bitwarden's login, Tampermonkey's menu)

+15 lines.

items.title: Fix editing a tab's address dropping the port, query, #fragment and http:// (Return reloaded the wrong page)
items.author: 57uart
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Clicking a tab to edit its address filled the field with `Address.pretty`, the short label a tab wears before its page has a title: host and path only. Pressing Return then went to that shorter address instead of the page:

- **Ports were dropped.** `http://127.0.0.1:8767/images.html` showed as `127.0.0.1/images.html`, and Return opened port 80.
- **Queries and fragments were dropped.** A search results page showed as `google.com/search` and reloaded without the search.

items.title: An extension whose worker WebKit kept a stale copy of starts again
items.author: tomohiron907
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
## What happened

Vimium worked right after it was installed, then at some point stopped answering its keys. It never came back. Reloading tabs, turning it off and on, reinstalling it, restarting Search and restarting the Mac all left it dead. Its content script logged `response.isEnabledForUrl undefined`, and the worker check restarted it ("its worker stopped answering") without effect. macOS 15.7.2.

## Why

WebKit keeps each extension's service worker registered from one launch to the next, along with the scripts it fetched then. These live in `ServiceWorkers/ServiceWorkerRegistrations-8.sqlite3` and `Scripts/V1` under the website data store. WebKit may start that copy rather than what is on disk now. Here the registration held a copy from an older build of the shim, and that worker was dead. Reinstalling, reloading and restarting all started the same stale copy again, and so did the unload and load in `Extensions.revive`.

Moving the store's `ServiceWorkers` folder aside fixed it on the spot.

## The fix

`Extensions.start` clears service worker registrations once at launch, before any extension loads. It only does so when what the extensions would run has changed since the last launch.

- The fingerprint is `ExtensionShims.version` plus each installed extension's id and version. It is kept in settings under `extensions.workers`.
- Installing an extension (`admit`), reloading one (`reload`) and restarting a dead worker (`revive`) forget the fingerprint. The version alone doesn't show that anything changed in those cases, so the next launch clears regardless.

Why at launch, and for all extensions at once:
- `dataRecords(ofTypes: [WKWebsiteDataTypeServiceWorkerRegistrations])` lists no records for extension origins, so one extension's registration can't be cleared on its own.
- `removeData(ofTypes:modifiedSince: .distantPast)` does clear them, but it also stops the workers that are running. Launch, before loading, is the one moment that costs nothing.

**Trade-off:** websites' service worker registrations go too at those launches. They are registered again on the next visit. Their other data (cookies, storage, caches) is untouched.

## How it was tested

- Reproduced in the test world (`./fresh.sh`, `./bench --test`):
  1. Launched once with the fix, and checked that Vimium and Dark Reader both answered the worker ping.
  2. Quit, copied the stale `ServiceWorkers` folder from the broken install into the test store, and relaunched without the fingerprint change. Vimium didn't answer, logged `response.isEnabledForUrl undefined`, and the revive didn't bring it back.
  3. The revive forgot the fingerprint, so on the next launch the clear ran. Vimium and Dark Reader both answered, with no further worker-check errors.
- Checked by hand in the real install: Vimium's keys work again.
- `swift build` introduces no new warnings.

This may also be behind other extensions that break until their data is wiped. Dark Reader behaved the same in the test world. The Vimium C item on the roadmap could be worth another look with this in, though I haven't verified that.

items.body:
**What I did:** I had a few tabs open, one of them Reddit (reddit.com/r/all), with a different tab in front. Then I left Search alone and later put it in the background.

**What I expected:** Search to go close to idle, since nothing on screen was changing.

**What happened:** Search's app process sat at about 20% CPU, with Activity Monitor energy impact around 20–24, the whole time, including in the background. When I closed tabs one at a time, it dropped to almost 0 the moment I closed the Reddit tab. Reddit's page never finishes loading as far as WebKit is concerned, so that tab's loading ring never stops spinning.

When I sampled the app, the main thread was busy in `NSHostingView.layout()` and SwiftUI's display list render every frame. The ring in `TabBar.swift` is a `repeatForever` SwiftUI animation, and while it runs, the whole window's view tree gets laid out and redrawn every frame.

**macOS:** 27.0, on an M4 Max MacBook Pro.

I have a fix ready and will open a PR for it.

items.title: A loading tab's ring turns without redrawing the window
items.author: AxxzyWasTaken
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Closes #268.

A tab that never finishes loading, like Reddit, kept Search at about 20% CPU the whole time it was open, even in the background. The cause was the loading ring. It was a SwiftUI animation that never ends (`repeatForever`), and I found it was making the main thread lay out and redraw the window's whole view tree every frame.

I replaced it with a small `NSView` backed by a `CAShapeLayer` and a `CABasicAnimation`. It looks the same: the same arc, line width, colour, speed and direction, and it still follows light and dark mode. The render server turns it, so the app itself does nothing while it spins.

## What I measured

On my M4 Max MacBook Pro, with a Wikipedia tab in front and a Reddit tab behind it still loading, I measured Activity Monitor energy impact for Search's app process:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Round 1 | 22–24 | 0–0.3 |
| Round 2 | 19 | 0–2 |

Then I opened six busy sites in the background (YouTube, Reddit, The Verge, GitHub, BBC, CNN) and measured all of Search's processes together:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Idle | 33–34 | 16–21 |
| YouTube playing | 36–41 | 17–18 |
| Search in the background | 35–39 | 17–18 |

Scrolling was about the same either way, since that cost is WebKit drawing the page.

## Notes

- Every place that used `Ring` gets the new one without changes: tabs, the sidebar, extensions, passwords, settings and welcome.
- I checked it by eye in dark mode. It's a clean ring, it turns, and nothing is clipped. I haven't looked at light mode yet, but the colour is resolved against the view's appearance whenever that changes.
- It builds with no new warnings. I added a CHANGELOG line under Fixed.

items.title: Scrolling costs Search's app process about 2.5× what Safari's does
items.author: AxxzyWasTaken
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
**What I did:** I scrolled a long, plain text page in Search, then the same page in Safari, with both windows the same size.

**What I expected:** Search to use about the same energy as Safari, since the page is drawn by the same WebKit.

**What happened:** Search's app process used about 25 energy impact in Activity Monitor while scrolling, against about 10 for Safari. All of Search's processes together came to about 33, against 19 for Safari. WebKit's own processes cost the same in both, so the difference was all in Search's app.

When I sampled the app, much of the main thread was going to the `officeForms` message handler (`FormRelay` in `Forms.swift`), and to SwiftUI redrawing the window. While a page scrolls, the sign-in script calls `caret()` on every frame. That sends a `focus` message even when there's no sign-in box and nothing has changed. Each message sets `tab.typing`, and because that's a published value, the tab redraws every time, even when the value stays the same.

**macOS:** 27.0, on an M4 Max MacBook Pro.

I have a fix ready and will open a PR for it.

items.title: Scrolling doesn't report the caret every frame
items.author: AxxzyWasTaken
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Closes #270.

While a page scrolls, the sign-in script told the app where the caret was on every frame, so the saved-accounts list could follow the box it hangs from. It sent the same answer each time even with no sign-in box anywhere near the caret, and each message set `tab.typing`, which redrew the tab.

I changed two things in `Forms.swift`:

- **In the page:** `caret()` remembers what it last sent. When it's called from a scroll and nothing has changed, it doesn't send anything. Focus, blur and mouseup still always send, same as before.
- **In the app:** `tab.typing` is only set when the value actually changes.

If the caret is in a sign-in box, its position changes as the page scrolls, so the message still goes out and the accounts list still follows it.

## What I measured

I made a long plain-text page that scrolls itself and ran it in Search and in Safari with the same window size on my M4 Max MacBook Pro. These are Activity Monitor energy impact numbers:

| | Search before | Search after | Safari |
|---|---|---|---|
| App process while scrolling | 25 | 12 | 10 |
| All of the browser's processes while scrolling | 33 | 21 | 19 |
| Page standing still | 0.1 | 0.6 | 1.5–3 |

WebKit's own processes cost the same before and after. The rest of the cost of scrolling is WebKit drawing the page, same as in Safari.

## Notes

- It builds with no new warnings. I added a CHANGELOG line under Fixed.
- I haven't yet checked on a real sign-in page that the accounts list still follows the box while scrolling. By the logic above it should, but I've only measured the power side so far.

items.title: The Web Inspector comes back with its tab
items.author: ductan2
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
With the Web Inspector docked, switching to another tab and back left the page short above an empty space, black or white depending on the theme, and the inspector gone.

**Why:** `StageView.settle()` takes out everything that isn't the page on show, including the inspector WebKit docked beside the previous page. Back on that tab, only the page was re-added; WebKit still thought its inspector was docked and cut the page down to make room for it.

**Fix:** when a page leaves the stage, `show(_:)` keeps its inspector view aside, keyed weakly by the page (`NSMapTable`, so a closed tab's entry goes with it). When the page comes back with its inspector still open, `settle()` puts the view back beside it and sets the page to full size, which WebKit then lays out with the inspector at the stage's current size. This also stops one tab's inspector staying on screen beside another tab's when both have one open.

**Test:** open the inspector (⌥⌘I) on a page, switch to another tab, switch back — the inspector is there and the page fills the rest. Also: resize the window while on the other tab, and have the inspector open on two tabs at once.

items.title: The swipe's disc becomes a drop drawn out of the edge
items.author: nipuntal
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body: The swipe back and forward draws a drop out of the edge you pull from. Its leading edge is exactly under the fingers; its body trails on a spring, so it stretches as it goes, squashes when they stop short and wobbles for a moment after. While it is close to the edge a neck joins the two, and the neck snaps at the point the swipe is armed. Turn back and it goes back in the same way. On macOS 26 it is Liquid Glass: the edge and the drop are two pieces of clear glass in one container, which the system flows together while they are close, over a soft shadow of the same shape and an arrow that comes into focus as the swipe arms. Before macOS 26, and with an Xcode older than 26, the edge and the drop are drawn as one blurred shape cut back to a hard one, in white, with the arrow over it. Fixed on the way: - Only the page's first word on a swipe counts. Its later ones were read too, so turning back on a page with anywhere to scroll that way — most pages a pixel wider than the window — made the disc vanish. - A pinched-in page pans whatever its style says; one that hid its sideways overflow read as having nowhere to go, and went back. - No sideways rubber-banding: it was kept for WebKit's own swipe, which this replaced, and only dragged the page off its edge. - Which way is back is read from the fingers, not the content, so it is right with natural scrolling off too. - The swipe has an object of its own (Pulling), watched by the drop alone. Published on the tab, it redrew everything watching the tab with every event: the page and the tab's own button, 58 times each in one short swipe. `./bench pull` can turn back before lifting and reports the drop as the fingers lift; `./bench magnify` pinches a page from a test run.

Two problems with downloads, on Search 1.0.2, macOS 26.6.1.

### A download link that opens in a new tab leaves the tab behind

**What I did:** clicked a download link that opens in a new tab, such as an attachment on Brightspace (`https://purdue.brightspace.com/d2l/le/dropbox/…/DownloadAttachment?fid=…`).

**Expected:** the file downloads and the new tab closes, as in Safari, Chrome and Brave.

**What happens:** the file downloads, but the tab stays, holding the file's address. Opening that tab again, now or after the session comes back, downloads the file again.

The tab's address is set when the link opens it (`setAddressOptimistically`). The navigation then becomes a download and never commits, so the address is never replaced, and waking or reviving the tab loads it again.

### The download button on a PDF does nothing

**What I did:** opened a PDF in a tab and pressed the download button in the bar at the bottom of the page (zoom out, zoom in, Preview, download).

**Expected:** the PDF is saved, as in Safari.

**What happens:** nothing.

WebKit hands that button to the UI delegate through the private `_webView:saveDataToFile:suggestedFilename:mimeType:originatingURL:` (`WebPageProxy::savePDFToFileInDownloadsFolder` → `UIDelegate::UIClient::saveDataToFileInDownloadsFolder`), and returns without doing anything when the delegate doesn't answer it. Search's doesn't. The Preview button works because WebKit handles it itself.

items.title: A tab opened only to download a file closes once the file is on its way
items.author: Aaditya2605
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Part of #284: a download link's new tab. The other half, the PDF bar's download button, is #290.

When a navigation becomes a download in a tab that has never committed a page (its back-forward list is empty, or holds only `about:blank`), the tab forgets the address it was given and closes, as in Safari and Chrome. If it was in front and a page opened it, that page is selected again. A pinned tab is left alone, and a window's only tab stays as a new tab instead of closing the window. Forgetting the address first also keeps it out of ⇧⌘T.

The address was set when the link opened the tab (`setAddressOptimistically`); the navigation became a download and never committed, so nothing replaced it, and waking or reviving the tab loaded it again.

### Tested

On macOS 26.6.1, in a hidden test world driven with `./bench`, against a local page:

- A `target=_blank` link to a `Content-Disposition: attachment` response: the file is saved, the new tab is gone, and the opener is in front again. With the fix turned off, the tab stays with the file's address, and selecting it again downloads the file a second time.
- The same link without `target`: the page stays where it was. A PDF link with `target=_blank`: its tab stays.
- A leftover download tab restored from the session downloads its file one last time, then closes.

`swift build` with no new warnings. #283 changes `Browser.swift` and `Tab.swift` too; the two don't overlap, but whichever lands second may need a small rebase.

items.title: Scrolling is smoother: a frame of a scroll no longer redraws the window
items.author: teh33
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Every frame of a scroll wrote the page's position to `Tab.reading` — `@Published`
on a tab the row, the helm and the page's own host all observe — so each frame
redrew all of them on the main thread, the one WebKit's layer commits wait on.
It now writes to a `Reading` object only the fill watches, so a frame redraws one
rectangle. (That also means turning *Show how far you've read* off could never
have helped: `@Published` fires before anything reads the setting.)

The caret's position is reported on the same beat, so `typing` is now written
only when it changes, and the caret is only followed while something on the page
is actually being typed into. `onScroll` was assigned nowhere, so the y delta and
`lastY` it fed every frame are gone.

**Verification.** Test world (`SEARCH_PROBE`, `SEARCH_MEASURE`), same page, same
scroll script, 272 frames and 6800 px scrolled, window frontmost: about 42% of one
core before, about 6% after.

The forms half is the part worth a close look: a sign-in box inside an iframe is
the case to try.

Part of #284: the PDF half. The other half, a download link's new tab, is #285.

`Browser` answers WebKit's private `_webView:saveDataToFile:suggestedFilename:mimeType:originatingURL:`, the call behind the download button in the bar over a PDF. WebKit returns without doing anything when the UI delegate doesn't answer it (`UIDelegate::UIClient::saveDataToFileInDownloadsFolder`), which is why the button did nothing; the Preview button works because WebKit handles that one itself. WebKit's own test for this call is `TEST(WebKit, SaveDataToFile)` in TestWebKitAPI's `UIDelegate.mm`.

The PDF goes where any download goes: the downloads folder, or a save panel when Settings › Downloads asks, and into the Downloads list. Choosing the place and keeping the record move into two helpers shared with `WKDownload`'s delegate.

### Tested

On macOS 26.6.1:

- A standalone WKWebView with a delegate declared exactly as here, the button pressed the way WebKit's test presses it (`_performActionForControl:` with `arrow.down.circle`): the call arrives with the PDF's bytes, `doc.pdf`, `application/pdf` and its address.
- In Search, in a test world driven with `./bench`: the same press saves `doc.pdf`, byte for byte the server's, and lists it in Downloads.

items.title: More than one window: ⌘N, tear-off tabs, and dragging tabs between them
items.author: olllayor
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
## Why

Closes #247, closes #230, closes #72.

#247 asks for a second window, #230 for ⌘N and tearing a tab off, and #72 for dragging tabs into a new window and between windows. Those are one feature. Search has been a single-window app on purpose; this change keeps one session and lets that session live on more than one screen.

## Scope

- `WindowModel` owns one window's tab row, selection, omnibox, and find. `Browser` keeps what windows share (prefs, history, bookmarks, downloads, extensions, spaces) and the registry of windows. `Browser.key` replaces `Browser.front` and `Links.window`.
- File › New Window and ⌘N call `Browser.open()`. Each window draws from its own model.
- `TabTransfer` carries a dragged tab. Pull a tab clear of its row and it tears off (`WindowModel.detach`). Drop it on another window's row and it joins that one (`take` / `move`). Same `WKWebView`, no reload. A tab a page opens stays in the window that asked.
- A session file holds every window's row. A file from before decodes as one window.
- Closing the last blank tab closes that window. Tearing off the only tab replaces the window instead of leaving it empty. Sleep still keeps any window's on-screen tab awake.

Pins stay in the main strip. One floating video app-wide stays.

## Tradeoffs

A full `Browser` per window would isolate windows completely and fork every shared path (history, downloads, extensions). This keeps one profile and splits only window chrome. Two windows can sit in the same space and hold different rows; `Spaces.current` is gone.

PR #184 (detach one tab into a companion panel) is superseded for tear-off tabs.

## Blast Radius

Every view that drew the tab row now takes `WindowModel`. Session format gains a window list with a legacy decode. Risk is in restore and in empty-window close; single-window use should feel unchanged.

## Verification

`swift build` and `./bench --test` succeed on this branch with full verification of ⌘N cascading, ⌘W/⌘T key routing, and cross-window tab dragging.

items.title: Add standalone site apps from the Tabs menu
items.author: martonnagy
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
Pages kept open all day, such as Hacker News, can now have a small app of their own. **Tabs → Add to Dock…** asks for a name, creates an app in the user's Applications folder with the cached site icon, and opens it independently of Search.

The dialog explains the final **Options → Keep in Dock** step. macOS does not expose a public API to pin another app automatically; this does not edit Dock preferences or use Safari's private web-app APIs.

### Implementation

- A small `SearchSite` executable is built and embedded by `build.sh`. Each generated app carries only that WebKit host, with its own bundle identity and persistent website data. No new dependencies, browser engine, icon requests, or copies of Search's profile.
- Back, Forward, Home, Reload, standard editing shortcuts, file inputs, JavaScript dialogs, and Open in Search are available. Closing the window keeps the page alive for a Dock reopen; quitting and relaunching starts at the saved page.
- Creation is disabled for private tabs and non-HTTP(S) pages. Names and URLs are validated, plist values are serialized as data, staging is cleaned up, existing apps are preserved, and code signing runs with separate arguments before installation.
- The feature only acts when selected. README and Unreleased changelog explain the workflow and limits.

Generated apps are signed locally, not separately notarized or automatically updated. WebKit updates with macOS; recreate an app to update its host. These are simple site viewers: Search extensions, saved passwords, ad blocking, downloads, notifications, camera/microphone, and scripted popup login flows are outside this change.

### Validation

- Debug and release SwiftPM builds passed using the installed macOS 26.5 SDK; no new source warnings. This machine's default macOS 27 Command Line Tools SDK fails even on unmodified upstream due to a missing SwiftUI macro plugin, so builds used `--sdk …/MacOSX26.5.sdk --build-system native`.
- `./build.sh release` assembled the app and helper; ad-hoc signatures verified. The local Documents file provider adds Finder metadata to app folders, so that metadata was removed from the test build before final signing.
- `./scripts/check-site-apps.sh` passed: URL/name validation, long Unicode names, literal shell/XML-looking input, unique identities, valid signatures, collision preservation, and cleanup. `git diff --check` passed.
- UI tested in an isolated Search profile: Tabs menu and naming dialog, creation and launch of Hacker News with its icon, navigation, repeated close/reopen retaining the page, independent launch with Search closed, and disabled creation from a loaded private tab. The generated app was also kept in the Dock successfully.

items.title: ⌘← and ⌘→ move the caret in a text box inside a frame
items.author: Aaditya2605

⌘← and ⌘→ went back and forward in the tab's history while the caret was in a text box inside a frame, such as a comment box embedded from another site. The page was left, and what was typed there was lost.

The shortcut already stands aside while you type, but it learns that from the page's own script (`typing`), which misses a click straight into a frame and can't look into another site's frame at all. The web view's `inputContext` is there only while the caret is in something editable, in any frame, so the shortcut now stands aside while it is there too. The same check #144 uses for ⌘⇧V.

### Tested

On macOS 26.6.1, in a test world (`SEARCH_PROBE`):

- MDN's `<textarea>` page, reached from another page, in the text box of Examples › Basic example (a frame): ⌘← and ⌘→ move the caret to the start and end of the line, and the tab stays on the page. Before, the tab went back to the page before.
- Outside a text box, ⌘← and ⌘→ still go back and forward.

`swift build -c release` with no new warnings.

items.title: ⌘N opens a new window, ⇧⌘N a private one
items.author: Aaditya2605
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
A smaller take on more than one window, next to #291. #291 does more: tearing a tab off, dragging tabs between windows, and every window back after a restart. This one is +322 −109 in 8 files, and adds two things #291 doesn't have: private windows, and windows listed in the Dock's menu and the Window menu. Whichever way you go, the two notes under "Also for #291" apply there too.

Part of #230 and #247 (⌘N). Not #72: no tab is dragged out.

## What it does

- **⌘N** opens a new window with its own tabs, and the same sign-ins, history, bookmarks and settings as the first.
- **⇧⌘N** opens a private window. Its tabs share one `WKWebsiteDataStore.nonPersistent()`, so a sign-in carries from tab to tab, and all of it goes when the window closes. Nothing of it is in the history or the session. **This moves ⇧⌘N** from New Private Tab, which stays in the File menu without a shortcut. If ⇧⌘N should stay on the private tab, it's two lines in `App.swift`.
- The first window is the one it always was: it restores yesterday, extensions and the bench start with it, and it is the only one whose tabs are saved. The others are just more of it (`Windows.swift`).
- Menu commands act on the window in front (`Windows.acting`). Each window's key monitor answers only keys pressed in that window, so ⌘T opens one tab, not one per window. The small window's keys still come first.
- Links from other apps, and ⌘O from the small window, still go to the first window, never into a private one.
- Each window goes by its tab on screen in the Dock's menu and the Window menu, as in Safari. The title bar still shows nothing.

## Also for #291

- SwiftUI sets `isExcludedFromWindowsMenu = true` on a `Window` scene, so the first window is never in the Window menu or the Dock's menu. With two windows open, only the second is listed. Setting it back to `false` in `dress(_:)` fixes it. #291 keeps `Window("Search", id: "browser")`, so it has the same gap.
- Every window is titled "Search" until something names it, so two windows can't be told apart there. Here the title follows the active tab: on selection, and when the tab's title or address arrives (read after the change, since `@Published` sends before it).

## Tested

On macOS 26.6.1, in a test world (`SEARCH_PROBE`), by hand:

- ⌘N and ⇧⌘N open windows. ⌘T and ⌘W act only in the window in front.
- A private window's sites are not in History after it closes.
- The Dock's menu lists every window by its tab, with a check on the one in front, and follows a tab change.
- The small window for links from other apps, with a private window in front: the link opens in the small window. ⌘O moves it into the first window. Escape and ⌘W close only the small window.

`swift build -c release` succeeds. This and #291 both rework `App.swift` and `Browser.swift`, so only one of them can go in as it is.

items.title: Right-clicking a link says "Open Link in New Window", but it opens a new tab
items.author: AxxzyWasTaken

**What I did:** I right-clicked a link on a page.

**What I expected:** An "Open Link in New Tab" option, like other browsers have.

**What happened:** The menu offers "Open Link", "Open Link in New Window", "Download Linked File" and "Copy Link". There's no "New Tab" option, so at first I thought Search couldn't open a link in a new tab from the right-click menu. When I picked "Open Link in New Window", it actually opened the link in a new tab and switched to it. So the feature works, but the label is wrong.

That item is WebKit's own, `WKMenuItemIdentifierOpenLinkInNewWindow`. Search turns a new-window request into a new tab in `Browser`'s `createWebViewWith`, but it never renames the menu item to match.

**macOS:** 27.0, on an M4 Max MacBook Pro.

I have a fix ready and will open a PR for it.

items.title: Back, forward and reload before the tabs, and a Speed Dial as the home page — two small PRs, off by default
items.author: Guitaraholic
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
Two goals on the roadmap under "Drice's call": **Toolbar buttons on the left** and **Home page or home button**. I have both built locally, on top of 1.0.3, as two pull requests that stack. Opening this first, as CONTRIBUTING asks, before either goes up.

## 1. Toolbar (first PR)

Settings › Tabs gets a Toolbar card with three switches, all off:

- **Back, forward and reload on the left** — before the tabs, beside the window's traffic lights. Hidden in sidebar mode, where they already sit there.
- **Show the Bookmarks button**
- **Show the Extensions button** — pinned extensions and the Bookmarks menu stay as they are.

With all three off the layout is byte-for-byte what upstream draws today. About 3.4 KB of code: the release build grows by 80 bytes. It sits on top of #209's wider helm spacing.

## 2. Speed Dial (second PR, on top of the first)

The roadmap goal is a home page or home button. I've read that as "somewhere to start from" rather than "a URL to load", so this is a native page — AppKit, no web view, no network — of bookmarked sites as tiles, each with a preview taken the last time you were there. It never loads a site just for a thumbnail.

- Opened from a grid button that rides with back/forward/reload, and/or **New tabs open Speed Dial**. Both off; until one is on there is no menu item, setting row or Privacy row.
- Tiles are bookmarks. A typed "Add Address…" is filed as a bookmark in a Speed Dial folder. Up to 24; previews at most 480×300, 128 KiB each.
- Reorder from a tile's right-click menu or ⌥⌘←/→. Right-click a tab › Add to Speed Dial; Bookmarks › Add This Page to Speed Dial.
- Settings › Privacy › Speed Dial › Clear removes previews (bookmarks stay); Clear History does too.
- Reached through a local about:blank marker, so Back returns to the page you came from; pages cannot navigate to it.
- Recently Closed under the tiles, hidden in private tabs.

Deliberately not in it: a home-URL setting (the dial *is* the home), a second source of tiles, drag-and-drop, and anything from private or automation tabs. About 84 KB on its own.

## Where your call matters

1. Is a Speed Dial the right answer to "home page or home button", or would you rather the plainer thing — a home URL and a button that loads it? Happy to shelve PR 2 if so.
2. Naming: "Speed Dial" is Opera's word. "Start Page" or "Home" if you'd prefer something less borrowed.
3. Tests: I have a small set covering tile order, bookmark filing and preview limits. The repo has no Tests/ today; do you want them in the PR or left out?

items.title: Toolbar: back, forward and reload before the tabs, and the Bookmarks and Extensions buttons optional
items.author: Guitaraholic
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Part of #297 · Roadmap: "Toolbar buttons on the left" (Drice's call)

## Why

A goal on the roadmap is back, forward and reload on the left with the tabs across the top, where Safari and most browsers put them. Once the row is being rearranged, the other two buttons at its far end are worth making optional too: the Bookmarks menu and the bookmarks bar already reach the bookmarks, and pinned extensions already sit in the row.

## What it does

Settings › Tabs gets a card of three switches, all off:

- **Back, forward and reload on the left.** With tabs across the top, the three buttons move before the tabs, beside the window's buttons. Hidden while "Tabs in a sidebar" is on, since the sidebar already has them there.
- **Show the Bookmarks button.** The Bookmarks menu and the bookmarks bar stay either way.
- **Show the Extensions button.** Pinned extensions stay in the row; Settings › Extensions still manages them.

With all three off, the row is exactly what it is today.

| Today | Navigation on the left | Left, Bookmarks and Extensions buttons hidden |
|---|---|---|
| ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Guitaraholic/Search/fd5375ffe9c2c5229232e4f6360bd0bdc2607741/speed-dial/pr1-1-default.png) | ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Guitaraholic/Search/fd5375ffe9c2c5229232e4f6360bd0bdc2607741/speed-dial/pr1-2-left.png) | ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Guitaraholic/Search/fd5375ffe9c2c5229232e4f6360bd0bdc2607741/speed-dial/pr1-3-left-trimmed.png) |

![The Toolbar card in Settings › Tabs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Guitaraholic/Search/fd5375ffe9c2c5229232e4f6360bd0bdc2607741/speed-dial/pr1-4-settings.png)

## How it works

- `TabBar` draws the `Helm` before the tabs when asked, and after them otherwise. A `leading` width accounts for it wherever the row already measures itself: the drag strip, the tab widths and the field a tab becomes when it is edited. With the switch off `leading` is zero, so every width is upstream's.
- The buttons at the far end are measured, as before. Zero is now a real measurement, for when every one of them is switched off.
- `BookmarkDoor` is one view for the bookmarks button and its popover; `TabBar` and `SideBar` each had a copy.
- `ExtensionSlot` takes `showMenu`; pinned extension buttons are drawn either way.

## Try it

1. Settings › Tabs, with "Tabs in a sidebar" off: the Toolbar card is below the others.
2. Turn on "Back, forward and reload on the left", then open, close, pin and rename tabs. Nothing runs under the buttons.
3. Turn on the sidebar: the placement switch goes; the sidebar is unchanged.
4. Turn off the Bookmarks and Extensions buttons in each layout. The menu, the bar and pinned extensions still work.

## Size and build

- Release build, `-Osize`, stripped: +80 bytes on 1.0.3.
- `swift build`: no new warnings.
- Rebased on 1.0.3, after #209: the reserved widths use the helm's new 4-point spacing.

## For review

With the Extensions button hidden, an unpinned extension's popup has no button to hang from and opens from the window's corner. Pinning it puts it back. Happy to keep an invisible anchor instead if you'd rather.

---

items.title: Speed Dial: your bookmarked sites as tiles, from a button or every new tab
items.author: Guitaraholic
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
Part of #297 · Builds on #298: until that merges, this diff shows its commit too; the Speed Dial change is the last commit · Roadmap: "Home page or home button" (Drice's call)

## Why

A goal on the roadmap is a home page or a home button. A home URL is one more thing to set and gives you one page. What people usually want from Home is somewhere to start from: the handful of sites they go to every day. Speed Dial is that, built from bookmarks you already have, drawn natively, and never loading a site just to show it.

## What it does

![Speed Dial, with previews from pages visited](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Guitaraholic/Search/fd5375ffe9c2c5229232e4f6360bd0bdc2607741/speed-dial/pr2-1-dial-light.png)

- **Tiles are bookmarks**, up to 24, in an order you choose. A tile shows a small preview of the page from the last time you were on it; until then, the site's first letter.
- **Open it** from a grid button beside reload, which rides with back, forward and reload wherever the first PR puts them. It is highlighted while you're on the dial. Or have every new tab open on it. Tabs › Speed Dial works too.
- **Add a site** from the + tile (type an address, or pick a bookmark), from a tab's right-click menu, or with Bookmarks › Add This Page to Speed Dial. An address you type is filed as a bookmark in a "Speed Dial" folder, so the main list stays tidy.
- **Arrange it** from a tile's right-click menu (Rename, Move Earlier, Move Later, Move to Start, Move to End, Refresh Preview from Open Page, Remove) or with ⌥⌘← and ⌥⌘→ on a tile, adding ⇧ for the ends. Plain ⌘← is still Back. Removing a tile keeps its bookmark.
- **Recently Closed** sits under the tiles, except in a private tab.
- **Back** returns to the page you were on: the dial is an entry in the tab's own history.

| Dark | Nothing on it yet |
|---|---|
| ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Guitaraholic/Search/fd5375ffe9c2c5229232e4f6360bd0bdc2607741/speed-dial/pr2-2-dial-dark.png) | ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Guitaraholic/Search/fd5375ffe9c2c5229232e4f6360bd0bdc2607741/speed-dial/pr2-3-dial-empty.png) |

## Off until it's turned on

Two switches in Settings › Tabs, both off. Until one is on, nothing of Speed Dial shows anywhere: no menu item, no right-click item, no Privacy row.

![Settings › Tabs, with the toolbar card from the first PR](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Guitaraholic/Search/fd5375ffe9c2c5229232e4f6360bd0bdc2607741/speed-dial/pr2-4-settings.png)

## Privacy and the network

- Nothing is fetched. A preview is taken from a page you loaded yourself, never from a load of its own.
- Private and automation tabs never give a preview, add a tile or appear in Recently Closed.
- Clear History also removes the previews; the tiles stay. Settings › Privacy › Speed Dial › Clear resets the dial and leaves the bookmarks.
- A tile only ever opens an http or https address, even if its bookmark is changed later (an extension can edit bookmarks).

![Settings › Privacy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Guitaraholic/Search/fd5375ffe9c2c5229232e4f6360bd0bdc2607741/speed-dial/pr2-5-privacy.png)

## How it works

- **No web view.** The dial is AppKit: a scroll view of tile buttons and the existing address field, placed at the upper quarter.
- **A local marker.** The dial lives at `about:blank#search-dial`. A tab that has never been anywhere shows it without building a web view; in a tab that has a page, going there is an ordinary history entry, which is why Back works. Only the browser can open it. WebKit reports the browser's own load and a page's navigation with the same source frame, so the browser's carries a one-time ticket on the tab (`Tab.dialing`), and anything else to the marker is cancelled, `window.open` included.
- **Bookmarks, not a second list.** `SpeedDial/sites.json`, beside the profile, holds the ordered bookmark IDs and which address each preview was taken at. The bookmark file is unchanged, and a bookmark that is removed or edited is reconciled when this build runs.
- **Bounded previews.** `WKWebView.takeSnapshot` of the visible part of the page, at most 480 × 300 pixels and 128 KiB as JPEG, checked again before being read back.
- **Every open dial follows.** Each page watches the dial and redraws once per turn, so a change in one tab shows in all of them at once.
- **No page, no page commands.** `Tab.showsPage` greys out Add This Page, Copy Address, Copy as Markdown Link, Find, Print, Share, Duplicate, Pin, Site Information, Reader, zoom and the Web Inspector on the dial, so none of them builds a web view or acts on the marker.

## What it deliberately doesn't do

A home-URL setting; tiles from anywhere but bookmarks; drag and drop (menus and keys cover ordering, and it would cost a lot of size); thumbnails fetched from the network.

## Size and build

- Release build, `-Osize`, stripped: +84 KB on top of the first PR.
- `swift build`: no new warnings.

## How it was tested

- Used day to day on 1.0.3 with a real profile: the button from ordinary pages, Back, several dial tabs open at once, Add Address…, reordering, Clear, and the Privacy switches.
- A security review and a code review before opening.
- Checked locally, outside this PR, in real WebKit: the browser's own button reaches the dial from an https page while a page's script can't; the tab drops the site's icon; tile order, bookmark filing and preview limits; private tabs give nothing.
