items.title: Import from Comet, alongside Chrome, Arc, Dia, Brave and Edge
items.author: gabrielemeksiz-ui
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Comet (Perplexity's browser) is Chromium underneath, and keeps its profile the way every other Chromium browser on the Mac does: `~/Library/Application Support/Comet`, the profile's `Login Data` in `Default/`, the key to it in the keychain as `Comet Safe Storage` / `Comet`.

That is the same shape as Chrome's and Dia's, so this is one line in `Chromium.known` in `Sources/Search/Import.swift`. Nothing else is needed: the reading, the keychain lookup, the PBKDF2/saltysalt stretch, the bookmarks JSON and the history reading after it are the ones already there.

Verified against a real Comet profile (Comet 152 on macOS 27, Apple silicon), with this change in place: 155 passwords, 68 bookmarks and 2 982 history rows read by the same reader, and the two files the conversion wrote for it (bookmarks.json, history.json) decoded by Search's own `Bookmark` and `Visit` types.

This answers the roadmap item "Import from Comet".

Also updated, since they name the browsers one by one:

- `Sources/Search/Settings.swift`, the Settings footer line;
- `README.md`, the passwords bullet;
- `CHANGELOG.md`, under Unreleased › Added.

Two notes for the reviewer:

- `folder: "Comet"` and not `"Comet/User Data"`: Comet keeps its profile directly under its application-support folder (`Comet/Default/Cookies`, `Comet/Default/Login Data`), and `Source.files` looks for `Login Data` one level inside `root`, so `Comet/Default/Login Data` is found as it is.
- The keychain item is `Comet Safe Storage` with account `Comet`, which is what `security find-generic-password -s "Comet Safe Storage"` reports.

Build: `swiftc -typecheck` over `Sources/Search/*.swift` with the macOS SDK returns zero errors, and warnings that are all pre-existing (deprecated `WKProcessPool`, a non-Sendable closure in the tab layout). `swift build` itself stops on this machine's Command Line Tools before compiling any source — `Package.swift`'s `.swiftLanguageMode(.v5)` is unknown to the bundled `PackageDescription` — so the check above is the one that was available. Nothing was changed to work around it.

items.title: Native messaging hosts registered with Vivaldi or Opera are read too
items.author: gabrielemeksiz-ui
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Search reads the native messaging hosts an extension may talk to in five places: Chrome's, Chromium's, Edge's, Brave's and Arc's `NativeMessagingHosts` folder. Vivaldi and Opera keep theirs the same way, in `~/Library/Application Support/Vivaldi/NativeMessagingHosts` and `~/Library/Application Support/com.operasoftware.Opera/NativeMessagingHosts`, and neither is read — so an extension whose host app registered itself with one of those two answers "Specified native messaging host not found" when it asks for it.

Both are already browsers Search knows by name: its import list has Vivaldi, and Opera's folder is where a Chromium-shaped profile lives on this Mac. This makes the folders it reads name the same browsers the import list does.

Two lines, no new dependency, nothing else touched: `Sources/Search/ExtensionNative.swift`, and a line in `CHANGELOG.md` under Unreleased › Fixed.

Found while chasing a ChatGPT side panel that wouldn't start on this Mac. That one turned out to be the other side's: the ChatGPT desktop app ships `installManifest.mjs`, which writes its `com.openai.codexextension` manifest into Chrome's, Chromium's, Edge's, Brave's, Opera's and Vivaldi's folders — and on this Mac it had never run at all, so the app's own checker (`check-native-host-manifest.js`) says "Correct: no" for all six. Installing it by hand into Chrome's folder, with the host binary the app bundles for exactly this, is what made the panel start; it is Search reading Chrome's folder that let that work. A report went to OpenAI for the installer; this pull request is the part that belongs to Search.

Checked with `swiftc -typecheck` over `Sources/Search/*.swift` (zero errors, only the pre-existing warnings); `swift build` can't run here, see the note in #301.

items.title: Passkeys: the WebAuthn PRF extension is dropped (no prf in getClientExtensionResults)
items.author: arvakme
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
**What I did**

On a site that uses the WebAuthn PRF extension (passkey-derived keys, e.g. for client-side encryption), created and used a passkey in Search:

```js
// registration
await navigator.credentials.create({ publicKey: { /* … */, extensions: { prf: {} } } });
// sign-in
const cred = await navigator.credentials.get({ publicKey: { /* … */, extensions: { prf: { eval: { first: salt } } } } });
cred.getClientExtensionResults().prf
```

**What I expected**

`getClientExtensionResults().prf` to be `{ enabled: true }` after registration and `{ results: { first: ArrayBuffer } }` after sign-in, as Chrome and Safari on iOS 18 give for the same passkey (saved in 1Password).

**What happened instead**

The macOS passkey sheet appears and the sign-in itself succeeds, but `prf` is missing from the client extension results, so the site can't derive its key and treats the passkey as unsupported.

**Why**

`Passkeys.swift` carries the ceremony itself through `ASAuthorizationPlatformPublicKeyCredentialProvider`, but it doesn't forward `extensions.prf` to the request (`ASAuthorizationPlatformPublicKeyCredentialAssertionRequest.prf` / `…RegistrationRequest.prf`, macOS 15+), and the page script only ever returns `credProps` in `clientExtensionResults`. `getClientCapabilities()` also reports `extension:prf` as false.

AuthenticationServices has supported PRF for browsers since macOS 15, so the fix looks small: pass `eval` / `evalByCredential` through, read `.prf` from the platform assertion / registration, and hand the outputs back to the page. I have a patch and can open a pull request.

macOS 27.0, Search 1.0.3.

items.title: Passkeys: carry the WebAuthn PRF extension through
items.author: arvakme
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Closes #312.

## What

Search carries passkey ceremonies itself through `ASAuthorizationPlatformPublicKeyCredentialProvider` (`Passkeys.swift`), but the WebAuthn PRF extension was dropped both ways: `extensions.prf` never reached the request, and the page script only ever returned `credProps` in `clientExtensionResults`. Sites that derive a key from a passkey (client-side encryption, end-to-end encrypted vaults) get no `prf` result and treat the passkey as unsupported, while the same passkey works in Chrome and in Safari on iOS 18. `getClientCapabilities()` also reported `extension:prf: false`.

## The change

- **Page script**: `get` forwards `prf.eval` and `prf.evalByCredential`, `create` forwards `prf` (an empty `{}` asks whether the new passkey supports it). Salts go through as base64url, untouched: macOS hashes them as the standard says. `evalByCredential` without `allowCredentials` rejects with `NotSupportedError`, as the spec and AuthenticationServices both require. It all rides the existing `search-passkeys-ask` / `-answer` bridge as plain strings.
- **Requests** (`#available(macOS 15.0, *)`, the package still targets 14): `assertion()` sets `ASAuthorizationPlatformPublicKeyCredentialAssertionRequest.prf`; `registration()` sets `…RegistrationRequest.prf` to the given values or `.checkForSupport`.
- **Answers**: the delegate reads `.prf` from the platform assertion / registration and hands back `first` / `second`, plus `enabled` on a registration.
- **Results**: `getClientExtensionResults()` builds fresh `ArrayBuffer`s on every call (the existing JSON copy would drop bytes); `toJSON()` carries them as base64url, per the WebAuthn JSON serialization.
- **Capabilities**: `extension:prf` is reported on macOS 15 and later.
- No new dependencies; `CryptoKit` (system) is imported only to read the `SymmetricKey` outputs. Changelog line under Unreleased › Fixed.

## Testing

- [x] `swift build`: builds, no warnings from `Passkeys.swift`.
- [x] The new API names typechecked against the macOS SDK (`prf` on the platform assertion/registration requests and credentials, macOS 15+).
- [x] The page and bridge scripts, run in a stubbed page with a fake native reply:
  - `get` sends `eval` + `evalByCredential`; `create` sends `prf: {}`
  - results come back as `ArrayBuffer`s (a fresh copy per call) and as base64url in `toJSON()`
  - a registration reports `{ enabled: true }`
  - nothing is sent or returned when a site doesn't ask for `prf`
  - `evalByCredential` without `allowCredentials` rejects with `NotSupportedError`
  - `getClientCapabilities()` reports `extension:prf: true`
- [ ] A real ceremony through the macOS sheet. A local build doesn't have the passkeys entitlement tied to your Developer ID profile, so I couldn't run it end to end. To try: a passkey in iCloud Keychain or 1Password, `get` with `extensions: { prf: { eval: { first } } }`; `getClientExtensionResults().prf.results.first` should be a 32-byte `ArrayBuffer` that is the same each time for the same salt.

Happy to reshape any of it if the direction doesn't fit.

items.title: The interface can be read in Chinese: a language file beside the binary, and a switch in Settings
items.author: songqii
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
## What

Search's interface can now follow the Mac's language, with Simplified Chinese as the first translation. Follows from #304.

The mechanism is deliberately small:

- **English is not stored anywhere.** A sentence's own words are the lookup key, and a language file (`Localization/*.lproj`) replaces the sentences it knows. A key no language knows passes through in English — so English needs no file, translations can land a page at a time, and nothing here changes what an English user sees.
- **`Tongue.swift`** carries the idea: `Text(title.said)` for the few shared atoms (`Line`, `Pill`, `Segmented`, `Quiet`, `Door`'s help…) where a panel hands in a plain String, and `"New Tab".saidNow` at the one place a sentence must stay a String (a tab's label) — looked up at the source, so page titles are never touched.
- **`build.sh`** copies each `Localization/*.lproj` into the bundle and lists them in `CFBundleLocalizations`. Adding a language is one case in `Tongue` and one folder.
- **Settings › General › Language**: Follow Mac (the default, and the behaviour until now), English, or 简体中文 — a dropdown, so more languages fit later. It writes the same per-app `AppleLanguages` entry System Settings writes, and offers *Relaunch now* when the choice and the screen disagree.

zh-Hans carries 270 sentences: the menus, the tab strip and its menu, every Settings page, the bookmarks/history/downloads/passwords panels, the extension pages and their errors, the welcome, the message under a page that never loaded.

## Known edges

- Sentences built at runtime with interpolation ("3 bookmarks from Chrome") stay English for now; they want format keys, which felt like a second change.
- A language change takes a relaunch — macOS's own rule for per-app language; the *Relaunch now* pill is `Updater.relaunch()`.
- The `bench` socket's strings are left in English on purpose.

## Testing

- `swift build` and `./build.sh` clean; an English Mac sees byte-identical UI (every hook falls through to the key).
- Verified on macOS 26: switched to 简体中文 via Settings, relaunched, walked the menus, tab menu, all Settings pages, the panels and an error page in Chinese; blank tabs read 新标签页 while page titles stay as the sites wrote them.

I'd suggest the language files live exactly where they are rather than a String Catalog: the app is a SwiftPM executable whose bundle `build.sh` assembles by hand, and identity-keyed `.strings` keeps the diff reviewable line by line. Happy to move it if you'd rather have `xcstrings`.

items.title: Fix NordPass sign-in returns to extension pages
items.author: SimonDesdevises
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
NordPass completes its web sign-in, but returning to its extension page fails with `NSURLErrorDomain -1008`: the ordinary tab does not use the extension's `webViewConfiguration`. This change replaces the view at that boundary, retaining the callback URL and the popup's opener and display metadata.

The handover accepts only main-frame GET navigations from HTTPS to resources exposed by the loaded extension's `web_accessible_resources`. It uses WebKit's source security origin, or the same provisional navigation's native server-redirect callbacks when the source document is still blank. Unlisted origins, private resources, ambiguous paths and unsupported dynamic URL declarations do not receive a handover. Private tabs are excluded, and a navigation revision check prevents a queued replacement from taking over a tab that has since navigated elsewhere.

Fixes #98. Includes the Unreleased changelog entry and removes the resolved roadmap item.

### Validation

- 33 policy checks and 9 native WebKit scenarios pass with `python3 Tests/ExtensionNavigation/run-tests.py` (SDK selected with `SEARCH_TEST_SDK`). The baseline reproduces `-1008`; successful returns preserve query and fragment, and disallowed returns never replace the view.
- `swift build --sdk /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/SDKs/MacOSX26.5.sdk --scratch-path .build/nordpass-sdk26` succeeds. Existing warnings in unchanged code and the local Command Line Tools linker paths remain. SDK 26.5 was used because the local default SDK 27 fails to load the SwiftUI macro plugin.
- Manually confirmed NordPass 7.10.10 sign-in, master-password unlocking and the keep-unlocked switch in an isolated Search profile, including after removing the temporary popup diagnostics.

The native fixtures compile the two production helpers and supply their own view-replacement delegate; they do not instantiate the full Browser. Real NordPass validation complements those checks. Test setup and scope are documented in `Tests/ExtensionNavigation/README.md`.

items.title: Add keyboard shortcut to promote a link peek into a full tab
items.author: bhanni01
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
## Summary
When a link is opened in peek mode (Shift + Click), pressing `Esc` closes the peek, which works well. However, there's no keyboard shortcut to do the opposite: promote the peek into a regular tab. Right now the only way is to click the button in the peek view.

## Current behavior
1. Shift + Click a link to open it in a peek.
2. Press `Esc` → the peek closes ✅
3. To keep the page, you have to move the mouse and click the "open as tab" button. There's no keyboard equivalent ❌

## Expected behavior
A keyboard shortcut that converts the current peek into a full tab, mirroring how `Esc` dismisses it. This keeps the peek workflow fully keyboard-driven: peek, then either dismiss or keep.

## Suggested shortcut
Some options (open to whatever fits existing keybindings best):
- `Cmd/Ctrl + Enter`
- `Shift + Enter`
- `Cmd/Ctrl + O`

Ideally it would also be shown in the button's tooltip so it's discoverable.

## Why
Peek is great for quickly checking a link without breaking focus. Having a close shortcut but no "keep" shortcut makes the flow feel incomplete and forces a switch from keyboard to mouse at the exact moment you've decided the link is worth keeping.``

I'm happy to open a PR for this.

items.title: Close other tabs with ⇧⌘K, a downloads button, a ten-card switcher, and sessions and colours that survive quitting
items.author: sethmorton
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
Stacked on #260 (⌃Tab switcher) and #262 (colour and folders). Review the last commit only (3c5ac97). The earlier commits belong to those two PRs and will drop out of this diff once they merge.

## What changes

- **⇧⌘K closes every other tab.** Pinned tabs close too. The current page stays. The session is written right away, so closed tabs stay closed after a relaunch. Listed in the shortcuts card.
- **Downloads button.** An arrow beside Bookmarks, in the top bar and at the foot of the sidebar. Same panel as ⇧⌘J. It lights up while the panel is open.
- **Switcher.** It follows light or dark appearance instead of always being dark. It shows at most ten cards at once, most recently used first. Older tabs are reachable by scrolling or by continuing with ⌃Tab.
- **Sessions survive quitting.**
  - Quitting now also saves the rows of spaces that aren't on screen.
  - The active tab is counted after private and bench tabs are filtered out. Before, the saved index could point at the wrong tab.
  - Session writes go through one serial queue. A slow background save can no longer land after the final save on quit.
- **Colours survive quitting.** `spaces.json` written before the Clear control has themes with no `clarity`. Those failed to decode, and the whole list fell back to a plain default. `Spaces.read` now migrates once: it adds `clarity: 0`, checks that the whole list decodes, then writes it back in the current format. Quitting also saves a colour drag that was never finished.

## Checks

- `swift build -c release` passes.
- `swiftc Sources/Search/Session.swift Tests/SessionCheck.swift -o /tmp/search-session-check && /tmp/search-session-check`: 1,000 background saves followed by one final save, and the final one wins. Deleted spaces stay deleted.
- Run in an isolated `SEARCH_PROBE` world:
  - 15 tabs plus a bench tab, quit with ⌘Q, relaunch: all 15 come back with the right active tab. The bench tab is left out.
  - A pre-Clear theme: dots, strength and grain are kept, and `clarity` is added.
  - The switcher: ten cards in light and in dark, and older tabs reached by scrolling.
  - ⇧⌘K leaves one tab, and that still holds after a relaunch.
  - Both downloads buttons open the panel.

items.title: Move tabs between Spaces
items.author: luca-dupont2
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
## Problem

Tabs are tied to the Space where they were opened. When a tab belongs to a different space, users currently have to reopen it manually.

## Changes

- Add **Move to Space** to tabs’ context menus when Spaces are enabled, with the current Space omitted from the destination list.
- Add **New Space…** to that menu. It opens Search’s existing Space creation flow, moves the tab into the Space after creation, and switches to it.
- Preserve the tab’s URL, title, pin, name, and restorable page state when moving between Spaces.
- Rebuild the WebKit view with the destination Space’s data store when its sign-in store changes.
- Ask before a move that changes sign-in stores when the page has unsaved form entries; canceling keeps the original page and its entered values intact.
- Keep the action unavailable for bench tabs and extension-host pages.

## Verification

- ./build.sh completed successfully. The build emitted existing Swift warnings, including warnings in unchanged code in a touched file; the new move logic introduced none.
- Manual QA in an isolated profile covered the single-Space menu, creating a Space from the tab menu, moving active and inactive tabs, moving pinned tabs, moving between shared and separate sign-in stores, and canceling or confirming the unsaved-form warning.
- git diff --check passed.

## Screenshots

The first image shows the New Space form opened from a tab’s **Move to Space** menu. The second shows the tab in its new Research Space.

![New Space form](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luca-dupont2/Search/97fec5e4ca2f3fc3656e4dec331e1eb3d8aff54e/.github/pr-screenshots/move-tabs-new-space-form.png)

![Example Domain moved into the Research Space](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luca-dupont2/Search/97fec5e4ca2f3fc3656e4dec331e1eb3d8aff54e/.github/pr-screenshots/move-tabs-new-space-result.png)

## Scope

Spaces are off by default. Enable **Settings › Tabs › Spaces** to use this feature. Moving internal extension-host and bench tabs is not included.

items.title: How should tabs be organized within a Space?
items.author: Takuto1121-ja
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
I’m trying to figure out the intended way to organize a larger number of tabs within a single Space.

For example, I might have a `Book` Space containing tabs for different categories:

- Mystery
- Manga
- Children's books
- Cookbooks

I’d prefer to keep these under one `Book` Space rather than creating a separate Space for every category, but once there are many tabs, it becomes difficult to visually distinguish the different groups.

I can think of a few possible approaches:

- Optional tab folders, perhaps behind a setting for people who want them
- Lightweight section labels or separators inside the tab list, without introducing full tab-group behavior
- Small category markers on individual tabs, such as a short label, symbol, or subtle visual marker

For example, section labels could look something like:

```text
Book

── Mystery ─────────
tab
tab
tab

── Manga ───────────
tab
tab

── Children's books ─
tab
tab

── Cookbooks ───────
tab
```

Or category markers could keep the list completely flat:

```text
[Mystery] tab
[Manga] tab
[Children's] tab
[Cookbook] tab
```

These are just examples rather than specific feature requests.

I know Search intentionally avoids traditional tab groups/folders and tries to keep the tab column simple, so I’m mainly curious:

**What would be the Search-style way to handle this kind of organization within a Space?**

I’d be interested in whatever approach best fits Search’s design philosophy.

items.title: Add support for auto-hiding the sidebar
items.author: Sparker0i
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
### Summary
Add an option to auto-hide the sidebar so it stays out of the way while browsing. It would slide out when the pointer reaches the window edge and collapse again when the pointer leaves.

### Motivation
- The sidebar takes up a fixed amount of horizontal space, and that hurts most on smaller displays and split-screen layouts.
- People who are used to a full-width page view (for example, on docs, notebooks or dashboards) currently have to pick between a permanently visible sidebar and a manual collapse.
- Other vertical-tab browsers offer this, and it's a common request.

### Proposed behavior
- Add a setting, off by default so existing behavior doesn't change, to enable "Auto-hide sidebar".
- When enabled, the sidebar is hidden and the page content uses the full window width.
- Moving the pointer to the left (or right, depending on sidebar position) edge of the window reveals the sidebar as an overlay, so the page doesn't reflow or resize.
- The sidebar hides again shortly after the pointer leaves it. A short delay avoids flicker.
- The sidebar stays open while a tab is being dragged, a context menu is open, or an input in it (such as search) has focus.
- Add a keyboard shortcut to toggle the sidebar or reveal it temporarily.

### Alternatives considered
- Manually collapsing the sidebar every time. This works but is tedious, and it doesn't give a quick way to peek at tabs.

items.title: Open browsing-data clearing controls with ⌘⇧Delete
items.author: siiddhantt
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
## Problem

I'd like a keyboard shortcut to reach Search's existing browsing-data clearing controls.

On current `main` (`491f321`), ⌘Y opens History and **Clear…** reveals separate actions for history, cookies/sign-ins, and cache. There is no ⌘⇧Delete binding. This is based on reading the current code, rather than a runtime bug reproduction.

## Proposed behavior

- **⌘⇧Delete** (Command + Shift + the Mac's backward-delete key, ⌘⇧⌫) opens History with its existing **Clear…** controls already expanded.
- If History is already open, the shortcut reveals those controls in place.
- Opening the controls does not delete anything. The user still explicitly chooses **Clear** for history or cache, or **Sign out of everything** for cookies/sign-ins.
- Expose the same action in the History menu as **Clear Browsing Data…**, with the shortcut shown.
- ⌘Y continues to open the ordinary history view.

This would reuse the existing UI and clearing actions, keeping the change small and adding no dependencies.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The shortcut and menu action reach the same clearing controls.
- [ ] It works from a normal page, the address field, and a focused page text field, and while History is already open.
- [ ] It remains available with an empty history, since cookies or cache may still need clearing.
- [ ] Opening or dismissing the panel clears no data; Escape dismisses it.
- [ ] Plain Delete and other editing shortcuts keep their existing behavior.
- [ ] Clearing history, cookies/sign-ins, and cache remains separate, with the existing labels explaining their effects.

## Scope and related work

Time-range selection and new deletion behavior can be separate proposals. This request is only for reaching the existing controls from the keyboard.

Relevant code: [HistoryPanel and its clearing controls](https://github.com/driceroland/Search/blob/491f3214063212fac176a7ad95467f0821040451/Sources/Search/Recall.swift#L42), [History menu](https://github.com/driceroland/Search/blob/491f3214063212fac176a7ad95467f0821040451/Sources/Search/App.swift#L158).

Related: #36 adds configurable shortcuts. This command should remain compatible with that work.

I'd like to contribute a small PR for this if the direction fits.

items.title: Open browsing-data controls with ⌘⇧Delete
items.author: siiddhantt
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Fixes #336.

Adds **History → Clear Browsing Data…** and ⇧⌘⌫ to open the existing clearing controls, including while History is already visible or a page editor has focus. Opening the controls deletes nothing; History, Cookies and sign-ins, and Cache retain their separate explicit actions.

History now has one optional presentation mode: closed, browsing, or clearing. Existing open/close paths use that state, so Back returns to browsing and one Escape closes the whole panel without leaving stale clearing state. The shortcut uses backward Delete, preserves the existing page-first handler, and is listed in Settings and the changelog.

This revision replaces the initial implementation with a rewrite directly on upstream `main` (`491f321`): one commit, five files, no dependencies, test framework, or bench API changes.

## Validation

Re-run on the rewritten implementation, macOS 26.6.1 / Apple silicon / Swift 6.3.3, in an isolated test profile. Interactive checks below were performed through native UI automation, not by a human tester.

- `swift build` passed; no new warnings compared with the main-branch build. `git diff --check` passed.
- Visited **https://example.com/** in a normal tab and confirmed its real history entry appeared. ⇧⌘⌫ opened the three clearing controls from the page. Repeating the shortcut kept them open; Back restored the normal footer; the shortcut expanded already-open History; one Escape closed it; ⌘Y then showed ordinary History.
- Compared the saved history file before and after those open/dismiss interactions: byte-for-byte unchanged. Explicitly clicked **History → Clear** in the panel: the visit disappeared, the UI showed “Nothing yet,” and the saved history became an empty array. The shortcut still opened the controls with empty history.
- Visited **https://www.wikipedia.org/**, focused its search field, and typed `shortcut`. Ordinary Delete produced `shortcu`; ⇧⌘⌫ then opened the clearing controls and preserved that input. Visually inspected the panel over the live page.
- In the address field, ordinary Delete removed only the final character. ⇧⌘⌫ opened the clearing controls, and one Escape dismissed History.
- A scripted contenteditable fixture with a page key handler confirmed Search consumed ⇧⌘⌫ before the page. Six scripted negative checks confirmed plain Delete, ⇧Delete, ⌘Delete, extra Option, extra Control, and forward Delete did not open History.

The menu entry was confirmed present, but direct menu activation remains unverified because the native UI tool returns stale menu targets. Cookie/sign-in and cache deletion were not exercised; their existing implementation is unchanged.

## Related shortcut work

Merge checks against #36 (`5d85459`) and #225 (`aea59cd`) add no additional `App.swift` conflict blocks compared with their existing conflicts against main. This is not a claim that those PRs are conflict-free. If #36 lands first, this action needs registering in its new shortcut registry during rebase. The History-menu overlap with the multiwindow work in #294 will also need resolving if that lands first.

Time-range selection remains a separate feature, as scoped in #336.

items.title: Add recently used (MRU) tab switching for Ctrl+Tab
items.author: NANAMINER
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated

items.body:
It would be great to have an option for Ctrl+Tab to cycle through tabs in most recently used order, rather than their physical order in the tab bar.

For example:

I'm currently on Tab A
Before that, I was using Tab D
Before that, Tab B

Pressing Ctrl+Tab once should switch from A → D. Pressing it again while continuing to cycle should go D → B, etc.
This makes Ctrl+Tab work more like an app switcher and makes it much faster to jump back and forth between recently used tabs, especially when many tabs are open.

The current sequential behavior could stay as the default if desired, with something like:
Settings → Tabs → Ctrl+Tab cycles through tabs in recently used order

Ctrl+Shift+Tab could cycle through the same MRU list in the opposite direction.

I use this behavior constantly in other browsers, and it's one of the main things I miss in Search so far.

items.title: Korean UI and foldered persistent sidebar pins
items.author: yunseongmin
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
## Problem Statement

Search v1.0.3 has a compact top pin shelf and regular tabs, but its pins keep the last visited address rather than a fixed home address. It has no persistent full-row sidebar tabs or folders, and its interface has no Korean localization. The user wants a Zen-inspired organization model without changing the browser pages themselves.

## Solution

Keep compact top pins and give the shelf a fixed four-column grid. Add full-row sidebar pins that can be grouped in one-level folders, alongside regular tabs that disappear when explicitly closed. Both persistent pin types remember a home address independently from the address currently being browsed and return to that home when closed. Localize the complete Search interface to Korean when macOS prefers Korean, with English as the fallback for other system languages.

## User Stories

1. As a Search user, I want four top-pin columns at every pin count, so that additional pins always wrap to the next row.
2. As a Search user, I want a top pin to remember the address it had when pinned, so that browsing elsewhere does not replace its home.
3. As a Search user, I want closing and reopening a top pin to return to its saved home address, so that the pin remains a reliable shortcut.
4. As a Search user, I want to reorder top pins without changing their saved homes, so that I can keep frequently used sites in a stable order.
5. As a Search user, I want to convert a regular tab into a full-row sidebar pin, so that an important site can remain available without occupying the compact top shelf.
6. As a Search user, I want to convert between a top pin and a sidebar pin, so that I can change how a site is displayed without losing its saved home.
7. As a Search user, I want to put sidebar pins in one-level named folders, so that related persistent sites stay together.
8. As a Search user, I want to create, rename, and delete folders, so that I can keep my sidebar organized as my work changes.
9. As a Search user, I want to drag a sidebar pin into a folder and move it through a menu, so that both direct manipulation and an explicit command are available.
10. As a Search user, I want deleting a folder to leave its pins in the unfiled sidebar group, so that organizing items never removes the sites themselves.
11. As a Search user, I want closing a sidebar pin to release its page and return to its home when reopened, so that persistent entries do not keep unused pages alive.
12. As a Search user, I want to unpin a sidebar pin into a regular tab, so that I can remove persistence while keeping the current page.
13. As a Search user, I want closing a regular tab to remove it, so that temporary work does not accumulate.
14. As a Search user, I want Search's existing open-session recovery to continue across app restarts, so that quitting the browser does not discard tabs I left open.
15. As a Search user, I want each Space to keep its own top pins, sidebar pins, and folders, so that separate tab sets stay organized independently.
16. As a Korean-speaking user, I want all Search interface text translated when macOS prefers Korean, so that menus, settings, dialogs, onboarding, and tab actions are usable in Korean.
17. As a user in another language, I want the existing English interface to remain the fallback, so that localization does not force Korean on everyone.
18. As a Search user, I want visited websites to keep their own original language, so that the browser translates its controls without changing page content.
19. As a Search user relying on VoiceOver, I want localized labels and help text for the new pin and folder controls, so that their actions remain understandable.
20. As a Search user upgrading from v1.0.3, I want my existing pins and open tabs to survive session migration, so that the new fields do not invalidate my saved session.

## Implementation Decisions

- A tab is exactly one of a regular tab, a top pin, or a sidebar pin; it cannot appear in multiple groups at once.
- The home address is captured when a regular tab becomes persistent. Navigating does not change it. Converting between the two persistent types preserves it; unpinning clears persistence and keeps the current page.
- Closing either persistent pin type resets the tab's visible and pending address to its home address and releases the old WebKit page. The next selection loads the home address.
- Existing top pins loaded from an older session use their saved current address as the initial home address. Missing optional sidebar and folder data defaults to no sidebar pins or folders.
- Sidebar pins may be unfiled or placed in one-level folders. Folders belong to the current Space. Deleting a folder moves its pins to the unfiled group.
- Folder operations include create, rename, delete, drag-to-folder, and menu-based movement. Folders are expanded by default; nested folders are out of scope.
- A regular tab is removed when explicitly closed, while Search's existing session recovery for tabs still open at app quit remains intact.
- Korean localization follows the operating system's preferred language and uses the existing English text as fallback. Website contents are not translated.
- The highest behavioral seam is Browser tab lifecycle and folder actions, persisted through Session. UI-specific layout and drag interactions are verified through the built macOS app.

## Testing Decisions

- Test only external behavior: tab category transitions, home-address restoration, folder membership and deletion, per-Space persistence, old-session decoding, and localization fallback.
- Add focused automated coverage for the pure session representation and the Browser lifecycle seam where the current app architecture permits it; do not assert private view layout implementation details.
- Manually verify in the built app: four-column wrapping, close/reopen of both persistent types, folder create/rename/delete and drag/menu moves, regular-tab close, Space isolation, and Korean/English language selection.
- The repository currently has no test target or test files. Build/type-check and the required UI smoke flows are the existing baseline; a test target should be added only if the lifecycle can be exercised without coupling tests to app startup or live WebKit.

## Out of Scope

- Nested folders, cross-device sync, import/export of Zen data, split view, and Zen-specific browser features.
- Translating website contents or changing Search's search engine, history, bookmarks, or account data.
- Changing normal-tab restoration across app restarts.

## Further Notes

- Target the checked-out Search v1.0.3 source. Existing optional session fields must remain backward-compatible with its saved JSON.
- Persistent address restoration is a fresh navigation; it does not promise to restore the previous page's back-forward history after the pin is closed.

items.title: Dock an extension's side panel beside the page
items.author: AngKS
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
Search fills in `chrome.sidePanel`, but `sidePanel.open()` and the toolbar button both open the panel's page as an ordinary tab. From inside that tab, `tabs.query({active: true})` and `captureVisibleTab` see the panel, not the page someone is reading, so an assistant, notes panel or reader cannot sit beside the page.

I would like the panel to be a column on the right of the page, the way Chrome docks one, and for `sidePanel` to answer the calls extensions already make:

- a path may carry a query and a hash (Bitwarden's panel is `popup/index.html?uilocation=sidepanel#/…`)
- changing the path updates the panel that is already open
- `setPanelBehavior({ openPanelOnActionClick: true })`, which extensions set once from `onInstalled`, still works after a relaunch
- a tab the extension disables hides the panel, and the panel comes back with that tab
- `close`, `getLayout`, `onOpened` and `onClosed` exist

No Settings switch: the column only appears because an installed extension asked for one. One panel at a time. It is not restored at launch.

This is the side panel part of the extension APIs on the roadmap (#12).

items.title: Dock an extension's side panel beside the page
items.author: AngKS
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
Closes #351.

Search fills in `chrome.sidePanel`, but until now `sidePanel.open()` and the toolbar button opened the panel's page as a tab of its own. That is the one place a side panel cannot work from: a panel exists to look at the page beside it, and a tab in front *is* the page in front. `tabs.query({active: true})` from the panel answered with the panel itself, and so did `captureVisibleTab`. Any extension that reads the page you are on from its panel broke in exactly that way.

The panel now opens as a column docked on the right of the page, the page's height, resized by pulling its edge (280–640 points, remembered as `panel.width`), with the extension's icon and name over it and a cross to close it. The page is loaded in a view built from the extension's own configuration, as its popup already is, and told to WebKit the same way: in the browser's window, but not among its tabs. From inside it, the tab in front is the page, `tabs.getCurrent()` is nothing, `windows.getCurrent()` is the browser's window, and a `runtime.connect` port reaches the worker.

`sidePanel` answers the calls extensions already make:

- `open({ tabId })` or `open({ windowId })` shows the panel, and rejects when no path is set, or when neither id is given. `open()` does not require a user gesture.
- A path may carry a query and a hash, so Bitwarden's `popup/index.html?uilocation=sidepanel#/…` loads that page.
- `setOptions({ path })` navigates the panel that is already open.
- `setPanelBehavior({ openPanelOnActionClick: true })` and the window's options are remembered across launches. Extensions set the flag once, from `onInstalled`.
- `setOptions({ tabId, enabled: false })` hides the panel on that tab and shows it again when you return. Said of some other tab, it leaves the panel you are looking at alone. A tab given its own path shows only on that tab.
- `setOptions({ enabled: false })` with no tab closes the window's panel and leaves it disabled, so the button does not bring it back.
- `close`, `getLayout` (the right-hand column), `onOpened` and `onClosed` are filled in. The worker hears the open and close events.
- `window.close()` from the panel page puts it away, including after the page has navigated.
- The button toggles the panel when the extension asked for that and the action has no popup.
- A reload or removal takes the panel with it. Links out of the panel open as tabs and the panel stays. A website the panel sends itself to goes to the row, and the panel keeps its page. A download from the panel is a download.
- One panel at a time. It is not restored at launch. No Settings switch: the column only appears because an installed extension asked for it. `getLayout` reports the right side; there is no left-hand option and no panel-picker menu.

Also in this branch, found while running the tests: a bench client that closes its end before a slow answer arrives had the answer's `write()` raise SIGPIPE and kill the app. The accepted socket now sets `SO_NOSIGPIPE`. Its own commit, if you would rather take it separately.

## Checked

`tests/sidepanel.py`, against a `SEARCH_PROBE=1` run of `build/Search.app`, with fixtures under `tests/sidepanel/` (a panel, an extension with no panel, and one that sets the button only from `onInstalled`). All of the checks pass, including the ones above: the docked column, what the panel sees of the page, a path with `?` and `#`, a tab hiding its own panel, a disabled panel staying down, the button still opening after a relaunch, and the width surviving a relaunch. `swift build` introduces no new warnings.

items.body:
The feature is useful especially on HiDPI displays where chrome is running at a normal resolution but you want content to be scaled. 

This PR improves upon #177 by allowing more granular setting increments while dealing with more edge cases. 

Settings > General has a Page zoom line: − and + either side of the value in an outlined pill, stepping 5% at a time from 50% to 300%, each going grey at its end. Away from 100%, a Reset button beside it takes it back there, as pressing the value does.

It is where every site starts. A size set on a site with ⌘+ and ⌘− is still remembered for that site and wins over it; a site zoomed back to the default keeps nothing and follows the default from then on. ⌘0, Actual Size and the number in the site card go back to the default rather than to 100%.

Changing it resizes every open page without a size of its own at once; a sleeping tab takes it when it wakes, before its page draws a frame.

The original implementation is Shashwat Aggarwal's, in #177: the setting, its pageZoom key and Tab.defaultZoom are theirs. On top of it, the steps and Reset in place of a menu, and tabs in every space follow a change, not only the one on screen.

Checked in a test world with each page's innerWidth: pages follow the default live and after a relaunch, a site's own zoom is left alone, and the steps land where they should, − going grey at 50%.

items.title: feat(tabs): cycle Ctrl+Tab in recently used order
items.author: olllayor
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
## Why

Issue #345 asks for Ctrl+Tab in recently used order. Sequential order forces a walk across the whole row to get back to the last tab. The change adds the MRU walk behind a switch and keeps the row walk as the default.

## Scope

- `Preferences.mruTabs` (`tabs.mru`) in Prefs.swift.
- `Browser.stepMRU(_)` plus `Browser.landMRU()` in Browser.swift.
- Ctrl+Tab routing and Control release in App.swift.
- Settings switch in Settings.swift and a CHANGELOG line.
- Menu Next/Previous Tab and Cmd+Shift+brackets stay sequential. Cmd+K is untouched.

## Tradeoffs

The walk runs off a snapshot taken on the first press. Re-sorting on each press would bounce between the two newest tabs instead of walking further back. The snapshot clears when Control is released.

## Blast Radius

Only the Ctrl+Tab path reads the new setting, and only when it is on. Default behavior is unchanged. The setting persists per install like the other tab switches.

## Verification

`swift build` passes with no new warnings. Walk logic and wrap arithmetic reviewed against `step(_)`. Space switches reset the snapshot. Manual test on hardware passed. Ctrl+Tab walks most recent first, a quick tap toggles the two newest, and release lands where the walk stopped.

Closes #345.

items.title: The tab switcher shows every space, a row for each, and takes the pointer
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
Reworked as asked: only additions on top of #24's switcher, which is now always on, so there's no switch to reuse. Two things, both in the switcher: rows per space, and the pointer. The second grew out of trying the first: with ⌃ held, a click on a card didn't land. Happy to split it into its own PR if you'd rather review them apart.

## Rows per space

With spaces on:

- ⌃Tab shows a row for each space, in ⌃1-⌃9 order, under the space's icon and name. Each row holds that space's five latest, in the same order the space on screen gets (the tab it was showing, then the ones last left).
- ⌃↑ and ⌃↓ go to the row above or below at the same place, ⌃← and ⌃→ go round the row, and Tab/⇧Tab walk the row the pick is in.
- Letting go of ⌃ on another space's card, or clicking it, switches to that space and then the tab.
- Cards shrink so every row stays in the window, down to 96 pt wide.

Without spaces, or with one, the grid is the one #24 left.

## The pointer

With or without spaces:

- Resting the pointer on a card picks it, once the pointer has moved: a panel that opens under a still pointer leaves the pick to the keys.
- A click on a card takes it, ⌃ held or not. Outside the panel, a click puts the switcher away.

⌃ is held for as long as the switcher is up, so every click on it is a ⌃-click, which AppKit treats as a right-click rather than a click the card's `Button` can be counted on to take. So the window's event monitor catches the left mouse down while the switcher is up and matches it against each card's frame (reported with a preference key, in the window's top-left coordinates). Hover goes through the same frames. The buttons stay, for VoiceOver.

## Notes for review

- **Five a row with spaces**, so each space is one row and up/down mean "the next space". Without spaces it stays ten in a 5-wide grid.
- **`step` takes the spaces' rows** on the first press and builds each with the same order as `candidates`, pulled out into `order(_:first:limit:)`. `shown` replaces `candidates` where the code means every tab on show (finish, preview caching, capture), so parked tabs get pictures too.
- **`commitTabSwitch`** switches space first when the picked tab is parked.
- **The space switch calls `tabSwitcher.left`** in `enter()`: the row swaps before `activeID` changes, so its `didSet` can't find the tab being left, which would otherwise drop out of the order and miss its picture.
- In the rows view, the pick's highlight moves with `matchedGeometryEffect`, since #24's offset maths assumes one grid with no row names.

## Tested

In a `SEARCH_PROBE` world with spaces. Through `./bench press` and screenshots: rows in order with pictures for parked tabs, ⌃↓ into the next space at the same place, Tab staying in that row, pressing a card in another space's row. With the real pointer: moving onto another space's card picked it and lit its row's name, and a ⌃-click on a card that wasn't picked switched to that space and tab. Not checked: the grid without spaces after the change (only moved into an `if`, plus the pointer, which uses the same frames).

items.title: Two-finger panning on a canvas or whiteboard goes back a page
items.author: arvakme
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
**What I did:** On a canvas or whiteboard page — Claude Code's canvas, and the same happens on Excalidraw, tldraw or Figma — I pan sideways with two fingers on the trackpad, the normal way to move around the board.

**What I expected:** The board pans, as it does in Safari and Chrome.

**What happened:** The back/forward disc comes in from the edge, and letting go takes the tab back (or forward) to the previous page, leaving the board.

**Why, as far as I can tell:** the swipe watcher in `Swipe.swift` only counts a sideways swipe as the page's when something under the pointer has `overflow-x: auto/scroll` room to scroll. A canvas app pans with its own non-passive `wheel` handler that calls `preventDefault()`, and has no overflow to scroll, so every swipe reads as free. Safari and Chrome both treat a `preventDefault()` on the wheel event as the page claiming the gesture and skip history navigation.

macOS 27.0, Search built from `main`.

items.title: Two fingers sideways on a canvas pan it instead of going back
items.author: arvakme
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Fixes #360.

A canvas or whiteboard (Claude Code's canvas, Excalidraw, tldraw, Figma) pans on two fingers sideways through its own non-passive `wheel` handler, and nothing under the pointer has overflow to scroll. The swipe watcher only looked for overflow, so it told the web view the swipe was free, the back/forward disc came in, and letting go left the board.

The watcher now also counts a sideways wheel event as the page's when the page called `preventDefault()` on it, which is how Safari and Chrome decide the same question. That can only be read once every handler has run, and the watcher's capture listener runs first, so it looks after dispatch with a `setTimeout(0)`. This also covers a canvas that calls `stopPropagation()`, which a bubbling listener on `window` would miss. The overflow check and the "once per change of mind, at most ten times a second" throttle are unchanged.

## Testing

- `swift build`: clean, no new warnings.
- The watcher script, pulled from `Swipe.swift`, run in a real `WKWebView` with the same `officeScroll` handler and synthetic sideways `WheelEvent`s:

| page | `main` | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| plain page | free | free |
| `overflow-x: auto` with room to scroll | taken | taken |
| canvas with `preventDefault()` | **free** | taken |
| canvas with `preventDefault()` + `stopPropagation()` | **free** | taken |
| canvas with a passive listener only | free | free |

Not covered: a real trackpad gesture in the running app — synthetic `NSEvent` scroll phases aren't something I can drive from a script.

items.title: Sites sign you out after a while: WebKit's tracking prevention clears their data
items.author: arvakme
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
**What happens:** now and then I'm signed out of sites I signed in to in Search, or a web app has forgotten its state, without clearing anything myself. It hits sites I open less often than daily.

**Why, as far as I can tell:** it looks like WebKit's Intelligent Tracking Prevention, which is on in every Search data store, as in Safari. From [`ResourceLoadStatisticsStore.cpp`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/NetworkProcess/Classifier/ResourceLoadStatisticsStore.cpp) (`registrableDomainsToDeleteOrRestrictWebsiteDataFor`, `shouldRemoveAllWebsiteDataFor`, `shouldRemoveAllButCookiesFor`):

- a domain classified as prevalent, with no user interaction within the last 30 days of browser use, loses **all** its data, cookies included, so you are signed out;
- a domain scheduled for "all but cookie" removal loses its script-written storage (localStorage, IndexedDB), where many web apps keep their session, once its interaction has expired.

Search's own ITP database on my Mac (`~/Library/WebKit/com.officecommun.search/WebsiteData/ResourceLoadStatistics/observations.db`) already has several sites I sign in to either marked `isPrevalent` (large sites that also serve third-party content and sign-ins, such as google.com and x.com) or `isScheduledForAllButCookieDataRemoval` (sites I reach through an OAuth redirect). So they are all on course to lose their data if I don't open them for a while.

I didn't manage to reproduce the removal end to end: I couldn't make ITP record anything in a bare `WKWebView` harness, even with the testing SPIs that move time forward. So this is the mechanism and the evidence in the database, not a captured removal.

**What might help:** a switch, off by default, that turns tracking prevention off for Search's data stores (`_setResourceLoadStatisticsEnabled:`, the same switch as Safari's "Prevent cross-site tracking"). The built-in blocker would still stop known trackers. People who want Chrome's behaviour, where a site keeps its sign-in until it expires, could turn it on.

macOS 27.0, Search 1.0.3.

items.title: Sites you rarely open can keep you signed in, a switch in Settings › Privacy
items.author: arvakme
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Fixes #362.

WebKit's Intelligent Tracking Prevention is on in every Search data store, as in Safari. When a site you signed in to goes unopened for a while, ITP clears its script-written storage. If WebKit has classified the site as prevalent, its cookies go too. Either way you come back signed out.

This adds **Settings › Privacy › Keep sign-ins on sites you rarely open**, off by default. Turned on, it switches tracking prevention off, through `_setResourceLoadStatisticsEnabled:`, the same switch as Safari's "Prevent cross-site tracking", in:

- the shared store, set from `Preferences.init` before the first page loads;
- every space's own store, as `Spaces.store(for:)` makes it;
- all stores already made, at once, when the switch is flipped while Search is open.

While the switch is off, WebKit's flag is never touched, so nothing changes for anyone who doesn't turn it on. The row sits under the ad blocker and says what turning it on costs: sites keep what they stored, as in Chrome, and the blocker still stops known trackers.

## Testing

- `swift build`: clean, no new warnings.
- The private selector exists on the macOS 27 WebKit. Both the default store and one made by identifier read back `false` after being set off, and `true` after being set on again.
- In the built app, two `SEARCH_PROBE` worlds loaded the same four sites through `./bench`. In the one with the switch left off, WebKit's `ResourceLoadStatistics/observations.db` recorded 54 domains. In the one with the switch on, no `ResourceLoadStatistics` database was created at all, and every page loaded normally.

Not covered:
- Flipping the switch in Settings while Search is open. That path goes through `Spaces.everyStore`, but I didn't drive it by hand.
- ITP actually removing a site's data. I couldn't get ITP to record anything in a bare `WKWebView` harness, so #362 rests on the WebKit source and on the ITP database of a real Search profile.

items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry

### Summary

In #140 Search registered `public.html` and `public.xhtml` document types in `Info.plist` so macOS can list Search as the default web browser. However, opening local files from the Finder did nothing because `Links` only accepted URLs with an `http` scheme prefix, and `WKWebView` requires `loadFileURL(_:allowingReadAccessTo:)` to load local documents and their accompanying assets.

### Changes
- `Sources/Search/Links.swift`: Update `application(_:open:)` and `handle(getURL:reply:)` to accept `file:` URLs (`url.isFileURL`) in addition to `http` and `https` URLs.
- `Sources/Search/Tab.swift`: Ensure file URLs are loaded via `loadFileURL(url, allowingReadAccessTo: url.deletingLastPathComponent())` across tab creation, restores, and reloads; compute tab monogram for file URLs using the file name initial.
- `CHANGELOG.md`: Add entry under `### Fixed`.

### Verification

- Executed verification script covering URL scheme filtering, tab monogram generation, and `WKWebView` file URL loading for both HTML and XHTML files.

items.author: DagimAlemayehuu
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry

### Summary
Follow-up to #95: when a link arrives in Search from an external application (Mail, Slack, Notion, Discord, terminal), Search can remain behind the originating app, and if its window was miniaturized to the Dock, `window.makeKeyAndOrderFront` does not de-miniaturize it.

- In `CHANGELOG.md`: added entry under `### Fixed`.

### Verification
- `swift build` passes with exit code 0 and 0 errors.
- Verified window de-miniaturization and activation flows in standalone test script.

items.title: Window › Move & Resize works on Search's window (#286)
items.author: karadoganyi
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
Fixes #286.

**Why it was greyed out.** `dress` keeps the window unmovable (fb79151) so that a tab dragged along the top moves itself and not the window. The tab row sits in the title bar, and SwiftUI's views under the tabs let AppKit move the window from them. macOS greys out Move & Resize, and beeps at its shortcuts, for a window that isn't movable.

**What changes.** The window stays unmovable at rest, exactly as on main. It's let go only while macOS may be asking (`HeldStill` in Stage.swift):
- while a menu is open;
- while a key with ⌃ is handled, since every Move & Resize shortcut has fn and ⌃.

It's held still again on the next turn of the run loop.

**Why not movable at rest.** I tried that first, holding the window still only during a press in the title bar. A press on a tab's top half was then taken by macOS as a drag of the window, before the app heard of it, and the tab never moved.

**Known limit.** A Move & Resize shortcut remapped to a key without ⌃ still beeps.

**Tested**
- New bench command `bench tiling` asks the window which Move & Resize commands it would let be picked. On main, none can be picked in any state. With this change:

  | State | Commands that can be picked |
  |---|---|
  | At rest | none |
  | Menu open | all nine |
  | While a ⌃ key is handled | all nine |
  | Next turn | none |

- New bench command `bench drag X1 Y1 X2 Y2` posts a drag through the app's event queue. A drag on a tab, on the empty strip or on the page leaves the window unmovable throughout, as on main.
- By hand, with a mouse and keyboard, on macOS 26:
  - fn-⌃-→ and fn-⌃-F tile the window.
  - Window › Move & Resize › Left works.
  - A tab dragged by its top half or its bottom half moves along the row, and the window stays put.
- `bench menu` now closes the menu it opens, which would otherwise leave the window movable for the rest of a test run.
- `swift build`: no new warnings.

The changelog line is under Unreleased › Fixed. The roadmap item is left for `./ideas done`.

items.title: A page's own Print… works: window.print() brings up the sheet
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
When a page printed itself, nothing happened. WebKit sends `window.print()` to a private UI delegate method, `_webView:printFrame:pdfFirstPageSize:completionHandler:`, and Search didn't implement it. ⌘P was dead on those pages too: the page gets it first (`pageFirst`), keeps it, and calls `print()`. I hit this on aadhar.sh, where Notepad's File › Print… and ⌘P both call `print()`.

## What changes

- `Browser` implements the method and puts the system's Print sheet on the page's window, the same way it already handles `_webView:saveDataToFile:…` for the PDF download button.
- It prints the frame that asked, through `-[WKWebView _printOperationWithPrintInfo:forFrame:]`. That selector is checked with `responds(to:)` first, and a WebKit without it prints the whole page.
- The page waits while the sheet is up, as in Safari. The completion handler runs from the sheet's `didRun`, through a small `PrintSheet` object kept alive by the sheet's context. While the page waits, WebKit draws the pages to print directly, which is how it expects this callback to be used.
- Only a page in a window can ask, and only when no sheet is already up, so a background tab can't put a Print sheet in front of you.
- `printPage()` and the new method build the print job in one place, `Browser.printing(_:frame:)`, with the same print settings as before.

## Tested

`./build.sh`, then a visible `SEARCH_PROBE` world on `aadhar.sh/writing/colophon`:

- Before: `window.print()` showed nothing (`./bench probe` listed no Print window).
- After: the Print sheet comes up on the window. While it's up, the page's script is held (an `eval` blocks). After the sheet closed, the page carried on and the line after `print()` ran.

Not checked: pressing Cancel or Print by hand. The test window's sheet closed while I was polling, and I didn't script clicks on it. Also not checked: `print()` called from inside an iframe (that path goes through `forFrame:`).

## Changelog

I left CHANGELOG and ROADMAP to you, as usual. A line for Fixed, if it helps:

> A page's own Print… button, and ⌘P on a page that keeps the key for itself, bring up the Print sheet. `window.print()` did nothing before.

items.title: extensions hear what their background sends their pages
items.author: dttdrv
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
WebKit hands none of an extension's pages a runtime message its worker or another of its pages sent. it's every message, not some: a listener added straight through WebKit's own onMessage.addListener, under the shim, hears nothing either. Bitwarden waits on those for its sync (ForegroundSyncService timed out on every sync) and for its passkey window, which opened blank, so passkey sign-ins through Bitwarden failed on every site.

each message the worker or a page sends now also goes over the shim's search-messages channel, and a page that didn't hear it from WebKit within 50 ms takes it from there. one WebKit did deliver is skipped, so nothing arrives twice if WebKit starts delivering them.

checked in Search Dev with Bitwarden 2026.9.2: a doFullSync from its page now gets fullSyncFinished back, a second page hears the worker's and the first page's messages once each, and registering on webauthn.io brings up Bitwarden's save passkey screen where it was blank.

items.title: Esc on a new, empty tab (⌘T) should close it and return to the previous tab
items.author: bhanni01
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
## Summary
After pressing ⌘T to open a new tab, pressing Esc minimizes the window instead of cancelling the new tab. I'd expect Esc to dismiss the new tab and return to the tab I was on, as if I'd pressed ⌘W.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Be on any page.
2. Press ⌘T to open a new tab.
3. Without typing anything or navigating, press Esc.

## Expected
The new, empty tab closes and the previous tab is selected again.

## Actual
The window gets minimized.

## Why
The README says `esc` puts away whatever is open, and a fresh ⌘T tab that hasn't gone anywhere is the thing that's open. Minimizing the window is surprising and loses your place. This matches how Esc already dismisses other transient UI (for example, the link peek).

## Scope
Only for a tab that was just opened with ⌘T and hasn't navigated yet. Once a page has loaded, Esc should behave as it does today.

I'm happy to open a PR for this.

## Summary
If I press ⌘T, start typing in the field, then switch to another tab (for example to look something up) and come back, what I typed is gone. I'd like the unsent text to stay in that tab's field until I send it or close the tab.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Press ⌘T and type something in the field, without pressing Return.
2. Switch to another tab.
3. Switch back to the new tab.

## Expected
The text I typed is still there, with the cursor at the end.

## Actual
The field is empty.

## Suggested approach
Keep the draft in memory on the tab itself, for as long as the tab is open. No need to write it to disk or cache: it's cleared when the text is sent or the tab is closed, so it never outlives the tab. This also keeps with Search's rule that nothing typed leaves the app until you press Return.

## Why
Opening a new tab, starting to type, then checking another tab for a word or link to finish the query is a common flow. Losing the text forces you to retype it.

I'm happy to open a PR for this.

items.title: fix: Better Tab Management
items.author: fschrhunt
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
## What this fixes

**Dragging a tab moved the whole window (#60 is back in 1.0.4).** 41c242a made the window movable between presses so that Window › Move & Resize would work (#286), holding it still only from a mouse-down monitor. macOS starts a title-bar drag in the window server before the app hears of the press, so the monitor is too late. I measured it with real mouse events on macOS 27: a hit view refusing `mouseDownCanMoveWindow` doesn't stop the drag, locking `isMovable` on the mouse-down doesn't either (the window still moved 70 of 80 points), and locking it on hover is racy. The band macOS treats as title bar is also only the top 32 points, whatever the strip's height, so a tab grabbed by its upper half moved the window and one grabbed by its lower half reordered. The only thing that holds is a window that is never movable, as before 1.0.4. Fill, Center and Move & Resize go grey again; the roadmap entry says why.

**Reordering was glitchy.** The row reordered live while a tab was carried, and gave the carried tab its new place on the row's spring while its offset compensated instantly, so it jumped a whole place away from the pointer and drifted back at every swap. The carried tab also lost its grey whenever hover tracking dropped out mid-drag (it always does, while the button is down), so the tab it was passing printed through its title, and the drop shadow under it was clipped flat at the row's edge and read as a smudge. And the run's scroll view clipped the tab at its end.

**Dragging a tab out was blind.** The pill was cut off at the window's edge, and the drop happened with nothing on screen to say where.

## What it does now

- **Reorder:** nothing is reordered until release. The carried tab is drawn wherever the hand is, the tabs it passes slide one place over on a spring, and on release the row reorders once with every place and offset springing together, so the only thing that moves is the carried tab settling in. Flat grey pill, no shadow, never clipped; carried past the end, it takes the plus along; the first tab stops at the start.
- **Out:** past the row's edge the pill grows into a small picture of the page that follows the pointer anywhere, and the row closes up behind it. Let go in the open, the picture grows into a new window there. A pin never leaves, nor the last tab of the only window.
- **Back in:** over any window's row, including its own, the picture becomes a pill in that row under the hand, the tabs make way, and letting go drops it there. A window emptied by that closes, as Safari's does.
- Column and row alike, with pins and tab groups. Reduce Motion is honoured.

Also in this PR, because it bit me while building: with Xcode 27, Swift 6.4's new default build system stamps the binary as linked against SDK 14.0 (the deployment target), and macOS 26+ then gives the app the pre-26 look. `build.sh` asks for SwiftPM's own build system, which stamps the real SDK. No change on Xcode 26.

## Before

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5e34008c-a7a1-438d-8242-82bbc3f632cc

## After

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/66f4f992-21fe-4a95-91ff-649fd3e0e8ec

## Notes for review

- `Tear.swift` is new and holds the picture panel and the window-under-the-pointer logic. The model side is the existing `moveToWindow` / `receive` / `detach`, with a landing index and an "or close" added.
- `Browser.dragOut` is kept for the bench's `towindow … at` probe; the drag itself no longer goes through it.
- Tried by hand on macOS 27.0 with both layouts. I have not run the bench's move/drag scenarios on a hidden probe.

items.author: luca-dupont2

items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
## Summary

Add a thin progress line along the top of a loading page. It uses WebKit's estimated progress, so it gives more detail than the tab's loading ring and remains visible when the tabs are folded away.

The line is off by default. Turn it on in **Settings › General › Show page load progress**.

## Implementation

- Keep the line's animation state tied to its tab, including when the single-page stage switches tabs.
- Fill and fade only after WebKit reports a successful navigation. Stopped and failed loads disappear without implying completion.
- Follow macOS Reduce Motion and let clicks pass through the line. Peek pages receive the same completion signal.

## Screenshot

![Search showing the grey page-load progress line halfway across the top of the page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luca-dupont2/Search/b54db47632b8de0ee6964661a2fc346c2a5aa576/.github/loadline-progress.png)

Captured from an isolated Search window loading a local page with a deliberately delayed image request.

## Verification

- `swift build` passes with Xcode 27 after rebasing onto upstream `main` at `4a1ad84`. Compiler warnings remain on lines outside this change.
- `git diff --check` passes.
- The screenshot captures the line while the page is still loading.

items.author: quanru

## Summary

Fix [SingleFile 1.27.0](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/singlefile/mpiodijhokgodhhofbcjdecpffjipkle) in Search.

- Allow SingleFile's `browser` getter to replace the global accessor. Search previously made it nonconfigurable, so SingleFile's service worker failed at startup.
- Convert extension-owned `blob:` download URLs to `data:` URLs that Search's page-based WebKit downloader can read.

## Actual reproduction and verification

On the installed Search build, SingleFile reported `TypeError: Attempting to change configurable attribute of unconfigurable property` in `lib/single-file-extension-background.js:2506`. Pressing its toolbar button on `https://example.com/?before=1` produced no file. Screenshot immediately after pressing:

In an isolated Search test profile using this branch, I installed SingleFile 1.27.0 from the Chrome Web Store, left its default save settings in place, opened `https://example.com/?final=1`, and pressed its toolbar button. The badge showed “完成”; Search's Downloads listed the new HTML file. I opened the file and confirmed it contains `https://example.com/?final=1`, `Example Domain`, and SingleFile's `Page saved with SingleFile` marker.

![SingleFile after: completed HTML download](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quanru/Search/fix/singlefile-compat/.github/evidence/singlefile-after.png)
