items.title: A key the page didn't take stops at its stage, instead of beeping
items.author: Chahine-tech
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Fixes #402: on a page that reads the arrows itself without taking them, such as the game in that report, the Mac plays its "can't do that" sound on every press. Safari doesn't.

## What happens

A key the page doesn't take is given back by WebKit to the **superclass's** `keyDown:` on the web view, so no override of `PageView`'s own ever sees it, and from there it walks up the responder chain. Nothing above a page wants a plain key, since Search's own are taken by the window's key monitor before the page sees them and the menus take theirs as key equivalents, so it goes all the way up, falls off the end, and AppKit beeps.

That last part is worth spelling out, because the quieting `PageView` already has (1.0.1, for editors that put the text in themselves) cannot reach this: it waits for the same event to come back through `keyDown`, and for these keys it never does. Traced on the page from #402, holding and tapping the arrows:

| | |
|---|---|
| presses seen by the page | 163 |
| distinct events | 163 |
| re-delivered to `PageView.keyDown` | 0 |
| quieted by the existing mechanism | 0 |

So the key has to be stopped above the page. `StageView` is the first view of ours it meets, and it is the page's frame, so it stops there. Split View is covered by the same line: its panes are `StageView`s of their own (`PaneStage.swift`).

A key a stage holds no page for goes on up as before.

## Checked

- The beep is gone on the page from #402, by ear on a build of this branch. That is the only test for it.
- The arrows still scroll a page that can scroll: 80 px for two presses, sent through the whole app rather than handed to the view.
- The space bar still scrolls a page: 760 px per press. It never reaches this path, WebKit takes it in the page.
- `⌘L` opens the address field and `esc` closes it.
- `⌘F` behaves identically with and without the change, compared build to build. Commands with a modifier arrive as key equivalents, which this doesn't touch.
- `python3 Tests/split_view.py`: 89 passed, 0 failed. Worth running here rather than
  elsewhere, since a pane of a pair is a `StageView` of its own, so the harness exercises
  the very class this changes: the cards a page puts over its own half, find in one pane,
  the moves, the swap, a page sent to another Space.
- `swift build` with no warning introduced.

## Note

This is a known shape of WebKit's on macOS rather than something Search was doing wrong: an Apple forum thread about a game in a `WKWebView` reaches the same conclusion, that overriding `keyDown` on the web view itself does nothing and it has to be a view around it. https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/748152

`CHANGELOG.md` gets its line under Unreleased › Fixed, crediting @pyrossh for the report.

items.title: A test world set up the way the bench skill says refuses every command
items.author: Chahine-tech
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
Following the bench skill to get a test world listening gives a world that refuses every command, and stays refusing.

What I did, as `skill/search-bench/SKILL.md` says: `defaults write SUITE bench -bool true`, then `./fresh.sh again`. What I expected: `./bench --test tabs` prints the tabs. What happened, on the first call and every one after it:

```
error: a window came onto a screen in this test run — stop the probe: the app brought forward
```

**Why.** `fresh.sh:40` launches with `open -n`, which activates the app. `Bench.watchScreens` catches `didBecomeActive`, appends to `caught` and hides the app again. Nothing ever clears `caught` (only `append` at 2784 and 2796, read at 240), so every later answer carries `onScreen` and `./bench` exits 3 for the life of that process. The world has to be killed and launched again.

The harnesses never meet this: `Tests/split_view.py:54` launches with `open -n -g -j`, and `Tests/fresh_window.py` goes through the same machinery. Only `fresh.sh`, which the skill sends you to, launches in a way the guard catches.

**Measured** on main at 5112683, macOS 27, two fresh named worlds, one variable between them:

| launch | result |
|---|---|
| `open -n --env SEARCH_PROBE=…` (as `fresh.sh` does) | refused on the first call |
| `open -n -g -j --env SEARCH_PROBE=…` (as the harnesses do) | tabs printed, world usable |

Both with `bench` written to the suite and nothing else. `welcomed` makes no difference either way, which I had wrongly assumed first.

**Worth saying**: the guard only runs once the socket is up (`Bench.start`, line 110), so `./fresh.sh` on a world without the switch is fine, and someone who just wants to look at a build still can. It is the switched-on case, the one the skill describes, that cannot work.

**A fix, if you want it that way**: `fresh.sh` reads that world's own `bench` default and adds `-g -j` when it is on, so a world meant to be driven starts hidden and a world meant to be looked at doesn't change. Happy to send it as a pull request, or to put it in the skill instead if you would rather the script stayed as it is.

items.title: Responsive Design Mode: a tab laid out as an iPhone, a Pixel or an iPad
items.author: StefanTodorov32
items.decision: Later
items.note: Useful native developer tool; private WebKit emulation APIs and incomplete touch/screen emulation. Coordinate #460.
items.body:
Search has the Web Inspector, but it had no way to look at a page as a phone would. Safari's Responsive Design Mode belongs to the Safari app, not to WebKit, so a WebKit browser doesn't get it for free. This adds one, the way Chrome's device toolbar and Safari's mode work.

## What it does

**View › Enter Responsive Design Mode**, or **⌃⌘R**, next to the Web Inspector items. The tab in front goes into a frame in the middle of the stage, with a bar above it:

- **Device.** Responsive, which takes a width and a height typed in; iPhone SE, X, 14, 16 Pro and 16 Pro Max; Pixel 7, Galaxy S20 Ultra and S8+; iPad Mini, Air and Pro. Sizes and densities are Chrome's, with this year's iPhones added.
- **Size.** Width × height in CSS pixels, and the rotate button.
- **Zoom.** Fit, which never goes past 100%, or 50–150%.
- **Pixel ratio**, reload, and close.

The page gets the device's layout size, its `devicePixelRatio`, and the user agent its own browser sends. That is iPhone/iPad Safari for Apple devices, and Chrome's reduced Android user agent for the others. It reloads when the user agent changes. Each tab keeps its own device, asleep too, and a new one starts with the last device picked. Turning it off gives back the Mac's layout, density and user agent. In Split View each page has its own StageView, so each can have its own device.

## How

`Devices.swift` holds the presets, the per-tab `Emulation`, and the bar. `StageView` places a page that has an emulation in a device frame instead of across the whole stage. When the Web Inspector is docked, the frame goes in the space the inspector leaves.

It uses three names outside WebKit's public API, the ones Safari's own mode uses. Each is checked with `responds(to:)` before use, as `Inspector.swift` does:

- `_setViewScale:` draws the page smaller than its CSS pixels, so a phone fits a short window.
- `_setLayoutMode:` with `_WKLayoutModeDynamicSizeComputedFromViewScale`. Without it, the default view-size layout divides only the width by the scale. A phone zoomed to fit then had a `100vh` of 82% of its height, and anything fixed to the bottom sat that far up.
- `_setOverrideDeviceScaleFactor:`. WebKit multiplies this by the view scale, so the device's ratio is divided by the scale before it is set.

A WebKit without these names shows the page at full size, cut to the frame.

One more change: in `App.swift` the developer items of the View menu are wrapped in a `Group`. SwiftUI showed no twentieth item in that `CommandGroup`, so the new item, and with it its shortcut, never appeared.

## Tested

This is a `SEARCH_PROBE` run on this branch, started hidden. On a page reporting its own metrics, iPhone X gives `innerWidth` 375, `innerHeight` 812, `100vh` 812, `devicePixelRatio` 3 and the iPhone user agent, with a `position: fixed; bottom: 0` bar at the device's bottom edge. Turning it off gives back the window's width, a density of 2 and the Mac user agent. A page put to sleep wakes as the same device.

Before rebasing onto `main`, I also used it on 1.0.4 with real sites, and checked the menu item and ⌃⌘R through the actual menu bar. `swift build` gives no new warnings.

**Not simulated:** touch events, `pointer: coarse` / `hover: none`, and `screen.width`/`height`, which still report the Mac's screen.

## Notes

- **No Settings switch:** it's a menu command like the Web Inspector, and nothing changes until you ask for it. Happy to add a switch if you'd rather it be opt-in.
- **Shortcut:** ⌃⌘R was free. ⌥⌘R (Safari's) is Reload From Origin here, and ⇧⌘M (Chrome's) is Stop Sound. It can be changed in Settings › Shortcuts.
- **No issue first:** there's no issue for this yet, sorry. Glad to open one or cut this down if the direction doesn't fit.

items.title: Keep browser folder selection in memory and bound import reads
items.author: quanru
items.decision: Adapt after #507
items.note: Strong import candidate: session-only picker, descriptor checks, bounded JSON reads, permission feedback. Latest source addresses earlier review requests; revalidate native consent and UI.
items.body:
Keep a chosen Chromium data folder only for the current session, show its path in the import sheet, and bound JSON reads to 64 MB. Nothing about the selection is persisted. Passwords still use only the chosen browser's own Safe Storage keychain item, and test runs ignore the session selection.

### Security review changes

- Resolve the chosen root before storing it; resolve profile/file paths and refuse anything outside the root. `file()` now returns the resolved path.
- Local State, Bookmarks, Preferences and Secure Preferences use the same open/fstat helper as database snapshots. Open with O_NOFOLLOW, require a regular file, then verify the opened descriptor's native path remains inside the resolved root. Read from that descriptor, not a separately reopened URL.
- Enforce the 64 MB JSON limit on initial size and throughout streaming reads, including a file growing after the initial check. Unreadable or oversized bookmark files cannot authorize replacement of existing imports.
- Database and WAL/SHM snapshots refuse final symlinks and copy from their opened descriptors with exclusive destination creation. **A linked WAL or SHM fails the entire snapshot**, rather than silently omitting potentially committed data.
- Profile discovery after the native folder picker runs off the main thread. The import options show “From ~/…” when the session-selected folder is active.

### Validation

Current revision: `8877bf8f6e698711a8de153581b3a9a058c60027`, based on upstream `59c1b4e`, without rewriting history. Local validation passed all 24 BrowserDiscoveryTests, BrowserImportBoundaryTests and ImportFileTests, plus the Release build.

The added regressions cover a denied profile directory, discovery after permissions are restored, a regular file at the browser root, an empty profile, and a directory that cannot be listed while known files remain readable. Discovery retains other readable profiles when one is denied. Welcome shows access warnings even when another browser is available.

[Exact-head hosted Intel Mac validation](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/38209484376/job/114680225228) passed all 24 scoped tests and the Release build. Workflow commit `f252b68` checks out and verifies product commit `8877bf8`; this result validates the current PR revision directly.

This update does not revalidate native TCC, the folder picker, or the visible UI. All new tests use temporary directories, without reading real browser profiles or requesting password keychain access. Not every individual file-content read failure is covered.

The earlier macOS 27.0 (26A428) check found the released Developer ID app could not discover Chrome's protected data. After the data owner authorized the native picker in an isolated ad-hoc-signed diagnostic build, Chrome appeared and its History preview became readable. No import or password-key request was performed. This is historical evidence for the session-picker approach, not a fresh GUI check of the new source-path label or a guarantee for every signing/entitlement combination.

Depends on #507 landing first. The two import diffs have shared hunks; synchronize this branch with the merged discovery change before final integration. This PR remains independent of model-backed E2E.

### Permission feedback (#583)

Automatic Chromium discovery now retains directory-read errors instead of converting them to an empty result. Welcome and the import sheet share messages that distinguish permission refusal, missing folders, readable folders with no profiles, and other read errors. Permission refusal points to the session folder picker; existing profile boundary checks remain in place. This prepares the related change for post-1.0.5 review and does not claim a fresh visual check or coverage of every individual file-content read failure.

items.title: Pins brought over from Arc wear letters until each one is opened
items.author: Chahine-tech
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
Bringing things over from Arc gave me its spaces and their pinned tabs, which is lovely, and eighteen pins that all wear a capital letter. Two `G`, two `C`, two `D`, three `E`: a letter doesn't tell Gmail from GitHub. Settings › Tabs › Tabs show › Site icons changes nothing until I open each pin one by one, and then that one gets its icon.

The bookmarks that came over in the same import wear their sites' icons straight away.

**Why the two differ.** `Favicons.shared.adopt` is called in one place, `Browser.swift:226`, and `source.icons(...)` right above it at 224, both inside the bookmarks branch and both for `Bookmarks.urls(found)`. `takeArc` (1785 to 1823) makes the spaces, the pins and the asleep tabs without either, so nothing ever reads Arc's `Favicons` file for those addresses.

The rest already works. `tab.restore(url:title:)` calls `adoptIcon()`, which is `icon = Favicons.shared.cached(host)`, so a pin takes its icon from the cache without a page. It finds nothing because nothing was put there for it. Opening the pin loads the page, and `Favicons.fetch(for:)` asks the page what it declares, which is the only other way an icon arrives.

**So**: the same three lines the bookmarks branch runs, over the addresses `takeArc` brings in, would give every imported pin its icon at once. Arc's `Favicons` is right there in the profile, 30 MB of it on this Mac, and `Chromium.icons(in:for:)` already knows how to read it. Nothing would leave the Mac.

The comment above `adopt` says it is meant for this:

> An icon from somewhere else, another browser's cache, at import, kept as if the site had handed it over

Seen on main at 5112683, macOS 27, importing from Arc with spaces, pins and bookmarks all ticked.

I can send it as a pull request if you'd like it that way.

items.body:
**What I did:** with the tabs in the sidebar, clicked the tab I was on to edit its address, on a tab near the bottom of the column (window close to the bottom of the screen).

**What I expected:** the site card (Connection is secure, Copy Address, Print, Zoom…) under the address, or above it if there's no room, with the field still visible.

items.title: ← and → move the caret out of sight in a long address being edited in a tab
items.author: StefanTodorov32
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
**What I did:** with the tabs in the sidebar, clicked the tab I was on to edit a long address (longer than the row), then used ← and → to move through it.

**What I expected:** the text scrolls to follow the caret, as in any text field.

**What happened:** only the start of the address was ever visible. The caret moved in the part cut off past the row's edge, so it looked as if the arrows did nothing, and the end of the address could never be seen.

items.title: Favicon does not update when a site changes icons for dark mode
items.author: keyding
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
## What happened

In macOS dark mode, a pinned GitHub page shows a black GitHub favicon on Search's dark pin background, making it hard to see. The same site shows a white GitHub icon in Dia and Chrome.

This is an example of a general problem: some sites change their favicon after the page loads, including when the page's color scheme changes. Search can keep showing the earlier icon.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Set macOS to dark mode.
2. Open `https://github.com` in Search and pin the tab.
3. Look at its icon in the pins area. Compare it with the icon in Dia or Chrome.

Tested on macOS 27.2 with Search 1.0.4 built from `3da44ed`.

## Expected

Search follows the site's current favicon: GitHub's white icon in dark mode and black icon in light mode. The behavior should work for any site that updates its favicon, without a GitHub-specific rule.

## Actual

The GitHub icon is black in Search's dark pins area.

## Investigation

GitHub changes its icon link after load as its theme changes. Search currently discovers favicon links when navigation finishes and caches the result by host. It does not follow later icon-link changes. This is not explained by SVG decoding alone: GitHub also offers a PNG favicon for the active theme.

## Acceptance criteria

- Update the displayed icon when a page changes its favicon link after load, including a theme change.
- Keep light and dark icon variants from overwriting each other in the cache.
- Apply the behavior to sites generally, without a GitHub-specific icon or URL rule.
- Coalesce rapid icon changes so they do not cause excessive downloads.

items.title: Pins brought over from Arc wear their icons at once
items.author: Chahine-tech
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Closes #416.

`takeArc` made the spaces, the pins and the asleep tabs without ever reading Arc's own icon store, while the bookmarks branch adopts theirs as they come in (`Browser.swift`, `source.icons` then `Favicons.adopt`). A pin reads the icon cache as it is made, through `restore(url:title:)` and `adoptIcon()`, and nothing had been put there for it, so it wore a letter until its page was opened, which is the only other way an icon arrives.

The same `icons` and `adopt` now run over the addresses `takeArc` brings in: a space's favourites, which become pins, and its pinned tabs. The ones already made read the cache again once the icons are there. `takeArc` takes the source and the profile to do it, which both callers already had in hand.

## A harness for it

`Tests/arc_icons.py`, in the shape of the others: it writes a made-up Arc into the world's own `Import` folder, a `StorableSidebar.json` with one space, one pinned tab and one favourite, and the `Favicons` file Arc keeps its icons in, with a small PNG for each. Then it asks the import for its spaces.

```
  ok   the made-up Arc is found
  ok   its favourite is a pin and its pinned tab came too
  ok   both wear Arc's icon, with no page opened
  ok   nothing was fetched: no tab holds a page
4 passed, 0 failed
```

On main the third one fails with an empty list, so it guards the thing it is about:

```
  FAIL both wear Arc's icon, with no page opened []
3 passed, 1 failed
```

## Checked

Five runs, each on a world of its own, wiped first, built from this branch and from main in a separate worktree:

| build | icons kept after `import Arc spaces` |
|---|---|
| main | none, 2 runs of 2 |
| this branch | `example.com.png` and `www.iana.org.png`, 3 runs of 3 |

The two addresses cover both ways in: `www.iana.org` as a favourite that becomes a pin, `example.com` as a pinned tab. No page is loaded either way, and nothing goes to the network: the icons come off the disk, out of Arc's own file.

`swift build` adds no warnings.

items.title: Would you want Apple Passwords in the list under the sign-in field?
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Needs coordination
items.note: Native Apple Passwords integration is maintainer-owned exploration using an undocumented helper. Browse first needs its own signing/entitlement path; retain the extension fallback.
items.body:
Search already handles passkeys through Apple's browser API, and Apple Passwords works through the iCloud Passwords extension. I've been wondering whether passwords saved in Apple Passwords could show up in Search's own list under the sign-in field, next to the passwords Search keeps and the passkeys.

Two things came up while I looked into it:

- There's no public API for this. The only way I know of runs through the helper app Apple ships for its browser extension. That helper is undocumented, so any macOS update could break it.
- macOS only lets a Developer ID-signed app start that helper. On my Mac the kernel refused to launch it from a build signed with an Apple Development certificate ("Launch Constraint Violation"). So only release builds could use it, and contributors couldn't test it locally.

Some questions before spending cycles:

1. Do you want this in Search at all, given it depends on a private helper?
2. If so, should it sit behind a setting and start off?
3. Or would you rather keep the extension as the way to reach Apple Passwords?

Either way I'm happy to help, whether that's testing on a release build or polishing the extension path.

items.title: Pinned rows, as in Arc: pins kept as rows under the squares, and a line with Clear
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Maintainer landing reference verified in Browse ancestry
items.note: Inspect current code; the landing may be an adapted subset, not the original PR unchanged.
items.body:
Closes #183 ("Pins as a list", including the Arc-style pinned rows above New Tab).

Arc splits its sidebar into three tiers: app-like favorites, a pinned list, and tabs that come and go. Search already has the first and the last. This adds the middle one, off unless you turn it on in **Settings › Tabs › Pinned rows** (shown with the tabs down the side).

## What it does

- **Rows under the squares.** Right-click a tab for **Pin as Row**, or **Show as Row** / **Show as Square** on a pin you have. The Tabs menu has the same.
- **A row is a pin in every other way.** ⌘W puts it down, it's the same in every window, it never joins a group or a pair. Its hover cross is a minus, since it won't close. A click on it edits the address like any row, so going home lives in its menu as **Back to Pinned Page**.
- **The line.** A hairline between the kept tiers and the rest, with **Clear** at its end under the pointer. Clear closes the loose tabs below it through `close()`, so ⇧⌘T brings them back. Pins and tab groups stay. The page on screen goes last, after an empty tab takes its place, so no neighbour wakes only to be closed.

## How it's built

A row is a pin with one more field, `Tab.listed`, carried in `PinDef` and `Session.Entry` as an optional that's only written when true. Every existing `pin != nil` check keeps meaning the right thing for rows without being touched. A pins file with no rows is written exactly as before (`fresh_window.py`'s "pins file untouched" check still passes).

The row keeps the order squares, then rows, then everything else (`settlePin`, and `reconcilePins` for pins arriving from another window). So a square's cell in the grid is still its index in `tabs`, and `PinCarried` and ⌘1–⌘9 needed no change. A carry across tiers is refused while rows are shown. With the switch off, or with the tabs across the top, rows are drawn as squares, and a pin carried across the hidden line takes the kind it landed among, so turning the switch back on finds a valid order and loses nothing.

## Testing

- New `Tests/pin_tiers.py` (bench-driven, hidden, in a world of its own): 20 checks covering order, carry limits, switching kinds, pins.json and the session, restart, unpin, Clear from a loose tab and from a pin, the switch off, and the tabs across the top. 20/20.
- `fresh_window.py`: 7/7. `split_view.py`: 91/92. The one miss was slice 6's 30 ms motion sampling on even-out, which touches no pins and passed 3/3 on rerun.
- `PinCarriedTests`: pass. No new build warnings.
- Checked by eye in a visible test window: squares, rows, line, loose tabs, in that order. Not checked: Clear's hover appearance.

The bench grows a `listed` flag on `pin`, a `clear` split action, and `listed` in `state`.

## Not in this PR

- Arc's 12-hour auto-archive of loose tabs. It closes tabs on a timer, so it'd want its own switch.
- Arc import bringing Arc's pinned list in as rows (today it lands as loose tabs).
- The roadmap entry, which `./ideas` keeps.

items.title: The window moves by the top of the page, as in Arc and Dia
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
Arc and Dia let you move the window by grabbing a site's top bar, so the page reads as part of the window rather than a pane inside it. With the tabs down the side, Search's page already runs up to the window's top, but only the column's part of that edge moved the window. This adds the rest, off unless you turn it on in **Settings › General › Move the window by the top of a page**.

## What it does

- **Empty ground moves the window.** A drag that starts on an empty part of a site's top bar, or of any page's top 52 px (the strip's height, where a title bar would be), moves the window through `performDrag(with:)`, the same system drag `DragStrip` uses. It snaps and tiles as any window does.
- **What a hand would use stays the page's.** Links, buttons, fields, media, widget roles, anything the site gave its own cursor (how most clickable `div`s say so), and words that can be selected. Words marked `user-select: none` count as ground, since there's nothing to select.
- **A click is still a click.** A press on the ground is held until it's known: let go without moving and the page gets the whole click; past 3 pt of slack it's the window's and the page never hears of it. A double-click's second press, and any press with ⌘ ⇧ ⌥ or ⌃ held, goes straight to the page.

## How it's built

The page lives in another process, and whether a drag is the window's has to be known when the press lands. So the page says ahead of time. `GrabRelay` (new `Grab.swift`) puts a listener in Search's own world, main frame only, that works out on pointer moves (once a frame at most) whether the ground under the pointer is grabbable, and posts only when the answer changes. `PageView` keeps the last answer and decides on `mouseDown`.

What counts as a top bar: the page's top edge, and below it an element at least half the page wide whose top is the page's top and that is no taller than 120 px. Once the page is scrolled, only a fixed or sticky one counts, so an article passing under the top isn't taken for a header. Below 120 px the listener returns before touching the page, so moves over the body cost one comparison.

Off, nothing reaches a page and `PageView.mouseDown` takes the same path as before. Turning it on or off applies to open tabs straight away, the way Show where links go does.

## Testing

- New `Tests/page_grab.py` (bench-driven, hidden, in a world of its own): 18 checks covering the switch off, header ground vs. link/button/words/cursor/field/role, unselectable words, below the header, a sticky header scrolled, a page with no header, the relay reaching the view, and a click on the ground still reaching the page. 18/18, three runs in a row.
- The bench grows a `grab` readout of the view's flag.
- `fresh_window.py`: 7/7. `split_view.py`: 92/92 on one run, 90/92 on the other two, the misses both times slice 6's motion sampling (`swap: both pictures travel` and `even out`), which touches no mouse handling and doesn't turn this switch on.
- No new build warnings.
- Checked by hand in a visible window: dragging a site's header and a bare page's top edge moves the window; links and fields there behave as before.

## Not in this PR

- A double-click on the ground zooming the window as a title bar's does. Pages use double-clicks, so it would want a closer look.
- Leaving out a peek's page: its top bar moves the whole window too, which seemed harmless.

items.title: Are the browser's own questions deliberately system sheets, where a page's are not?
items.author: Chahine-tech
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
A question about a line in the design rather than a report, since I couldn't find it settled anywhere and it decides whether a change is worth proposing at all.

Every question in the app is a system sheet, whoever is asking. Nine of them:

| Where | What it asks |
|---|---|
| `Dialogs.swift` | a page's own alert, confirm and prompt, titled with the site |
| `Dialogs.swift` | a site that can't prove who it is |
| `Dialogs.swift` | a site asking you to sign in |
| `Browser.swift` | a page that wants to open another app |
| `Extensions.swift` | adding an extension, and an extension asking for more access |
| `Extensions.swift` | removing an extension |
| `Spaces.swift` | naming a space, a new space, and are you sure |

The one place that is not a sheet is Split View: there a page's question is a card over its own half, so the other page goes on working. That reads like something the shared window forces rather than a preference, since a sheet covers the whole window.

And `Dialogs.swift` says what the rule is about, which is the title rather than the chrome:

> The site's name as the title, so a page can't dress its message up as one from the system or from the browser.

So the question: **is the system sheet the deliberate voice for every question Search asks**, with the Split View card only what a shared window forces? It would be worth having written down, because the other reading is that these sheets are waiting their turn and someone will eventually offer to restyle them into the app's own cards, starting with the extension install. I'd rather not be that someone if the answer is no, and the hardening note about installing the extension a store page actually shows suggests it is no.

If the sheets stay, the only thing open is their wording. If they don't, the question applies to all nine at once rather than to any of them alone.

No change proposed here, and nothing needed if the answer is "deliberate, they stay".

*Edited: the first version of this said a page's questions are drawn in Search's own style. They are system sheets too, except in Split View. The correction makes the question a narrower one.*

items.title: Tabs that close themselves, as in Arc: kept by a pin, a name or a group
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Later
items.note: Optional clutter control with separate expiry bookkeeping and whole-split checks. Not a memory fix; exercise unsaved state and relaunch.
items.body:
The other half of Arc's model, after pinned rows (#426): every tab you open is temporary unless you say it's for keeping. Pinned rows gave kept tabs their own place above the line. This makes the tabs below the line temporary. Off unless turned on.

## Tabs that close themselves

**Settings › Tabs › Close tabs you leave alone**: Never (the default), or after 12 hours, a day, a week or a month without being looked at. A tab that runs out closes the way ⌘W would, so ⇧⌘T and History bring it back. With pinned rows on, the line with Clear is the boundary: everything under it closes on its own, and everything over it stays.

- **What stays:** a pinned tab (square or row), a named tab, or a tab in a group. Letting go of any of those restarts the tab's clock, so a pin you've had for weeks doesn't close a minute after you unpin it.
- **What never closes:** the page on screen, a private tab (nothing could bring it back), and anything busy the way a tab kept awake is: sound, a call, a download, a question waiting, something typed and not sent. `awake(because:)` hands its busy half to a new `busy(_:)` that both features ask, so the two lists can't drift apart. A Split View pair closes whole or not at all.
- **The clock survives a quit.** `Tab.touched` reset on every launch, so anyone who quits nightly would never see a tab expire. It's now saved as `Session.Entry.touched` (never later than now, in case the clock was wrong once). A pass at launch, and on coming into a space, closes what ran out before it's drawn. Sessions from before this start counting at launch, so nothing vanishes on update.
- **Other spaces:** rows kept in memory close their own tabs and rewrite their files. Those tabs skip ⇧⌘T, which would reopen them in the space on screen with that space's sign-ins; History still has them.

The roadmap has this as not planned, because "a tab you leave alone sleeps after half an hour and costs nothing, so there's nothing to clear away." Sleep does settle the memory. What it can't settle is the column itself: a row of forty tabs costs attention even when every one of them is asleep. That's the reason Arc does this, and the reason it only makes sense as something you turn on.

## Also

`Tests/pin_tiers.py` gets one line, `sv.SOCK`. Since 2432be9 the harness computes the socket path when the module loads, so a test that switches to its own world has to reset `SOCK` along with `SUPPORT`, or it watches the wrong socket and can't recognize its own probe. `closing_tabs.py` does the same.

## Testing

- `Tests/closing_tabs.py` (new): 21/21. Covers Never, each way of keeping a tab, private tabs, pairs, something typed (real keys, then the box emptied as a control), ⇧⌘T, unpinning and unnaming, the clock across a relaunch, the launch pass, and another space's row.
- On this branch merged with current `main`: `pin_tiers.py` 20/20, `split_view.py` 92/92, `fresh_window.py` 7/7.
- Not checked by eye: the Settings row. It's a menu `Picker`, like "Search with".

It has a CHANGELOG line under Unreleased. I haven't touched the roadmap, since it's written from the ideas database.

items.title: A link's small window comes alone, and its keys act on its page
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Adapt with #549/#554
items.note: Fix small-window launch/key ownership; preserves hidden saved windows rather than closing them. Supersedes closed #519. Test external launch and quit before main windows return.
items.body:
With **Settings › General › Open links from other apps in a small window** on, a link from Slack or Mail opened the small window with the browser's big window right behind it, and the small window's keys reached through to that big window. This PR makes the small window come alone and act on its own page.

Split per review: the new look of the small window's top line and Find in the small window (with `FindSession`) are on their own branches, to follow after 1.0.5 (see the bottom).

## The big window stays where it was

`Links.deliver` called `Browsers.ensureWindow()` before it checked the setting, so a closed window came back first and the small window opened in front of it. The setting is now checked first, in `Links.take`, and the small window opens with no browser window coming forward.

**A launch made by the link.** SwiftUI opens its window at every launch, a link's included, and asks nobody (`applicationShouldOpenUntitledFile` isn't consulted). An earlier version of this PR closed the browser's windows for such a launch. As review pointed out, that loses data: a window closed while another is open is retired (`Browsers.closing`), its tabs out of the session and `windows.json`, and windows restored behind it then went unsaved.

Now they are **put away, never closed**. A small window's link that arrives before launch finishes sets `Browsers.keepAway()`. `putAway()` takes every browser window off screen with `orderOut`: SwiftUI's own (known before `ContentView` ties it to a browser by its frame's autosave name) at `didFinishLaunching`, a turn later, and as each window is dressed. `open()` keeps last time's other windows off screen as they are restored. The windows stay open, with their tabs, and nothing about them is written differently.

`bringBack()` puts them all on screen together, restoring any not yet opened, the first time a window is wanted: Open in Search (⌘O), another link (`ensureWindow`), ⌘N, or the Dock icon (`applicationShouldHandleReopen`, which macOS would otherwise skip with the small window on screen). `save()` keeps last time's other records while they haven't been restored, so quitting before any window is wanted drops nothing.

## The small window's keys are its own

- **Its own key monitor.** Its ⌘W, Esc and ⌘O were handled by a browser window's monitor, and on a launch made by a link no browser window is on screen, so ⌘W fell through to File › Close Tab and closed a tab in a window nobody could see.
- **Copy, reload, zoom on its page.** Commands it didn't claim fell through to the menus, which act on the browser's front tab: ⌘⇧C copied the big window's page (or nothing) and said so there, ⌘R reloaded a page behind you. `LittleWindow.take` now answers Copy Address, Copy as Markdown Link, Reload, Reload From Origin, Zoom In, Zoom Out and Actual Size on its own tab, on whatever keys **Settings › Shortcuts** gives them. Copying and zooming say so at the small window's foot ("Address copied", "110%"), in the capsule the browser's window uses; the tab's `onZoom` had pointed at the browser's window behind it. The Markdown link is `Browser.markdownLink`, shared with the browser's own command.

## Testing

- New `Tests/little_window.py` on `split_view.py`'s harness, in a world of its own (`little-tests`), 20 checks. The small window: ⌘⇧C copies its address and says so and stops saying it, ⌘+ / ⌘- / ⌘0 zoom its page and say so there, ⌘W and Escape close it and leave the row alone, Open in Search moves its page into the row. **A launch with three saved windows:** every window kept away and none closed, `windows.json` still has all three after a quit without bringing them back, Open in Search brings all three back with the page in the row, and a plain launch after has all three with their pages. 20/20, three runs in a row.
- The same test with put-away swapped back to closing: 4 fail (windows closed, `windows.json` cut short, the first window's tabs replaced, a plain launch after coming back short), which is the loss review described.
- A test run takes no links from outside, so `SEARCH_LINK` stands in for one that launches the app. The bench's `press` takes `"little": true`, `little look` reads the small window without acting, and the `windows` readout says which are `away`.
- `fresh_window.py` 7/7, `close_panel.py` 9/9, `split_view.py` 92/92, `swift test` 47/47. Merged with `main` (#476's harness and the rest), no conflicts.

## Following after 1.0.5

Both stacked on this branch, ready to open as PRs once it lands:

- [`claude/small-window-look`](https://github.com/oddharsh/Search/compare/claude/search-popout-toolbar-style-5b8ff3...claude/small-window-look): the line takes the page's colour as Safari finds it, under glass on macOS 26, with even spacing and resting lights. `Little.swift` and `Lights.swift` only.
- [`claude/small-window-find`](https://github.com/oddharsh/Search/compare/claude/search-popout-toolbar-style-5b8ff3...claude/small-window-find): find's state moves into `FindSession`, and the small window gets its own find bar. 25/25 in `little_window.py`, `split_view.py` 92/92.

## Not in this PR

- Other menu commands pressed in the small window (Reading Mode, Hide Elements, Print, Share) still act on the browser's front tab.

items.title: One ⇧⌘T after Clear brings back everything it closed
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
The follow-up from #426: one ⇧⌘T right after **Clear** undoes the whole Clear, instead of bringing tabs back one at a time.

## What it does

- **Everything back, in place.** Each tab returns where it was, and the tab you were on returns to the front. A Clear made from a pin leaves you on the pin.
- **Only one tab loads.** The others come back asleep, as last session's tabs do, so undoing a Clear of 30 tabs loads one page.
- **The empty tab Clear left goes,** unless something was typed into it.
- **A Split View pair cleared together is a pair again.**
- **The menus say it:** File and a tab's menu read "Reopen 14 Cleared Tabs" while ⇧⌘T would do that, and "Reopen Closed Tab" otherwise. Shortcuts bind by id, so a rebound key still works.

## How

Ghosts from one Clear share a `batch` id. `reopen()` hands a batched ghost to `reopen(batch:)`, which replays the batch newest-closed first. Each ghost's index was taken in the row just before that tab left it, so the replay puts the row back step by step. A ghost also keeps the id of the tab it was, because a reopened tab gets a new id and a cleared pair has to find its other half. The pair is rebuilt directly rather than through `pair()`, which would take the focus and wake both pages.

The cap of 12 now counts undo steps, with a Clear as one step. Before this, clearing 14 tabs silently lost 2 of them before anyone could undo.

A single ghost from a Clear, picked in History › Recently Closed or through the extensions' `sessions.restore`, still reopens alone, as before.

## Testing

- `pin_tiers.py`: 29/29. It has 9 new checks:
  - an undo of Clear from a loose tab brings back the same row, the same tab in front, no leftover empty tab, and nothing left to reopen;
  - Clear of 14 tabs from a pin, with a pair among them: all 14 back in order, the pin still in front, the pair paired again;
  - the menu title in both cases.
- `split_view.py`: 92/92. `fresh_window.py`: 7/7. No new build warnings.

`pin_tiers.py` also gets `sv.SOCK = f"{sv.SUPPORT}/bench.sock"`. Since 2432be9, `split_view.py` reads its socket once at import, so without the line the test talked to `split-tests`' socket. #429 adds the same line in the same place.

items.author: karadoganyi

items.body:
Nothing in Tests/ covered the password vault or the updater, and both matter
more than most code here. This adds 17 tests for the parts that need neither
the keychain nor the network. No source file changes.

What they pin down:
- Which host a login belongs to, including that an Android app's login
  (android://…@com.vendor.app/) gives no host.
- That the registrable domain never merges two tenants of a shared suffix, so
  one github.io site can't be offered another's saved logins, and that
  matching falls back to the exact host when no suffix list is available.
- How a password export is read: rows that can't be kept are counted as
  skipped, and quoted fields with newlines or doubled quotes stay one row.
- That a release needing a newer macOS isn't offered.
- That an unsigned feed is refused: garbage, and a valid appcast.json.zip
  with no code signature, both come back nil from Updater.opened.

Checked:
- swift test: 35 tests, 0 failures, no new warnings.
- The unsigned-feed test fails if the signature check is removed from
  Updater.opened, so it exercises the check itself and not a missing file.
- No test touches the keychain: every CSV row used is one that gets skipped.

Not covered: Updater.link and the CSV parser are private, so they are tested
only through Vault.take. Testing link directly would need it made internal;
I left that out to keep this tests-only. Happy to do it if you'd like.

items.title: Extensions loaded from a folder get Chrome's id from their path
items.author: AllDaGearNoIdea
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
An extension loaded from a folder now gets the id Chrome gives it, so a native messaging host shipped for it accepts it. Before, it got a random `local-*` id, which no host's `allowed_origins` lists. StopTheMadness Pro, for one, installs its Chrome extension as a folder inside its app, and its host lists only Chrome's id for that folder.

Reworked after review: the id comes from the folder's real path only. A manifest's `key` is ignored, since nothing checks it and Web Store public keys are public, so a folder could otherwise claim any extension's id along with its native hosts and stored data.

- `Crx.unpackedID(for:)` hashes the folder's `realpath` (a symlinked folder gets its target's id) and never reads `manifest.json`.
- Loading a folder already installed says "Already installed. Press Reload to take its changes" instead of adding a second copy.
- `management.getSelf` reads `fromStore` for `installType`, as the id no longer carries a `local-` prefix.
- Extensions loaded before keep their `local-*` id until removed and loaded again.

Where else the prefix or `key` could matter, checked:
- Nothing else derives an id from `key`: `load()` sets `uniqueIdentifier` and `baseURL` from `Installed.id`, and ids come only from `Crx.id(in:)` for store installs and `Crx.unpackedID` for folders.
- The only use of the `local-` prefix was `installType`. Update checks, Reload and Remove already go by `fromStore` and `source`, so a folder extension is never checked against the Web Store.
- Every install path still refuses an id already installed, and `admit()` checks again after the prompt.

The fixes for StopTheMadness's worker link and for replies cut off by a host's exit are now separate pull requests.

Test:
- `swift test --filter UnpackedIDTests`: the path id matches the one StopTheMadness's host lists (`paflpghjhdjaeapkeiophohkhagfcjih`), a `key` in the manifest is ignored, two folders with the same `key` get different ids, a symlinked folder gets its target's id
- `Tests/run-extension-files-tests.sh` passes, `swift build` adds no warnings
- StopTheMadness Pro loaded unpacked in a test world, with the other two fixes: id `paflpghjhdjaeapkeiophohkhagfcjih`, settings open without an error on 8 of 8 cold launches, no host process left behind. On main it shows "Native messaging port disconnected" on 3 of 3.

items.title: Configurable Sleep Policy
items.author: binaryfields
items.decision: Adopt as polish
items.note: Small sleep timing control with defaults and safety exclusions unchanged. Does not solve #520 or active-page memory growth.
items.body:
This PR adds support for fine-tuning how sleep is enforced in order to give user more control over resource usage.

### UX

In Settings > Tabs, a new control appears under 'Sleep tabs you aren't using' (only when that option is enabled):

- How soon tabs sleep - choices: Later, Normal, Sooner
- Helper text under the control explains the selected behavior 

### Policy

Only the idle wait time changes. The rules for which tabs sleep are unchanged.

| Policy | A tab sleeps after |
|--------|--------------------|
| Later | 2 hours |
| Normal | 30 minutes |
| Sooner | 10 minutes |

Low-memory conditions still override the selected pace:
- When macOS issues a memory warning, the wait drops to 5 minutes.
- When memory is critical, tabs sleep immediately.

The sleep.after preference continues to override the selected policy (used by the benchmark).

Existing setups are unaffected: the policy defaults to Normal, and the on/off switch for sleeping inactive tabs is unchanged.

### Exceptions

The following remain exempt (unchanged from main):
- The visible tab
- Pinned tabs
- Tabs that are playing audio, on a call, recording the screen, downloading, showing picture-in-picture, still loading, waiting on a dialog, or holding unsent typed text

items.title: After an import, the tabs across the top read as one row of nineteen marks
items.author: Chahine-tech
items.decision: Needs coordination
items.note: Three parts: import bookmarks-bar offer already inherited via #485; pin/tab separation and compact-tab background remain layout work. Do not mark the whole issue solved.
items.body: Coming from Arc, on main at 1ec28a0, macOS 27: one import brought 1 space, 6 favourites, 13 pinned tabs and 24 bookmarks into a fresh profile. That is one click, and it is what anyone arriving from another browser does first. It is also the first screen you meet afterwards, and the one where I would have gone back to Arc if I hadn't been reading the source at the same time. With the tabs down the left, the result is lovely: the pins are a grid of squares, a line under them, then the tabs as rows with their icons and their titles, and New tab written out. With the tabs across the top, the same session is 19 marks in a row with nothing to tell them apart, and the 24 bookmarks are nowhere to be seen. Three things behind that, each on its own. ## 1. Nothing separates the pins from the tabs across the top The sidebar tells them apart three ways at once: squares against rows, a line under the grid, and titles. The top strip has none of the three. A pin is a 16 point mark on a faint ground; a tab that has shrunk is a 16 point mark on nothing. The block of pins and the run of tabs read as one row of nineteen. The line already exists in the sidebar. The same line, standing up, between the last pin and the first tab, would say what the sidebar already says. ## 2. A tab that has shrunk to a mark has nothing behind it The reason for the pin's ground is in the code, and it is the right reason: > A letter with nothing behind it reads as debris. A pinned tab keeps a faint ground of its own so the block of them reads as one thing. A compact tab is exactly a letter with nothing behind it: a 16 point mark alone in a 59 point slot. The row has no boundaries, so it is hard to see where one tab ends, and it reads as a toolbar rather than as tabs. Losing the title past a dozen tabs is what every browser does and is not the complaint; losing the ground with it is what makes the row unreadable. ## 3. After an import, the bookmarks bar is still off 24 bookmarks came in and nothing says where they went. The panel offers **Show bookmarks**, which opens the bookmarks panel, so you see them once and never learn the bar exists. Someone arriving from Chrome, Firefox or Arc has no reason to think a bookmarks bar is optional, and that is the row they are looking for when they scan the top of the window. A second pill beside **Show bookmarks**, turning the bar on, would make it findable at the one moment it has something to show, without turning anything on by itself. ## Not the complaint The letters, which are a setting and which others have asked to keep; the titles going away past a dozen tabs, which every browser does; and my own bookmarks being two folders deep, which is Arc's doing. Happy to send any of the three as a pull request, or to split this into three issues if that reads better.

items.title: Light pages darkened while Search is dark, in their own colours
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Defer
items.note: 2,269 additions; broad page recoloring/observers and expensive site compatibility work. Reader dark mode is a smaller first step.
items.body:
Darkens the sites that stay light while Search is dark, the way Dark Reader does, in the site's own colours. A site with a dark look of its own is left as it is. Off unless turned on in **Settings › Appearance › Darken pages that stay light**.

## Against the review

- **Off unless turned on.** `pages.dusk` defaults to false. The line shows under Appearance whenever it's Dark or System.
- **Only where it's needed.** Nothing goes into a page unless darkening is on, Search is dark, and that page is light. A site not known yet is looked at from outside, with no script: a snapshot of its first frame (and again at `didFinish`), 48 pixels wide, and how much of it is light (`Dusk.look`). Light, and the page is darkened then, and every later page of the site from its first frame; dark, and it gets no script, observer or stylesheet. `dark_pages.py` checks that a dark page, and a page opened while Search is Light, has nothing of ours in it.
- **One site's verdict per page.** `arm(hiding:to:)` hands over only that host's choice and measurement, and the page checks the host is its own, so a redirect lands knowing nothing. The lists stay in Swift, and what's measured lasts the session only.
- **No second fetch.** Nothing is asked for again. A sheet from another site that can't be read (Amazon's and NYT's CDNs) is handled by what it colours: each element's computed colours that no twin reached are taken dark and set on the element as custom properties, which a few rules written once put to use. Small dark logos are only looked at when the page can already read them.
- **Cost.**
  - No timer that never stops: the one-second check runs until ten seconds after the load, and again for ten seconds when the page moves to another address of its own (Search tells it, on a same-document URL change).
  - No whole-document observer for the page's life: the same ten seconds. Only the `<head>`, for a new sheet, is watched for the page's life.
  - A stylesheet that doesn't only grow: when a watch ends, twins of sheets the page took out, marks no element carries, and attribute colours no element has are dropped.
  - What's added is taken in one batch a frame, every element read first and written after. Amazon had been working its whole style out a thousand times during load.
  - Once a page shows in its own colours it isn't measured again. Measuring set our sheets aside and back, four full style rebuilds a time, and sites change the classes on `<html>` constantly.
  - The filter's sheet is written only when its text changes. It was rewritten on every step while a page grew, and a rewritten sheet has the whole style worked out again (about 180 ms a time on NYT).
  - An element's style attribute is read for colours only when its text changes and names a colour. NYT animates transforms through it: 9,534 reads during load before, a regex check each now.
  - Something added inside something else added in the same frame is walked once, with what holds it.

The cost that's left, measured as the page's web process CPU over its first 12 seconds, darkened against a baseline that already has Search's script world, as every tab does (three runs each; NYT's ads move a run by a second or more):

| | Baseline | Darkened | Extra |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wikipedia | 470 ms | 700 ms | +230 ms |
| Amazon | 2,690 ms | 3,240 ms | +550 ms |
| NYT | 8,290 ms | 11,710 to 13,010 ms | +3,400 to +4,700 ms |

What's left on NYT is mostly work done as the page adds content during its load: new nodes checked for inline colours, logos and shadow roots, and colours from its CDN sheets read off the elements (it has sheets that can't be read, so those are painted). Tried and left out, each measured the same way:

- Rewriting the colours inside the site's own rules in place, instead of a rule beside each: the same cost within the noise, and it edits the site's stylesheets.
- A 3-second watch window instead of 10: the same cost. The work is in the load, not after it.
- No watching after the first pass: about 1,800 ms less on NYT and 300 ms on Amazon, but content added later (a comment box, a feed with inline colours) would show light. A new sheet in the `<head>`, and anything a stylesheet colours, would still be darkened.

## What it does

- **Measured on the page.** Before a page first shows in its own colours, its colours are sampled at nine points with ours set aside; a page that's mostly dark is left alone and Search remembers it for the session.
- **The site's design, in dark colours.** Every colour the site sets goes to a dark one of the same hue, so brand colours stay recognisable, and pictures and videos aren't touched. Dark logos drawn on nothing are turned light, writing laid over a photo keeps its colour, and frames and web components go with their page.
- **⇧⌘D**, or **Darken This Site** in the site card, switches it for the site you're on, at once, and it's kept. **⌥⇧⌘D** pauses it everywhere until pressed again or Search quits. A private tab is darkened and keeps nothing.

## How it's built

WebKit has no force-dark, and the paint-time filter Mail uses (`-apple-color-filter`) isn't parsed in a web view even with `_setColorFilterEnabled:` on (macOS 27.2).

**In the site's colours** (`DuskColours.swift`, macOS 15 and later): for every rule of the page's that sets a colour, a twin with the same selector in the same order, grouped the same way, in a sheet of its own after the page's, so the cascade settles each element as it did for the site. A twin is relative colour syntax, `oklch(from <the site's colour> <new lightness> c h / alpha)`, so the browser does the arithmetic for any colour the site names, variables and P3 included. Three lightness curves by the part a colour plays: grounds dark (a strong colour keeps more of its lightness), writing light, lines between. Style attributes, `bgcolor`, `<font color>` and SVG `fill` are twinned too; `multiply` blends go to `normal`; a site's transitions are held still while our sheets change. Each open shadow root gets twins of its own sheets.

**Frames** run the page script on their own document and wait: Swift tells each frame that asks whether its page is darkened, and again whenever that changes. A frame darkens only then, and only if it measures light itself.

**Turned over** (the filter) covers the page from its first frame until the twins are ready, and does all of it where the browser can't do relative colours (macOS 14).

## Testing

- `Tests/DuskHarness.swift`: the page script, read out of the sources, on 37 made-up pages in a dark web view, including a sheet from another origin served by a scheme handler, whose rules the page can't read, and a check that the site's own rules read the same darkened and after. A deliberately false check fails, so the checks are real. 37/37.
- `Tests/dark_pages.py` (bench-driven, hidden, a world of its own): off by default; turned on, the light page up is looked at and darkened without a reload; a light site from its first frame; a dark site left alone with nothing of ours in it; ⇧⌘D live, kept and cleared; ⌥⇧⌘D, including after the setting is turned on at runtime; Light and back; the setting off and on; a private tab. 26/26.
- Screenshots of Amazon, eBay, Wikipedia, Hacker News, NYT and W3Schools' Try it editor against the site as it made itself.
- No new build warnings.

## Known limits

- The CPU cost above, on pages as heavy as NYT.
- The first visit to a light site in a session shows its first frame light before it's darkened: nothing is in the page to do it sooner.
- On a site's first page, frames aren't darkened until the next page; they get the script from the first frame of the pages after.
- Colours an unreadable sheet gives on hover, or to something a class change brings later, show as the site made them.
- Closed shadow roots can't be reached, and colours inside `@keyframes` aren't twinned.

## Not in this PR

- The roadmap entry, which `./ideas` keeps.

items.title: Focus the address field after Cmd-L opens it
items.author: quanru
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
## What changed

When ⌘L shows the address field over a page, SwiftUI may update the `NSTextField` before AppKit attaches it to a window. The old code marked the focus request as answered immediately, even if `field.window` was still nil. The URL appeared, but typing went to the page and did not edit it.

The field now retries the request when it attaches to a window and marks it answered only after AppKit gives it a text editor. The existing behavior of selecting the whole URL, editing within it, and using Esc to return to the page remains.

## Actual verification

- Before, in Search Beta on `https://example.com/path?query=abc`: ⌘L displayed the URL, but typing `z` did not change the field.
- After installing this change in Search Beta: ⌘L selected the whole URL; typing `https://example.com/edited?x=1` replaced it. Moving the caret after `edited` and typing `-again` changed the field to `https://example.com/edited-again?x=1`. Esc closed the field and left the original page at `https://example.com/path?query=abc`.
- `swift build -c release --arch arm64` passed. The updated Search Beta was signed with the user's Apple Development certificate and passed `codesign --verify --deep --strict`.

items.title: ⌘W closes the panel in front, in the same order as Escape
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
With Settings open, ⌘W closed the page behind it. In Chrome, Settings is a tab and ⌘W closes it; here it's a panel over the page, so ⌘W went past it and closed the tab you couldn't see.

The Home page line that was here moves to a PR of its own, since it waits on a product decision.

## What changed

⌘W reached the app three ways: the key handler in `ContentView.take`, the File › Close Tab item, and the `file.closeTab` command. Each closed the active tab, and only the key handler knew about Peek. All three now call `Browser.closeFront()`, which closes, in order:

- a peek
- then the panel that's up, through `Browser.closePanel()`: release notes, What's New, Settings, Bookmarks, Passwords, Bring Things Over, History, Downloads
- then the tab

Escape uses the same `closePanel()` after its own peek check, with the panels in the order Escape already had. The two keys agree on what's in front, and Escape behaves exactly as before.

Welcome and the Hidden on This Site popover are left out. Welcome covers the whole window as a first-run walk-through, and the popover is meant to sit beside the page while you look at it.

`.gitignore` also gains `__pycache__/`, which the probe scripts leave in `Tests/`.

## Testing

- New `Tests/close_panel.py` (bench-driven, hidden, in split_view.py's test world): ⌘W over Settings, History, Downloads and Bookmarks closes the panel and leaves the tabs alone, then ⌘W with no panel closes a tab. 9/9.
- Builds clean, with no new warnings.

items.title: Disconnect stale ports after confirmed extension worker recovery
items.author: quanru
items.decision: Gated integration
items.note: Use the latest passive once-only disconnect implementation, not closed #514 polling/replay. Strong fixture evidence, but dead/failed-start, delayed cold start and overlapping page checks remain unverified.
items.body:
Content-script and extension-page runtime ports receive one `onDisconnect` when their native worker is confirmed to have been replaced. This includes the content-script reach requested from #514, without its polling, reply deadlines, replay queue or automatic reconnect.

### Behavior and compatibility

The existing worker check remains responsible for recovery. Swift publishes passive retirement notifications to the extension pages and isolated content-script world, including recovery requested by another extension page. Whole-context teardown retires old observers; same-context background replacement retires only ports bound to the previous background lifetime. Healthy wake and cooldown refusal disconnect nothing. Native disconnects and retirement notifications are deduplicated; manually opened fresh connections remain usable.

Automatic recovery reuses the context to preserve existing WebKit API object identity. Native host/socket resources still close explicitly. Ports are weakly held; closure, extension removal and document exit cancel subscriptions. The content-script bridge can observe/cancel notifications but cannot request recovery or invoke privileged APIs.

Same-context background identity uses guarded private WebKit interfaces (`_backgroundWebView` and its creation callback). Content delivery relies on WebKit's shared isolated-world naming. These compatibility dependencies are documented in `Tests/ExtensionWorkerRecovery/README.md`; missing support degrades to native behavior rather than guessing a restart. Screenshots from the earlier history were removed.

### Current revision and reproducibility

Current head `b952ac3` incorporates the validated cross-origin/content-message fixtures directly, so reviewers no longer need to copy them from verification branches. This update changes only tests and their README: `Sources`, worker and extension-page scripts are unchanged from product revision `7ad610d`.

[Exact-head hosted Intel Mac validation](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/38363309647/job/115182398158) now passes at `b952ac34a2ec4b06bbf9731dc65adcfdae3bb296`, without fixture overlays. It passed seven scoped Swift lifetime tests, all shim/fixture/bridge/diagnostic checks, the Release build and the integrated native lifecycle fixture. The live result is **265 checkpoints passed, zero failed, three cases not covered**; these are checkpoints rather than independent E2E cases.

In this exact-head run, the worker stalled for 1,802 ms. The content script actually invoked its runtime request 200 ms after stall onset, returned its Promise in the same millisecond, and received the matching token/worker echo after 1,604 ms. The 18-second no-false-disconnect check, cross-origin audit, both explicit revives, cooldown refusal and idle/wake replacement passed. Final retained-port counts were `[1, 1, 1, 0]`; fresh connections echoed and the owned probe was cleaned up. The outstanding native fault, delayed-cold-start and extension-page health-check cases remain listed below.

To reproduce on macOS 15.4+, build with `./build.sh release`, then run `python3 Tests/ExtensionWorkerRecovery/live.py`. On Intel, first copy `build/intel/Search.app` to `build/Search.app`. The README lists the local checks and coverage limits. All live traffic is local and the hidden launcher uses an isolated owned probe with bounded cleanup; no model service or real profile is used.

### Hosted native evidence

- [Original exact-product job](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/37915564391/job/113770767691): build, shim/fixture checks and live recovery passed at `7ad610d`. Two explicit revives and a 160-second idle/wake worker replacement retired original content/page ports exactly once; fresh connections echoed. The separate upstream comparison stopped on main's old `null` revive return contract, so that workflow is not a clean differential proof.
- [Cross-origin child-frame job](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/38259720540/job/114846823898): product `7ad610d` plus fixture `95b0cf8`, 264 checkpoints passed, none failed. The parent uses `localhost`, its child `127.0.0.1`; admission confirms cross-origin `contentDocument` denial. Relayed observations verify both origin and frame identity and preserve the child's actual callback audit, without reconstructing counts.
- [Content-message overlap job](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/38263205701/job/114858731320): product `7ad610d` plus fixture `d341d6c`, 265 checkpoints passed, none failed, three cases not covered. A real worker stall lasted 1,802 ms. The content script actually called `runtime.sendMessage` 201 ms after stall onset, returned its Promise in 1 ms and received the matching token/worker echo after 1,604 ms. The timestamp is recorded at invocation, not when arming the timer. Actual overlap and reply delay are mandatory assertions.

After that overlap, 18 seconds of observation produced no false disconnect or native recovery. Two explicit revives, cooldown refusal and the 160-second idle/wake checks also passed. The original cross-origin document and isolated fixture survived; retained content/page ports ended with counts `[1, 1, 1, 0]`. Fresh manual connections echoed. Counts above describe checkpoints, not independent E2E cases.

### Failed experiment and remaining acceptance gaps

The [strict extension-page timer experiment](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/38233569310/job/114758628215) remains failed evidence. Its worker stalled for 1,803 ms, but the page timer's message started exactly when the stall ended and replied in 14 ms. That experiment did not establish overlap; its red result is not a production recovery failure. Coupled scheduling is a possible explanation, but process/thread identity was not measured. The [retained diagnostic log](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/38233569310/artifacts/11739973914) remains available.

The successful content-script overlap does **not** enter the extension page's `checkWorker` path. Independent health-check overlap, a genuinely unresponsive worker/failed-start recovery, and delayed cold startup remain unverified live. Slow startup without false disconnect has shim-only coverage. These outstanding checks remain part of the requested acceptance; the current evidence does not complete the entire checklist.

The PR remains queued for review after the 1.0.5 release freeze.

### Fault-injection feasibility — 2026-10-14

A [read-only hosted process inventory](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/38522029621/job/115713699855) ran on macOS 15.7.9 (24G830), WebKit 20621.3.11.11.3, with product `b952ac3` and diagnostic overlay `0482691`. The only source overlay is a test-mode-guarded background-view PID getter in `Bench.swift`; it does not change recovery or invoke process-control APIs.

Three consecutive samples identified the background view and **both retained extension pages in the same WebContent process**. The ordinary parent page used a different process; the cross-origin child frame's separate PID was not measured. This confirms that process-level suspension or termination cannot isolate the worker from the two extension-page observers in this fixture. Such an experiment would also stop or destroy the pages whose original callbacks must be measured, so it would not satisfy the requested live acceptance. Process sharing alone does not establish thread sharing or explain the previous page-timer delay.

The job passed its Release build and 24 admission/observation checkpoints, including initial real echoes and owned-probe cleanup. It did **not** run failure recovery, slow startup or health-check overlap. No signal, suspension or termination was issued. [Retained PID samples and admission log](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/38522029621/artifacts/11874715945).

Further native fault coverage needs a background-specific mechanism that demonstrably leaves the original extension-page documents and ports alive. Before classifying any such experiment as worker-only, it must verify document identity, unchanged observer process/liveness, actual backend failure, and the production wake/check route that recovers it. Delaying application listener registration while the shim ping remains healthy is not delayed WebKit cold-start coverage. These cases remain outstanding, rather than being replaced with a process-kill test that destroys the observers.

items.title: Support multi-selecting tabs and copying their links
items.author: quanru
items.decision: Adopt after core tab work
items.note: Multi-tab selection/copy; preserve split pairs and modified dragging. Latest metadata says mouse drag still needs visible validation.
items.body:
Select several tabs with ⌘-click or ⇧-click, including whole Split View pairs, and copy their addresses from the existing tab context menu.

The normal Close, Pin and Move to Group actions remain available. Selected pins use a selection wash distinct from the active pin. The command is “Copy Addresses” and the copied feedback has its singular form. Selection uses a simultaneous tap gesture so tab dragging keeps its existing gesture path.

Revision: `561a7f7bfdbebc87d7e8d12160dfdcf7012c4a9d`. Merged upstream `59c1b4e` without rewriting history and resolved the changelog conflict, retaining both entries. The requested entry remains under Unreleased › Added.

[Exact hosted Intel Mac validation](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/38109510093/job/114381957277): 2 TabSelectionTests and the Release build passed. The separate verification branch is not part of this PR. Modified mouse dragging is not claimed as visually verified; the maintainer plans to check ⌘/⇧ dragging on the release candidate, as discussed in the review.
