items.title: Avoid duplicate address field in unpaired Split View tabs
items.author: quanru
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
## Cause
With Split View enabled, `SplitStage` renders the address field for every focused pane, including an ordinary unpaired tab. `ContentView` also rendered its window-level field whenever `activeSplit == nil`. Cmd+T on an unpaired tab therefore showed two vertically offset fields.

## Fix
Render the window-level field only when Split View is disabled. Split View continues to use its pane-level field. The existing `Breath` effect and field styling stay intact.

## Verification
- Confirmed the affected Beta profile has `splitView = true`.
- `swift build` passed.
- Built, signed, installed, and launched Search Beta 202609291327 with the isolated Beta profile intact.
- Visual confirmation remains pending because the computer-use native pipe fails to start.

items.title: Avoid duplicate extension actions in webpage context menus
items.author: quanru
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
## Cause
SingleFile registers both webpage and tab context menu entries. WebKit already supplies extension actions in the webpage's native context menu, while Search appended `WKWebExtensionContext.menuItems(for:)` there as well. That API retrieves tab menu entries, so a webpage right-click showed SingleFile twice.

## Fix
Stop appending tab extension items to the webpage menu. Keep WebKit's native webpage menu actions.

## Verification
- Confirmed the user sees the duplicate when right-clicking webpage content, and only one SingleFile extension is installed.
- `swift build` passed.
- Built, signed, installed, and launched Search Beta 202609291332 with the isolated Beta profile intact.
- Visual confirmation remains pending because the computer-use native pipe fails to start.

items.title: Drive Search from an agent: an MCP server over the bench
items.author: redbear7
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
The roadmap's "Later" list has **Drive Search from an agent — an MCP server over the bench**, and #14 already taught agents to use `./bench` through a skill. I've built that MCP server in a fork and used it daily for a few days, and would like to ask whether you want it upstream, and in what shape, before opening any pull request.

## What it is

`mcp/search_mcp.py`: one Python file, standard library only, that speaks MCP over stdio and talks to the running app through the existing bench socket. `claude mcp add search -- python3 mcp/search_mcp.py` and an agent can open pages, read them, click and type, and see what the page did. It starts its own test world (`SEARCH_PROBE=agent`), so the browser someone actually uses is never touched.

Tools: open / navigate / wait / tabs / close / text / eval / screenshot / click / type / press key, plus a few new bench verbs behind them:

- **snapshot** — the page as a list of what can be read or acted on, each with a ref (`k3x.e12`) that click and type accept; same-origin iframes included, cross-origin ones named; hidden inputs listed with their value masked.
- **console** and **network** — console messages and uncaught errors; every request the page makes, the page itself included, with its status (a `_setResourceLoadDelegate:` delegate, the same SPI family `paintUnseen` already uses), plus fetch/XHR headers and body previews on request.
- **dialog** / **upload** — answer alert/confirm/prompt and file choosers by policy instead of leaving them held on a background tab.
- **wait_for** — text, a visible element, a URL, or network idle.
- **viewport** — render a tab at a phone width, optionally with an iPhone Safari user agent.

Everything new only runs in a test world and on bench tabs: `Store.testing`, the same gate `tap` and `select` use. Someone who never runs a test world never sees any of it.

## Why it's worth having

I compared it with Playwright's MCP server (Chromium) on the same tasks, same model and prompt, graded against answer keys built from the site's source:

- ordinary tasks (menus, forms, notices, links, errors): both 5/5;
- **secrets**: on a page with an access token and a CSRF field, Playwright's runs put the raw values into the agent's transcript 21 times; Search's none, because tool output is scrubbed before it reaches the model (credential-shaped values in headers, bodies, URLs, HTML and eval results);
- **what Safari users see**: Search renders it — it *is* WebKit; Chromium can only infer it;
- after the network and snapshot additions, the remaining gaps closed (request statuses, hidden fields, phone width); Playwright is still a few seconds faster per task.

## How I'd split it

If you're open to it, small pull requests in this order, each one thing, each with its CHANGELOG line:

1. The MCP server over the existing bench verbs — Python only, no app change.
2. snapshot with refs (iframes, hidden inputs).
3. console and network, with statuses for every load.
4. dialog and upload policies; windows a bench tab opens become bench tabs.
5. MCP-launched test worlds shown instead of hidden (`SEARCH_VISIBLE=1`, so animations and timers run), and tap/key answering after the page has handled the event.
6. viewport.
7. Output scrubbing, and `browser_html` (the rendered HTML saved to a file, scrubbed).

Questions before I start:

- Is an MCP server something you want in this repository, or should it live next to it and only the bench verbs come in?
- Is the resource-load delegate SPI acceptable, given that only test worlds use it?
- Any part of the list you'd rather not have?

items.title: GitHub PR Files page intermittently stays blank for tens of seconds
items.author: quanru
items.decision: Needs reproduction/information
items.note: Recorded stalls also occur in bare WKWebView; author qualified foreground/login/VPN comparisons. No validated Browse-side speed fix.
items.body:
### What happens

Opening this GitHub PR's Files/changes URL in Search can leave the content area blank for a long time before the page appears:

https://github.com/web-infra-dev/midscene/pull/3198/changes#diff-4df0b567c2495d8b7f29ac04869bdf7f6ab93a9ffb04e8663738dc4fdfeb0d90

The URL redirects from `/changes` to `/files` while retaining the fragment. On the same Mac, the reporter says Ego Lite (Chromium) opens it much faster. The delay is intermittent, but has reached tens of seconds in Search. The visible symptom is a blank content area, not just a slow spinner after the page is already displayed.

### Reproduction and measurements

- macOS 27.0; Search 1.0.4 (a locally built Beta, build 202609291332).
- Open the URL above in a new tab. Repeat with a fresh/isolated Search test profile if the first attempt is fast.
- In an isolated Search test world with no installed extensions, `bench wait` took about **50 s** in one run, **16 s** in another, and **3 s** in a later warm run. This makes installed extensions an unlikely sole cause.
- An independent, minimal `WKWebView` loading the same URL (without Search's scripts or extensions) took about **38 s** to finish in one run, but roughly **6–12 s** on later runs.
- In a traced isolated Search run, `didCommit` occurred at 14:51:46.712, WebKit's first visually nonempty layout at 14:51:50.037, and `didFinish` at 14:52:04.353. The page continued loading for about 14 s after the first frame. A separate warm run reported first contentful paint at 4.35 s, document response end at 2.37 s, and load event at 6.77 s.
- The PR itself has 7 changed files (158 additions, 7 deletions), so this is not an unusually large diff.

### Expected

The PR Files page should become visible and usable without a prolonged blank interval. It would help to determine whether the slow phase is in network transfer, GitHub's page scripts/styles, WebKit rendering, or Search-specific setup, and whether Search can mitigate it.

### Notes

Search hides a new `PageView` until WebKit reports its first visually nonempty layout (with a `didFinish` fallback). That could affect how a slow first paint looks, but a controlled run with the view hidden versus visible did **not** show a consistent extra delay from this mechanism. I have not found a reliable Search-side fix yet. GitHub has documented a separate Safari-specific PR page performance issue in the past (https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/170758), but I cannot establish that it is the same cause here.

items.title: Supporting profiles
items.author: 0xbentang
items.decision: Needs coordination
items.note: Spaces already isolate cookie stores when explicitly created that way. Shared profiles with separate history/bookmarks/extensions do not exist; define privacy semantics before extending.
items.body: In Arc, you can associate profiles to different spaces. Seems like profiles is not even supported in Search? Is there any plans on this? Thanks!

items.title: Allow choosing custom User Agent
items.author: Rahuletto
items.decision: Available
items.note: A per-tab user-agent control is welcome upstream but shares plumbing with #412. Coordinate to avoid implementing two per-tab emulation states.
items.body:
Safari on macOS has a built-in way to switch the User Agent in the Develop menu with list of presets (like Safari, Chrome, Microsoft Edge, etc..) and even custom string. It applies per tab and restarts on restart. 

Search is built on WebKit and WebKit already has APIs for it
https://developer.apple.com/documentation/webkit/wkwebview/customuseragent
https://developer.apple.com/documentation/webkit/wkwebviewconfiguration/applicationnameforuseragent

For Safari User Agent feature:
https://developer.apple.com/documentation/safari-developer-tools/develop-menu

This will be really handy to tweak the UA to tweak than to install some extension to do it instead.

items.title: The hidden column's shadow leaves with it
items.author: karadoganyi
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Fixes #441.

When the folded column slides back out of the window, its shadow stayed along the window's edge after the column was gone, then vanished at once. The tabs across the top, folded away, did the same at the top edge.

Why: `.transition(.move(edge:))` moves the column by its own width, but its `.shadow(radius: 20, x: 4)` draws about 24 pt past that width. So the slide ended with the shadow still inside the window, and it only went when SwiftUI removed the view.

The fix fades the shadow over the same transition: `.move(edge:)` combined with a `.modifier` transition whose off-screen state has the shadow at nothing (`FoldShadow` and `.casting` in Fold.swift). The shadow gets lighter as the column slides and is gone when the column is.

The slide itself is unchanged. Moving the column further, so the shadow slides fully out, would pull it away from the window's buttons, which ride in its corner by exactly the column's width on the same spring.

The strip still casts its shadow from a ground behind the row, as before, not from every title.

Checked, with `./bench film unpeek` / `film peek` in a hidden test world:
- Column: before, frames at about 0.54 s and 0.70 s show the column gone and a shadow band along the left edge (darkness about 70/1000 at the edge), then a clean frame. After, every frame once the column has left is clean.
- Strip: the same band at the top edge before the fix, clean after.
- At rest, the shadow beside the column and below the strip measures the same values before and after, and the same again after sliding back out. Mid-slide, the column's edge is where it was.
- Reduce Motion, the column on the right and full screen are unaffected.
- `swift test`: 47 tests, 0 failures. `./build.sh` builds clean.

No unit test: the change is visual, and the bench films above are how it was checked.

items.title: Pins in every space: a pin kept in every space, above each space's own
items.author: karadoganyi
items.decision: Later; take #587 first
items.note: Global pins are a feature. The pin-move persistence fix was split into #587 and should be taken independently.
items.body:
From the roadmap's "Pins shared by every space" (Planned): pins every space shows, plus each space's own, as Arc's favourites sit above every space.

I built this without opening an issue first, so the design is yours to redirect. The three calls I'd most like your eye on are at the end.

## What it does

- Settings › Tabs › **Pins in every space**, off by default and shown only while Spaces is on. It isn't on the What's New card, since with Spaces off it would do nothing.
- With it on, a pin's right-click menu has **Keep in Every Space**, and on a shared pin, **Only in This Space**. Move to Space isn't offered for a shared pin, since it's already everywhere.
- A shared pin shows first in every space, above the space's own pins. Squares still come before rows: shared squares, own squares, shared rows, own rows.
- Each space opens a shared pin in its own cookie store, as each window already keeps its own tab for a pin. So Gmail in a Work space started afresh is the work account.
- Unpinning a shared pin takes it out of every space, the way unpinning in one window does for every window.
- Switched off, or with Spaces off, shared pins leave every space but stay in pins.json. They come back, asleep, when it's on again.
- With the switch off, nothing changes, and pins.json is byte for byte what it was.

## How

- **pins.json** gets one more key, `"shared": [PinDef]`, next to the per-space lists. `Pins` gains the shared list and small pure helpers (`share`, `unshare`, `split`, `row`, `sharedToWrite`, `decode`, `encode`), all unit-tested.
- **Rows:** `reconcilePins` builds each space's row from shared plus own while the switch and Spaces are on. `Tab.everywhere` marks a shared pin. It isn't saved in the session, since pins.json says which pins are shared.
- **Saving:** `writeSession` splits the row back into the two lists. It writes the shared list only from a row that holds a shared pin, so a row not yet rebuilt (the switch just turned on) can't wipe it.
- **Syncing:** a shared-list change goes to the other windows through `Pins.changed`. Every window rebuilds its row on screen and each space it keeps off screen.

## One fix to existing behaviour

The Move to Space fix (a moved pin becomes the destination's pin in pins.json too, so it survives a relaunch) is now its own PR, #587, for 1.0.5. Once it's on main, this branch is rebased without its copy.

## Going back to 1.0.4

1.0.4 reads the new file fine: it skips a key that isn't a space id. But if it then saves pins, it writes the file without the shared list. So downgrading and changing a pin loses the shared pins. That happens only on a downgrade.

## Checked

- `swift test`: 60 tests, 0 failures. `Tests/SearchTests/SharedPinsTests.swift` is new, with 13 tests on in-memory data.
- `Tests/shared_pins.py` is new: 24 checks in a hidden test world, using the split suite's harness. They cover:
  - sharing a pin, and a new space showing it asleep
  - a space started afresh signing in on its own
  - Only in This Space while the pin is another space's front tab
  - unpinning from every space
  - switch off and on, then a restart
  - Spaces off and on
  - deleting the current space
  - the block order after Show as Row
  - a pin moved to a space not on screen
  - a second window keeping its tab and page when a pin is shared from the first
- Also run: `Tests/split_view.py` 92/92, `Tests/pin_tiers.py` 20/20, `Tests/fresh_window.py` 7/7, `Tests/close_group.py` 5/5. `./build.sh` builds with no new warnings.
- The column's order in two spaces was checked with `./bench picture`. I haven't seen the right-click menu on screen.

Bench additions for the test: `pin` takes `everywhere: true|false`, the split state reports `everywhere` and `pinStores`, and `ui sharedpins on|off`.

## Questions for you

1. Should each space sign in to a shared pin its own way, as built, or should there be one session for all spaces?
2. Is a switch in Settings › Tabs right, or would you rather have the menu item alone whenever Spaces is on?
3. Should shared pins sit above the space's own, as built and as Arc does, or be mixed in?

Not included: the Arc import is unchanged (favourites stay each space's own pins), and there's no change to bookmarks, groups or tabs. ROADMAP.md is left for `./ideas`.

items.title: A sideways scroll swipes between pages only when the Mac's setting sa…
items.author: karadoganyi
items.decision: Adopt
items.note: Honor native swipe setting after forwarding scroll to the page. Test fixture positioning was corrected; real-device acceptance remains.
items.body:
Fixes #464.

With Swipe between pages off in System Settings › Mouse, a one-finger Magic Mouse scroll still swiped back or forward in Search. Inside a page with its own sideways scroll, like a Google Sheet, it went back a page once the sheet's scroll reached its edge.

Why: Search draws its own swipe from scroll events and turns WebKit's off (`allowsBackForwardNavigationGestures = false`). So it never asked the Mac whether a scroll may go between pages, the way Safari and WebKit's own swipe do.

The fix: `PageView.scrollWheel` reads the gesture only while `Swipe.followsTheMac` says so. That's `NSEvent.isSwipeTrackingFromScrollEventsEnabled`, the same check Safari, WebKit and Firefox follow. The page still gets every scroll event, since the check comes after `super.scrollWheel`, so a sheet keeps its own sideways scroll. There's no new setting in Search: it follows the Mac, as Safari does.

The mouse and the trackpad each count: AppKit answers for the device of the event being handled. It keeps the Mouse switch (`AppleEnableMouseSwipeNavigateWithScrolls`) and the Trackpad switch (`AppleEnableSwipeNavigateWithScrolls`) separately and picks one from `NSApp.currentEvent`. That's why it's read in `scrollWheel`, for that event, and never cached; the comment on `followsTheMac` says so.

"Hold a swipe to pick from history" goes through the same path, so it follows the setting too. Swiping between spaces over the tabs and moving the floating video are left as they are, since they don't go between pages.

## Checked

- `Tests/swipe_setting.py` (new) runs in a hidden test world. A test run stands in for the Mac's setting with `./bench ui swipepages on|off`, so nobody's System Settings are touched.
  - On: two fingers back go back.
  - Off: the same gesture stays on the page, and the page still gets the wheel events.
  - On again: it goes back.
- The "off" check failed before the fix: it went from `/b` back to `/a`.
- Moving the check above `super.scrollWheel` makes "the page still gets the scroll" fail, so that check holds the other half.
- `swift test`: 47 tests, 0 failures. `Tests/split_view.py`: 92/92. No new warnings.

Not tested by hand with a real Magic Mouse. @nourspace, if you can try a build, the thing to check is: with Swipe between pages off in System Settings › Mouse, scrolling sideways in a Google Sheet should never go back a page.

## Left as it is

- If the Mac's setting changed during a live gesture, a swipe already under way could be left half done until the next gesture the Mac allows. That needs a System Settings change while your fingers are moving.
- Why a Google Sheet's inner sideways scroll isn't recognized as "the page scrolls this way", so the swipe arms at all with the setting on, is a separate question. It's not part of this change.

items.title: Constrain page ideal size without changing window safe areas
items.author: quanru
items.decision: Hold: not reproduced
items.note: PR and main measurements/drawings matched in current comparisons. Do not merge a layout change without reproducing the clipping it claims to fix.
items.body:
Let the native page answer SwiftUI's offered size at `WebStage.sizeThatFits`, so its previous bounds do not become the browser layout's ideal size. This follows the alternative requested in review. The page GeometryReader is removed, and App.swift/window-root safe areas have no diff against current upstream main.

For fully specified finite proposals, the stage returns the proposed width and height; otherwise it leaves sizing to the existing representable behavior. Added an Unreleased changelog entry.

Revision: `b4a6fdf7590ac0896ed46f796aba39acffb4aed5`, synchronized with upstream main `35aa051`.

### Resize procedure under evaluation

Open a normal page, keep the tabs column visible, start at a 1180 × 780-point window, shrink through widths 700 and 560, then expand to 1180. Repeat with the column on the left and on the right. Observe whether the column/page or overlays are clipped by the window. Actual width may be constrained by the window's native minimum; record it rather than assuming the requested width was accepted.

[Current revision hosted check](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/38022552660/job/114126465036) builds Release, runs FindStageTests and records native page/window bounds through that sequence in a hidden disposable probe. [Unmodified-main comparison](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/38022476017/job/114126243439) uses the same observer. The observer and its logs are on a separate verification branch, not in this PR.

These are native layout measurements, not visual before/after evidence of address fields, panels, import progress or the tab switcher. The original clipping scenario and those overlays still need visual confirmation; successful bounds checks alone do not establish that the original defect was reproduced and fixed. The report will retain any failures and the exact measured widths.

### Comparison result — 2026-10-10

Both the exact current head and unmodified main passed their Release builds, FindStageTests and all eight native width measurements. The measurements were identical: with the column on the left, page frames were `[232, 0, 948, 780]`, `[232, 0, 468, 780]` and `[232, 0, 408, 780]` at actual window widths 1180, 700 and 640; on the right, page x was 0 with the same widths. A request for 560 points was constrained to 640 by the native minimum.

**This sequence did not reproduce clipping on main**, so it does not establish an old-fails/new-passes fix. The sizeThatFits alternative builds and preserves these measured bounds, but visual reproduction of the original clipping and overlays remains outstanding. I have not closed this PR as already fixed or claimed visual acceptance based on these results.

### Additional native drawing comparison — 2026-10-12

The [PR revision job](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/38233569310/job/114758628396) and [current upstream job](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/38233569310/job/114758628705) both built Release and repeated the resize sequence above. Current upstream was `59c1b4e`; the PR remained `b4a6fdf`.

Each captured 12 hidden native window drawings: column left/right, actual widths 700/640, and normal/Settings/import-sheet states. I inspected all 12 PR drawings, then compared each original PNG against its upstream counterpart: every pair is byte-identical. All eight page-frame measurements also match and remain in bounds. Probe state independently confirms the requested Settings/import-sheet state.

Download the [PR screenshots and measurements](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/38233569310/artifacts/11739403650) and the [upstream counterparts](https://github.com/quanru/Search/actions/runs/38233569310/artifacts/11739558855). They are native hidden drawings from the existing `picture` bench route, not screen recordings. They do not cover real-screen resize animation, address-field editing, the tab switcher or active import progress. No new FindStageTests run is claimed for this drawing comparison.

This provides additional overlay evidence but still does **not** reproduce the original clipping or prove a behavioral benefit from this PR. The original trigger remains unresolved; this is not presented as fixed or ready to merge on that basis.

items.title: Remove All… in the passwords panel (#469)
items.author: karadoganyi
items.decision: Adopt after rebase
items.note: Bulk password deletion. Latest comments supersede stale body: authentication, cancel default, background deletes, success counts and test cleanup are addressed. Rebrand test keychain label.
items.body:
Closes #469.

Passwords kept in Search could only be removed one at a time, with the Remove that shows on each account. Someone who brought in 246 as a stopgap and has since moved to Bitwarden had 246 clicks ahead of them.

## What it does

- The passwords panel's foot gets **Remove All…** beside the count, or **Remove 12…** while the search box narrows the list. It's hidden when the list is empty.
- It removes exactly what the list shows: all of them with no search, only the matches with one. A search for one site never takes the rest with it, and the button and the question both say how many.
- It asks first: "Remove 246 Passwords? They're taken out of your keychain. Only the passwords Search keeps are removed: password managers, other apps and other browsers keep theirs. This can't be undone." After you confirm, it asks for Touch ID or your password, as showing or copying one does. Return is Cancel.
- Each removal is the existing `Vault.forget`: Search's own label, site and account. Nothing Search doesn't keep can be touched.
- The list of sites never to offer saving for is left as it is.

## Also fixed: Esc on a question over a panel

Pressing Esc on the question didn't cancel it. The window's own key handling took Escape first, closed the passwords panel, and left the question up with Return on its first button, **Remove**.

`take(_:)` in App.swift now leaves a key typed into a sheet to the sheet. The bug was older (removing a bookmarks folder had the same path), but this is the first mass delete shown over a panel.

## Test hooks (test runs only)

- `Ask.sure` takes a test run's answer (`./bench ui confirm on|off|ask`), since a probe started hidden can't show a sheet to click.
- `./bench passwords [TEXT] [remove]` narrows the list and presses the button.
- `press` can target the window's sheet, and `probe` reports whether one is up.

## Checked

  - A search for "bank" shows 2.
  - "No" removes nothing.
  - "Yes" removes only the 2 shown.
  - No search removes the rest.
  - A real question with Esc pressed on it leaves the panel open and every password in place.
- Each check was shown able to fail. Removing every kept password instead of the shown ones fails "only the two the list showed". Taking the Esc line out fails "the panel under the question stays".
- Removing 246 made-up accounts took about 1 s, on the main thread.

Not checked in a test: that Esc then closes the question. That needs the question to be the key window, which a hidden probe never has. It's AppKit's own behaviour for an alert's Cancel, but worth a look by hand.

## Left as it is

- The line after removing counts what was asked to be removed. If the keychain refused some (a locked keychain, items written by a differently signed build), it would overstate.
- The ~1 s for 246 runs on the main thread. #380 moved bulk keychain writes off it for imports; the same could be done here if you'd like.

items.title: Settings › General › Home page, while an extension offers a page
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Adopt as polish
items.note: Keep explicit user choice among new-tab extensions; no to a new extension should not undo the old choice. Test actual two-extension UI.
items.body:
Split out of #452, as asked there. It waits on the product decision; this is the version to decide on.

## The rule change

This changes which extension's page new tabs show. Before, only the newest extension that asked counted. A no to it hid an older extension you'd said yes to, so installing something and declining its page quietly undid your earlier pick.

Now the newest extension you said yes to wins, and a no only answers for the extension you said it to. Picking one in Settings, or picking Search's own, answers no for every other asker, so one extension owns new tabs at a time and none of them asks again.

## The line

An extension "changing the home page" is `overrideNewTabPageURL`: Search has no home page apart from the new tab. The only way back was a hover-only **Stop in New Tabs** on the extension's row in Settings › Extensions.

- **Settings › General › Home page**, under Bring things over, only while an extension offers a page. It's a menu: **Search's own**, then each extension that asked. With none, the line and its hairline aren't there.
- `Extensions.setNewTabPage(_:)` makes the choice. `newTabPageID` and `newTabAskers` replace the private `newTabCandidate`.
- The row in Settings › Extensions (its Show/Stop in New Tabs button and its "shows in new tabs" detail) reads `newTabPageID`, so it agrees with General.
- The first-time prompt points at Settings › General › Home page. It now asks for any extension that asked and hasn't been answered, not only the newest.
- **A new extension is asked even while another has new tabs.** Before, `newTab()` opened the holder's page and returned before `offerNewTabPage`, so a second extension was never asked and only Settings could switch. The prompt now names the extension that has new tabs, and a yes swaps the tab just opened if it's still on that page.
- ⌘T onto the blank tab a window opens with (which `newTab()` reuses) never asked either, and does now. That's usually where the first ⌘T after adding an extension lands.

## Testing

- New `Tests/newtab_choice.py` (bench-driven, hidden, in split_view.py's test world): two unpacked extensions, each with only a new tab page. A is asked and shown; B, added while A has new tabs, is asked, and a yes shows B in that tab and the next; a no to B keeps A and isn't asked again. 8/8. With the offer taken back out of the extension path it's 3/8: B is never asked and ⌘T keeps showing A.
- Builds clean, with no new warnings.
- Not tested: the Home page line on screen, with or without an extension offering a page.

items.title: One ⇧⌘T after Close Group brings the whole group back
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
**Depends on #432.** This builds on its batch undo, so until #432 lands the diff here includes it. The changes of its own are the last two commits, 12371d3 and 09c12bb.

The follow-up suggested on #432: Close Group's tabs come back with one ⇧⌘T, the way a Clear's now do.

## What it does

- **The whole group back in one step:** every tab in its place and in its original order, in a group named as it was and where it was among the others.
- **The page you were on comes back in front,** if it was in the group. Otherwise you stay where you are.
- **No lost tabs:** a group of 13 or more no longer loses its first tabs to the 12 steps ⇧⌘T keeps.
- **The menus say "Reopen Closed Group"** while that's what ⇧⌘T would do.

## How

- `closeTabGroup` now closes its tabs inside `closingTogether`, the helper Clear uses. So they share a batch, and the tab on screen is marked to come back in front.
- The code that brings a closed group back moves out of `reopen(_:)` into `regroup(_:)`. Now both `reopen(_:)` and `reopen(batch:)` put a tab back into its group, bringing the group back from `closedGroups` first.
- Reopening one tab of the group by name from History › Recently Closed still works as before, and a later ⇧⌘T brings the rest back into the group it recreated.

## Testing

- `close_group.py`: 10/10. It now presses ⇧⌘T once where it used to press three times, and checks the tabs' order and that nothing is left to reopen. A new case closes a 13-tab group with the page on screen inside it; one ⇧⌘T brings all 13 back in order, with that page in front.
- `pin_tiers.py` (Clear goes through the same helper now): 32/32. `fresh_window.py`: 7/7.
- `close_group.py` now runs in a world of its own (`close-group`), as `pin_tiers.py` does. Before, it shared `split-tests` with the split suite, so another checkout running that suite at the same time could answer on its socket with a different build.

items.title: A swipe back from a small window's first page closes it
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Later
items.note: Swipe-to-close small window. Manual back-stack testing incomplete; only swipe should close, not stray mouse back buttons.
items.body:
A small window for a link from another app now closes with a swipe back from the page it opened on. Back from there is back to before the window existed, so that's what the gesture does.

## What it does

- **Swipe back on the first page closes the window.** The same 70pt reach and quick flick as any back swipe, and turning round before letting go still cancels.
- **The disc shows a cross instead of an arrow** when letting go will close the window. Small windows didn't show the disc at all before, so now every swipe in one gets it.
- **Pages clicked through inside the window go back as usual first.** Only the page it opened on closes it.
- **Only the swipe closes it.** A mouse's back button and Logi Options+'s back do nothing on the first page, as before. They close with no disc and no chance to change your mind, and ⇧⌘T can't reopen a small window, so a stray press would lose the page.
- **Open in Search (⌘O) turns it off.** Once the page is a tab in the browser's row, back on its first page does nothing, as with any tab.

## How

- `PageView` gets `leave`, what back means with nothing to go back to. The swipe no longer gives up at the first page when `leave` is set; on release it calls it. The call waits a turn of the run loop, since it closes the window the swipe's own view is in.
- `Tab.leave` holds it and hands it to the page each time the page is built, as `onPull` is, so a rebuilt page keeps it. `LittleWindow` sets it on open and clears it on keep and on close.
- `Pull.leaves` tells the disc to show the cross.
- The disc and the held-swipe history list move out of `Page` into a `Swiping` view, which `LittleView` now puts over its page too.

## Testing

- `./build.sh` builds clean, with no new warnings.
- Tried by hand in a build of this branch: a link from another app opened in a small window, and a swipe back on its first page closed it.
- Not checked by hand yet: stepping back through pages clicked inside the window before the swipe that closes it.

items.title: A dev build is named for its branch, on a yellow icon
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Adapt concept only
items.note: Distinct development name/icon is useful, but this PR explicitly retains the production bundle ID and profile. Pair with actual data isolation; port Browse branding.
items.body:
`./build.sh` now makes a dev build named for the feature it's built from, on a yellow icon. A build from a worktree can't be mistaken for the installed Search running beside it, or for another worktree's build.

This came up because a dev build left running took the links clicked in other apps, and nothing on screen said which Search had them. Every copy had the same name, the same icon and the same bundle id.

## What it does

- **Named `Search-<feature>`** in the Dock, ⌘Tab, Finder and the menu bar. The feature is the branch's last part, minus the six-character hash a worktree's name ends in:

  | Branch | Name |
  | --- | --- |
  | `claude/split-view-4a6927` | Search-split-view |
  | `claude/dev-build-look` | Search-dev-build-look |
  | `fix/omnibox-double-layer` | Search-omnibox-double-layer |
  | detached HEAD | Search Dev |

  `SEARCH_FEATURE=name ./build.sh` picks the name directly.
- **A yellow icon,** the way Chrome Canary marks its builds: the mark on a yellow plate, and in Dark mode, a yellow mark on the ink plate. It's readable at 16pt.
- **Releases are unchanged.** `release dmg` and `release ship` are always plain Search with the white icon, and asking for a dev build in a DMG is an error. `SEARCH_DEV=0 ./build.sh` makes the plain one locally.
- **The docs say so:** the README's build section, the usage block at the top of `build.sh`, and the bench skill. The skill notes that the process is still named `Search`, so it should still pick processes by their executable path.

## How

- The name is a localised one: `en.lproj/InfoPlist.strings` plus `LSHasLocalizedDisplayName`. Without it, the Dock, ⌘Tab and Finder show the bundle's folder name. This way the folder stays `build/Search.app`, which `fresh.sh`, the bench skill and `Tests/split_view.py` open.
- The plain `CFBundleName` and `CFBundleDisplayName` stay "Search". macOS only uses the localised name when the plain one matches the folder name. When they differ, it assumes someone renamed the app by hand and shows the folder name.
- The hash is only stripped when it contains a digit, so a branch ending in a word like `-decade` keeps it. The name keeps only letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, so it's safe in the strings file.
- `Icon/icon.swift` reads `SEARCH_DEV` for the plate colour, in both the `.icns` and the Icon Composer document.
- The bundle id stays `com.officecommun.search`, so a dev build shares the installed app's settings, sign-ins and extensions. While both run, a link from another app can still land in the dev build, but you can now see when it has.

## Testing

- On this branch, `./build.sh` makes "Search-dev-build-look". After `lsregister -f`, macOS reports that name through both `FileManager.displayName` and the URL's `localizedName`.
- `SEARCH_FEATURE=small-window-swipe ./build.sh` makes "Search-small-window-swipe".
- The naming block from `build.sh`, run in bash on the branches in the table above (plus `feature/decade`, and a name with a quote and a backslash), gives the names shown.
- `SEARCH_DEV=0 ./build.sh` makes "Search", with no `en.lproj` and no `LSHasLocalizedDisplayName`.
- `SEARCH_DEV=1 ./build.sh release dmg` stops with "a dev build doesn't go in a DMG".
- Checked the 256pt and 16pt@2x icons by eye.

items.title: Tests: each checkout tests in a world of its own
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
`split_view.py` gave every checkout the same world, `split-tests`, and the nine suites that run through its harness (`fresh_window`, `close_group`, `tab_switcher`, `site_search` and others) all use it. When two checkouts test at once (a worktree beside the main one, or another session's), they share one bench socket. So a run in one can be answered by the other's build. I hit this while working on #426: a test kept failing at random, with a `state` missing a key its build had added, because another checkout's older build was the one answering.

## What changes

The world is now the suite's name plus a tag taken from the checkout's path: `split-tests-4eb239dd`. A new `use(name)` sets `W`, `SUPPORT`, `SUITE` and `SOCK` together. A suite that wants a world apart from the split suite's can call `sv.use("pin-tiers")` instead of setting the four by hand (forgetting `SOCK` is how `pin_tiers.py` broke after 2432be9). Three suites get worlds apart from the split suite's, each with one call:

- `fresh_window.py` calls `sv.use("fresh-window")`. It quits and relaunches with a setting of its own in between.
- `close_group.py` calls `sv.use("close-group")`. It shared the split suite's world before.
- `pin_tiers.py` calls `sv.use("pin-tiers")` in place of its hand-set `W`, `SUPPORT` and `SUITE`. That also repairs it on `main`: it never set `SOCK`, so since 2432be9 it was watching the split suite's socket.

#429, #432 and #473 each add world lines to one of these two files, so whichever lands after this one takes `use()` in a small conflict.

The tag hashes the full path rather than the folder's name, because two checkouts can share a name (`~/repos/Search` and `~/noodling/Search`). The socket path grows by 9 characters, to 84 with a short user name, well under macOS's 104.

## Testing

- `split_view.py`: 92/92. `fresh_window.py`: 7/7, `pin_tiers.py`: 20/20 and `close_group.py`: 5/5, each in its own tagged world. All run directly, with no wrapper.
- While they ran, only `Search (split-tests-4eb239dd)` existed, never `split-tests`, and nothing was left behind.
- Three checkouts on one Mac get three different tags.

items.title: Full screen keeps the window's buttons in the column's corner
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Closed without merge flag: inspect before reuse
items.note: No adoption recommendation from closed state alone; may be declined, superseded, partially incorporated or incorporated outside GitHub merge.
items.body:
With the tabs down the side, full screen took the red, yellow and green buttons out of the column's corner and drew a ghost bar across the top of the window: a frosted band 28 points deep with a shadow line under it. The lights now stay in the column's corner, the way Dia keeps them in its sidebar, and the page runs clean up to the menu bar.

## What changes

- **The column keeps its corner in full screen**, with fresh system buttons in it (`NSWindow.standardWindowButton(_:for:)`), set where the real ones sit in a window. Red closes, green leaves full screen, and yellow is greyed out, as macOS greys it in full screen. The glyphs are the system's own.
- **Hover works.** The buttons ask their superview `_mouseInGroup:` only when their state changes; `needsDisplay`, on the button or every view inside it, redraws them as they were. So on hover each button is switched off and on again, and all three show ×, − and the full-screen arrows together.
- **macOS's title bar is hidden in full screen while the column is on.** Three layers of it, each found with a view and layer dump:
  - AppKit shows the title bar's frosted background again in full screen, even on a transparent title bar, and moves the container into a separate `NSToolbarFullScreenWindow` *after* did-enter-full-screen, resetting the container's hidden flag on the way. So the container's contents are hidden (the button row, which holds the background, and the decoration view), and `Lights` re-applies this on every full-screen layout through its existing frame watch.
  - The shadow line is a bare 16-point `CALayer` holding a shadow picture, in that window's content view, faded in with the menu bar. Neither `hasShadow` nor `titlebarSeparatorStyle` touches it. The window is a child of the full-screen window, so it's found through `parent`, and its content view is hidden.
- **A window restored straight into full screen gets its lights.** It never sent will-enter-full-screen to anyone listening. `Browser.fullScreen` is now read from the window at setup, and on did-enter too.
- **The #241 corner rule is gone.** In full screen, the folded column wouldn't come out of the top 60 points of the edge, so the pointer could reach macOS's buttons there. Those are hidden now and the column carries its own.
- **The strip across the top is unchanged:** its buttons stay macOS's, in the bar that comes down with the menu bar.

## Tested

In a test world (`SEARCH_PROBE=lights`) with the column on, in real full screen:
- The lights sit in the column's corner. Hovering shows all three glyphs, leaving clears them, and green leaves full screen (checked by eye).
- The shadow line: a temporary hook forced the shadow layer on and switched the fix off and on every 10 seconds. The line came and went with the fix.
- The hover redraw was chosen by rendering the buttons in a borderless window and capturing after each candidate call. Only a state change brought the glyphs.
- A window restored straight into full screen shows the column's lights.

Not checked: the menu bar set to hide in full screen versus always shown, and more than one full-screen window at once.

Refs #241

items.title: Bringing Arc over loses its shape, and its folders are dropped for good
items.author: Chahine-tech
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
Arc keeps three things down its side: the favourites as squares, then folders of pinned pages, then the day's tabs. Bringing it over gives back the first, and loses the shape of the other two unless a switch happens to be on.

| In Arc | What the import makes of it |
|---|---|
| the favourites | square pins, as they should be |
| its folders, mine are Basics and SRE | tab groups, but only when Settings › Tabs › Tab groups is on, and the names are dropped when it isn't |
| its pinned pages | ordinary tabs, never the row pins that were made for them |

## The folders are dropped, not hidden

`takeAsleep` reads the setting once and gives up the folder when it is off:

```swift
guard grouping, let folder else { return nil }
```

So the name never reaches the session. Measured on a world of its own, with my own Arc profile:

```
import with Tab groups off      groups: none      tabs in a group: 0
turn Tab groups on afterwards   groups: none      tabs in a group: 0
import with Tab groups on       groups: Basics, SRE   tabs in a group: 11
```

Turning the switch on later brings nothing back, because there is nothing left to bring back. You have to bring Arc over again to get your folders, and there is no way to know that from the app: the sheet says how many pinned tabs came in, and they did come in, flat.

## The pinned pages

`fff4ce1` added pins kept as rows, and the comment on `Tab.listed` says what they are for:

> For a pin, kept as a row under the squares rather than as a square: Arc's pinned list, below its favourites.

The import doesn't use them: `takeArc` hands the pinned list to `takeAsleep`, which makes ordinary tabs. The one place row pins were built for is the one place that doesn't produce them, and getting there by hand means right-clicking each tab and choosing Pin as Row, thirteen times here.

It would also answer the part of #449 that isn't waiting for the new layout: a row pin is drawn as a square across the top, so the pages I keep would sit on a ground where a tab I have just opened does not.

## Worth saying plainly

Making Arc's pinned pages into pins changes what they are: put down by ⌘W, the same in every window, never in a group. That is what they are in Arc, which is why it reads right to me, but it is a change in kind and yours to call. The folders being dropped is not a judgement call, it is a loss.

Happy to send either half as a pull request.

items.title: Settings pages open at their top, and an extension's actions in a … menu
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited

items.body:
Two small Settings fixes for 1.0.5. Split out on review: which extension new tabs go to stays with #472, and a new tab page of your own will come as its own PR after 1.0.5.

### Each page opens at its top

All pages shared one `ScrollView`, and only its contents changed. So going from a scrolled General to Tabs opened Tabs scrolled just as far, and its first lines were out of sight. `.id(page)` gives each page its own scroll view.

### An extension's actions in a … menu

The row carried Pin, Show in New Tabs, Options, Reload and Remove as `Quick` pills. In a settings page's width (about 420pt of row), five of them don't fit, so SwiftUI wrapped each one mid-word ("Toolba / r"). They're in a … menu now, always visible and also on right-click, with Remove last and marked destructive. `Quick` is unchanged, since the row no longer uses it.

### Checked

items.title: Small windows in the ⌃Tab switcher
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Later
items.note: Adds small windows to switcher; native ordering/interaction acceptance still needed. Base for #495.
items.body:
Split in three in review. This PR is the middle piece: small windows in the ⌃Tab switcher, and ⌃Tab inside small windows. Only people who turned small windows on see any of it.

- #493: new small windows cascade instead of stacking exactly.
- #495: keys in the switcher (⌃W, ⌃R, ⌃M, ⌃O), behind a Settings › Tabs switch that's off by default. It builds on this PR.

With links from other apps opening in small windows, I often end up with several at once, usually HN threads. There was no way to cycle through them. ⌃Tab inside one went to the page and did nothing. Every small window also opened dead center, so five of them sat exactly on top of each other and looked like one.

### Moons in the browser window's switcher

- The small windows sit beside the tab grid in a smaller panel of their own, front-most first, up to 9. Columns stay even, so 4 show as 2×2. Each card has a thin strip across the top, like the small window's own bar, and a page-title caption. The title is what tells two threads on one site apart.
- **A moon's size goes by its page's length**, on a log scale: a one-screen page is 60% of the column, and a page 16 or more screens long fills it. The page already reports its scroll to fill the tab's reading meter; it now also reports its height in screens. `Tab` keeps that number unpublished, so scrolling doesn't cause any new redraws.
- ⌃Tab walks the grid, then the moons. A quick ⌃Tab still goes back to the last tab and never lands on a moon.
- Picking a moon brings its window forward and leaves the row alone. Open in Search (⌘O) is still the only way to move a small window's page into your tabs.

### ⌃Tab in a small window

- It shows the same planet and moons: the tabs of the browser window in front as the planet, the small windows as moons. The walk starts on the moon you're in, and a quick press goes back to the small window you were in before. Walking on reaches the tabs, and picking a tab goes to it in its window.
- Escape puts the switcher away. Before, the same key press would have closed the window too.
- `TabSwitcher` now tracks a `home` card, the one the gesture started on, and the walk puts the moons first when home is a moon. The small windows share one switcher; each window has the overlay, and only home's window shows it.
- The browser windows' key monitors leave a small window's events alone. So letting go of ⌃ and clicks in a small window get a monitor of their own; otherwise they'd go to whichever browser window was active.

### Refactor

`TabSwitcherOverlay` no longer takes a `Browser`. It looks cards up by id and picks through a closure, so the same view serves both switchers. Click handling moved into `TabSwitcher.click(at:pick:)`, and `Browser.clickTabSwitcher` now calls it.

### Checked

- `./build.sh` with Xcode beta: builds, with no new warnings.
- New `Tests/little_switcher.py`, 16 passed. It opens hidden small windows and checks the moon order, walking from the grid into the moons, ⌃→ plus letting go of ⌃ bringing a moon forward, the planet and moons from inside a small window, ⇧⌃Tab from a small window going to a tab, Escape leaving the window open, and a 20,000px page's moon coming out bigger than a one-screen page's.
- `Tests/tab_switcher.py`, 4 passed, after the refactor.
- Layout checked with the bench's `picture` of the window, which is how the 3+1 columns got caught and changed to 2×2.
- The hidden probe caught a real bug: `NSApp.orderedWindows` also lists windows that were never shown, oldest first. `LittleWindow.stacked` now ranks only windows on screen by their front-to-back order.
- Not checked on a real screen: the most-recently-used order from actually moving between windows, and pointing at or clicking cards inside a small window.

The bench's `press` takes `"window": "little"` and `"letgo": true`, and `little` reports its own switcher's state and each small window's page length, for the test. The test server in `split_view.py` gains a `/long` page.

items.title: A worker that is a link to a file of its own package gets the shim
items.author: AllDaGearNoIdea
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
Split out of #440.

StopTheMadness Pro's `service_worker` is `background-143.js`, a symlink to `background.js` in the same folder. `prepare` leaves a worker that is a link alone, so it never got the shim, and early messages bounced back to the extension instead of reaching its host.

Now a worker that is a link to a regular file of its own package is replaced by a copy of that file, which then gets the shim as usual. A link is only replaced when its target and the folder it sits in both resolve inside the package, so a worker under a linked folder that leads outside is left alone and nothing outside the package is deleted or written. That last check is the gap from review: `unlink` now checks where the link's parent folder resolves, as `inside` does.

The shim's version now includes a preparation number, raised whenever `prepare` changes what it does to a package, so every installed extension is prepared again once on the next launch and ones installed before pick this up.

Test:
- `swift test --filter ExtensionWorkerLinkTests`:
  - a worker linked to a file in its package becomes a regular file with the shim at its top and the file's contents after it, and the file it pointed to is unchanged
  - a worker under a folder that links outside the package, whose own link points back into the package, is left alone: the outside link, the package file and a file beside it are all unchanged. With the parent check taken out this test fails, and the outside file is deleted and rewritten.
- `Tests/run-extension-files-tests.sh` passes, `swift build` adds no warnings

items.title: Bringing Arc over twice adds a second pin for a site whose address has moved
items.author: Chahine-tech
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
Bringing Arc over a second time gave me seven pins where Arc has six, with Gmail twice.

## Why

`takeArc` keeps a favourite out when a pin already holds the same address, compared as strings:

```swift
for favourite in favourites where !defs.contains(where: { $0.home == favourite.url.absoluteString })
```

A pin's `home` doesn't always stay the address it came in with. `pinDefs` writes `(tab.home ?? tab.pending ?? tab.address)`, so a pin that has lost its home is written down at the address it is on. Gmail is the kind of site that moves: `https://mail.google.com` answers at `https://mail.google.com/mail/u/0/#inbox`. The two strings differ, the guard lets the favourite through, and Arc's Gmail arrives beside mine.

## Reproduced

A world of its own, a made-up Arc profile with its six favourites, on main at d8c33c8:

```
first import              pins: 6   [Y, G, T, M, R, T]
a pin's home moved to https://mail.google.com/mail/u/0/#inbox
second import             pins: 7   [Y, G, T, M, R, T, M]
                            M  https://mail.google.com/mail/u/0/#inbox
                            M  https://mail.google.com
```

The second import reports `pins: 1`, so it believes it brought something new.

## Worth noting

Two pins for one site is not only a duplicate in the row: they are two pins in every window and in every space that has them, each with its own identity, and unpinning one leaves the other.

History had the same shape of problem and was given a proper comparison in 1.0.5 (localhost:3000 against localhost:4000, and the case of a path). The pins' guard is still an equality of strings.

Happy to send it as a pull request, though the right comparison is yours to pick: the address as the history compares them, or the identity the import already keeps in `ImportRecords`.

items.title: A native host's connection ends when its output closes, not when it exits
items.author: AllDaGearNoIdea
items.decision: Adopt early
items.note: EOF-driven native-host lifetime, waiter-before-write, callbacks-before-start, bounded incoming frames and child cleanup. Preserve all fake-host regression tests.
items.body:
Split out of #440.

A host that writes its reply and exits at once (StopTheMadness Pro sends about 160 KB of settings this way) could have the reply cut off. `HostPipe` treated the host's exit as the end of the connection, and the exit could reach the main queue while the last chunk was still in the pipe, so the port disconnected with a reply unread. StopTheMadness then showed "Missing settings".

The connection now ends when the host's output closes, which is what Chrome watches. The exit on its own no longer ends it: a host that exits with a child of its own still holding its output open is given 1.5 s, then the connection ends anyway and its input is closed. A host whose output closes is stopped as Chrome does: its input is closed and it gets SIGTERM, then SIGKILL if it is still running after 2 s. `stop()` goes through the same path. The end runs exactly once whichever way it is reached, so waiters are failed and `onExit` fires once.

Two more things from the review. `sendNativeMessage` registers the reply's waiter before writing, so a host quick to answer isn't missed, and for `connectNative` the port's `onMessage`, `onExit` and `Live.keep` are set before the host starts, for the same reason. A message from a host is capped at 1 MB, as in Chrome: a length header past that drops the connection and stops the host, where before a 0xFFFFFFFF header had up to 4 GB buffered.

Test:
- `swift test --filter HostPipeTests`, fake hosts (small python scripts using Chrome's framing) run through `HostPipe`. The first round, against main:

| Case | main | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| A reply still unread when the host exits (busy reader, 30 KB) | fails 20/20: reply lost, waiter told "Native host has exited." | passes 20/20 |
| A 200 KB reply, then an immediate exit | passes | passes |
| A long-lived host answering several messages, open until `stop()` | passes | passes |
| `stop()` on a running host: ends it, `onExit` once, no process left | passes | passes |
| `stop()` after the host exited: `onExit` once, no hang | passes | passes |
| A host exiting without a reply: waiters fail, `onExit` once | passes | passes |
| A host closing its output but staying alive | passes | passes |

- Added since the review: a host exiting with a child holding its output open (ends after the grace, a write then fails), one closing its output and ignoring SIGTERM (killed), one closing its output and stopping, 30 rounds against a host that replies immediately (fails with the old write-then-wait order), a request after the end, a 0xFFFFFFFF length header (connection dropped, waiter failed, host stopped), and a reply of exactly 1 MB (delivered). 13 of 13 on three runs, and the full suite 60 of 60.
- The 200 KB case alone doesn't catch it: the pipe holds about 64 KB, so the host is still blocked writing until the reader has nearly drained it.
- `Tests/run-extension-files-tests.sh` passes, `swift build` adds no warnings.
- StopTheMadness Pro loaded unpacked in a test world, with #440 and #481: settings open without an error on 8 of 8 cold launches, no host process left behind.

iCloud Passwords needs your test round, as it can't be tested outside a build signed as you ship it. Its helper, `PasswordManagerBrowserExtensionHelper`, carries a launch constraint: the parent must hold `com.apple.developer.web-browser.public-key-credential` or be one of the browsers Apple lists, and anything else has the helper killed at exec (SIGKILL, Code Signature Invalid). 1.0.4 passes through the entitlement and its provisioning profile. My builds, ad-hoc or signed with my Apple Development certificate, don't have it, on main as much as on this branch, so the helper never runs and the code this touches is never reached.

On a build with your certificate and profile:
1. Open iCloud Passwords from the toolbar, enter the code if asked, fill a saved password.
2. Leave it for about 2 minutes, then use it again.
3. Quit Search, and check `pgrep -fl PasswordManagerBrowserExtensionHelper` shows no helper left from Search.

items.title: Feature Request: Split Tabs and Full Extension Support
items.author: Creator101-commits
items.decision: Historical issue: closed; not independently revalidated
items.note: Closed state alone does not establish resolution; inspect body/discussion if reopening.
items.body:
I would like to request two major features for Search: split tabs and full browser extension support.

1. Split Tabs / Split View

Allow multiple tabs or pages to be displayed at the same time within the same browser window.

Requested functionality:

Vertical split: Display two tabs side-by-side.

Horizontal split: Display two tabs on top of each other.

Each split pane should be able to display and navigate its own tab independently.

Allow users to resize the divider between the two panes.

Allow an existing tab to be moved into a split.

Allow tabs to be moved between either side of the split.

Closing the split should return the tabs to the normal tab bar without closing the pages.

Ideally allow links to be opened directly in a split pane.

Possible tab context-menu actions:

Split Right

Split Down

Move to Split

Open Link in Split

Close Split

This would make it much easier to compare websites, keep documentation beside another page, or work with multiple related pages without constantly switching tabs.

2. Full Browser Extension Support

Add much more complete extension support, similar to how extensions work in Chrome and other Chromium-based browsers.

Right now, extensions cannot be used as fully as they can in Chrome. In particular, extension interfaces that are supposed to open in a sidebar or right-side panel do not work properly.

Requested functionality:

Support Chrome/Chromium browser extensions as completely as possible.

Support installing and managing extensions.

Support extension toolbar buttons and extension menus.

Support extension popups.

Support extension background scripts/service workers.

Support content scripts.

Support extension permissions.

Support extension keyboard shortcuts.

Support extension options/settings pages.

Support extensions that modify or interact with webpages.

Support extension context-menu actions.

Support extension notifications where applicable.

Support extension pages and other extension-provided interfaces.

Most importantly, support the Chrome Side Panel API / extension sidebars, so extensions can open their interfaces on the right side of the browser just like they can in Chrome.

For example, if an extension normally has an action such as "Open in Side Panel" in Chrome, the same extension should be able to open its UI in a persistent right-hand sidebar in Search.

The goal would be for extensions to behave as close to their normal Chrome behavior as technically possible, rather than only supporting basic extensions or limited extension functionality.

Together, split tabs and complete extension support would make Search significantly more capable for productivity and power-user workflows.

items.title: Bringing things over offers the bookmarks bar
items.author: Chahine-tech
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body: Closes the third point of #449, as asked there. 24 bookmarks came in and nothing said where they went. **Show bookmarks** opens the bookmarks panel, so you see them once and never learn the bar exists, and somebody arriving from Chrome, Firefox or Arc has no reason to think a bookmarks bar is optional. A pill beside it turns the bar on, and puts the sheet away so the row is seen where it will live. It only shows when it is worth showing: when bookmarks have just come in, and while the bar is off. Nothing is turned on by itself, and the switch stays in Settings › Tabs as before. ## Checked By hand, in a world of its own with a real Arc profile: - bookmarks came in, bar off: the pill is there, and one press turns the bar on and closes the sheet - bar already on: the pill is gone, so it never offers what is already on - the third case, an import with Bookmarks unticked, follows from the code rather than from my eyes: `marksLanded` is only ever set inside the bookmarks branch, so an import without them cannot raise it `swift build` adds no warnings. ## One thing you should see before merging The row is full. At the sheet's 580 points, a fourth pill does not fit, and something has to fold. Before this, **Or from a file another browser exported…** sat on one line; with the pill in, it takes three. Before, the row on one line each: After, with the pill in: I kept the new pill on one line on purpose (`.fixedSize`), because without it SwiftUI folded the new pill instead while leaving spare room in the row. But that is a choice about which of your pills folds, which is yours rather than mine. Two ways out, if you want one: - that last label is long, and shortening it would give the row back its line. I left it alone: it is your wording, and it predates this change. - or the offer could leave the button row and sit on the result line where the bookmarks are already announced, beside `✓ 24 bookmarks`. That reads better to me, but it is no longer the pill beside Show bookmarks you asked for, so I did not take that on myself. Happy to do either in a second pass.

items.title: A click on the tab you're on renames it; its icon opens the address
items.author: oddharsh

items.body:
## Why
A click on the tab you're on put its address in the tab. Clicking a tab's name reads as "rename this," the way a click on a file's name does in the Finder, so the address edit surprised people.

## Change
- The strip, the column and a split pair's halves now call one entry point, `Browser.beginTabClick`, where each used to call `beginTabEdit` on its own. It renames the tab through the existing Rename path. A blank tab has nothing to name, so it still goes to the address.
- The site's mark in the tab keeps the old job: the address in the tab, with the site card under it (`AddressClick` in `TabBar.swift`). Its tap is gated with a `GestureMask` rather than an `if`, so the mark keeps its identity and doesn't fade in when the tab comes forward. `.gesture(_:isEnabled:)` would be tidier but needs macOS 15, and the package targets 14.
- ⌘L and Site Information… in the tab's menu are unchanged.
- CHANGELOG line under Unreleased.

## Open question
The mark only shows when Tabs show is set to Site icons. With Letters, the in-tab address and site card are reachable only from the tab's menu (⌘L opens the window's field, without the card). If that's too hidden, a second click on a tab being renamed could switch it to the address.

## Verification
- `./build.sh` passed with the Xcode beta toolchain, with no new warnings.
- Not clicked through in the app yet: the gesture precedence (mark over tab) is untested by hand.

items.title: build.sh records the SDK the app was built with
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Verify before adopting
items.note: SDK stamp workaround targets a specific Swift Build toolchain. Inspect Browse LC_BUILD_VERSION before changing linked-on-or-after behavior.
items.body:
A copy of Search built with Xcode 27 draws itself as a macOS 14 app on every Mac. On macOS 27 that means the old window buttons and controls instead of 27's.

AppKit decides how to draw an app from the SDK recorded in its binary (`LC_BUILD_VERSION`). Swift Build, SwiftPM's default engine in Xcode 27, writes the deployment target into both of that field's versions:

| Built with | `minos` | `sdk` |
|---|---|---|
| `swift build` (Swift Build, default) | 14.0 | **14.0** |
| `swift build --build-system native` | 14.0 | 27.0 |
| Installed 1.0.4 (older toolchain) | 14.0 | 26.2 |

The compile steps already pass `-target-sdk-version 27.0`; only the number written at link time is wrong. The native build system would dodge it, but SwiftPM marks that one deprecated.

## What changes

`build.sh` sets the build version with `vtool` right after copying the binary into the app, before stripping and signing: the same minimum (`$MINIMUM`, 14.0) and the SDK `xcrun --sdk macosx --show-sdk-version` reports. So:

- **The oldest macOS is unchanged.** 14.0 in the binary, the plist and the appcast.
- **The look follows the SDK the build used.** From Xcode 27, a Mac on 27 gets 27's buttons and controls. A Mac on an older macOS draws its own OS's, as before. An older Xcode stamps its own SDK, so nothing changes there.

This opts the whole app into the SDK's linked-on-or-after behaviour, which is what an Xcode-built app gets anyway. It's worth a look around the app on macOS 27.

## Tested

With Xcode-beta (SDK 27.0), `./build.sh release` gives a binary that reads `minos 14.0, sdk 27.0`, and `codesign --verify --strict` passes. On macOS 27, the window's buttons draw in 27's glossy style, where the same code built without this drew macOS 14's flat ones. Found while working on #477.

items.title: The bench's save waits for pins.json too
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
`pin_tiers.py` failed once today at a load average of about 250. After `sv.sp("save")` it reads `pins.json` at once, and the file still showed a pin as a row that the app had already made a square. Two reruns passed 32/32.

The bench's `save` writes the session file on the spot (`writeSession(now: true)`), but `Pins.save()` goes by the `Disk` queue in the background. Nothing waited for it, so on a busy machine the test could read the file before the newest write landed.

## What changes

The bench's `save` now calls `Disk.drain()` after writing the session, the same call `applicationWillTerminate` makes on the way out. It waits for the serial disk queue to empty, so `pins.json` (and anything else queued, like bookmarks) is on disk before the bench answers.

Normal browsing is untouched: pins still save in the background. The drain only runs when a test asks the bench to save. No CHANGELOG line, since nothing a user sees changes.

## Testing

- `DEVELOPER_DIR=/Applications/Xcode-beta.app/Contents/Developer ./build.sh debug` builds clean.
- `pin_tiers.py`: 32/32 on 5 runs in a row, at a load average of about 215.
- `split_view.py`: 82 to 91 of 92 over 4 runs, at load averages of 100 to 263. Main without this change failed the same checks in 2 runs at 221 to 348, so the failures come from load and were there before this change:
  - `swap: both pictures travel` and `even out: the pages move to even halves`: all 8 motion samples come back empty, because the animation isn't on screen while they run.
  - `case_slice5b ran to the end`: `split answer` arrives before the page's question has reached the app, and the rest of that case is skipped (hence 82 or 83 passed).

  None of these paths call the bench's `save`, so the new `Disk.drain()` doesn't run in them.

items.title: A small window whose page never came says so, with Try again
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
A small window for a link from another app now says so when its page fails to load, and offers Try again, as a tab does. Before, it stayed blank.

Split out of #474 as asked there, so it can go into 1.0.5 on its own.

## Why it stayed blank

A small window's tab uses the browser to look after its pages, but it isn't one of the browser's tabs. The browser's failed-load handler, `fail(_:_:)`, looks up the failed page's tab with `tab(for:)`, which only searches `tabs`. So for a small window it found nothing, and never set the `failure` that a tab's stage shows. Just drawing `Trouble` in `LittleView` wouldn't have been enough: there'd never have been a `failure` to show.

## What changed

- **`Browser.littleTab(for:)`** finds a small window's tab by its page. `fail(_:_:)` falls back to it, so the failure is recorded.
- **`didCommit`** uses it too. Otherwise a page that loads after a failure (going back with a mouse's back button, say) would stay covered by the message, because `didCommit` is where a tab's `failure` is cleared.
- **`LittleView`** draws `Trouble` over the page when `tab.failure` is set, as `Page` does. `Trouble` loses `private` in Stage.swift so it can.
- **The bench's `little` command** reports each small window's `failure`, so this can be checked without a window on screen.

## Testing

- `./build.sh` builds with no new warnings.
- In a hidden test world (`SEARCH_PROBE=test`), `./bench --test little http://127.0.0.1:9/` gives `"failures": ["The page didn't load."]`. Small windows on example.com and example.org give none.
- Not checked yet: the message on screen, Try again bringing the page back once it can load, and the message clearing when a page loads afterwards.

## Note

#474 also changes `LittleView`, in the same spot. Whichever merges second needs a small rebase.

items.title: Tests: wipe() takes the world's WebKit stores with it
items.author: oddharsh
items.decision: Already upstream-merged; main inherited
items.note: Upstream main is an ancestor of Browse. This does not guarantee every historical hunk survives later changes.
items.body:
The follow-up suggested on #476: `wipe()` now also removes a test world's WebKit stores, as `fresh.sh` does, so a world's cookies and site data don't outlive it.

## What it removes

`stores()` names every store a world's runs can make, computed the way the app names them rather than found by looking:

- **Websites:** `WebsiteDataStore/<probeStore(1)>`, from the world's name (FNV-1a, as in `Store.probeStore`). WebKit keeps this folder under a lowercase name, and `stores()` uses that name exactly.
- **Extensions:** `WebExtensions/<probeStore(2)>`, which `fresh.sh` doesn't remove.
- **Each space with its own sign-ins:** `WebsiteDataStore/<space id>`. The ids come from the world's own `spaces.json` (every space whose `sharesSignIns` isn't true, never the first), plus its `spaces.erasing` for spaces deleted during the run.

It removes these stores before the folder and settings, because the space ids are read from them. It never matches stores by their look: a real Search's own spaces keep their stores in the same `WebsiteDataStore/` folder, named by their ids.

## Checked

- **The names match what the app makes.** A scratch world opened pages, made a space with sign-ins of its own, and made and deleted another. It created three stores (its website store and one per space), `stores()` named all three, and after `wipe()` none were left.
- **Both formulas match stores already on disk.** `split-tests` hashes to an existing extension store, and ten worlds' names hash to existing website stores.
- **The suites leave nothing behind.** `fresh_window` 7/7, `close_group` 5/5, `pin_tiers` 32/32, `split_view` 90/92 (the two misses are the timing checks that fail under heavy load, at a load average of 195). A snapshot of `~/Library/WebKit/com.officecommun.search` before and after showed no new store left by these runs. The four stores removed were this checkout's own leftovers from earlier runs, and nothing else was touched.

Stores that earlier runs left behind stay where they are. Some belong to worlds that other checkouts are still using.
